World.title: Two funerals, two flashpoints: politics intrudes on mourning
World.content:
“No life is worth losing for power,” Chief Chisunka warns as funerals become flashpoints and party accuses police of standing by

Traditional leaders, a Catholic priest and an opposition party chairman have issued pointed warnings against rising political violence ahead of the 13 August general election.

Their intervention comes after two funerals in Eastern and Southern provinces this week descended into standoffs over party politics.

Chief Chisunka of the Ushi people of Luapula said no life is worth losing for the sake of power. He called on politicians to rein in their cadres before the country is set alight.

“We don’t have to lose lives just for certain people to cling to power. Peace needs to prevail because the country has been a beacon of hope,” the chief told The Mast.

He said it was unfortunate that parts of the nation were experiencing bloodshed in what he described as a Christian country. Politicians, he said, needed to sober up and tame their cadres before Zambia is drawn into wider conflict.

The Ushi traditional leader called on chiefs countrywide to rise to the occasion and denounce political violence wherever it occurs.

Catholic priest Father Gladson Phiri echoed the call. He said the church and traditional leaders are best placed to lead the fight against political violence because they deal directly with the citizens who go on to engage in political activity.

“The church and traditional leaders are the ones that should champion the fight against political violence because they usually deal with the masses who in turn engage in various political activities,” Fr Phiri said.

He said clergy and chiefs needed to engage both politicians and the electorate on the dangers of violence, warning that the country risked being set ablaze if the trend continues unchecked.

The warnings came in the same week that two funerals turned into flashpoints, illustrating how deeply campaign season has begun to intrude on ordinary community life.

In Aslot Township, Chipata District, mourners stormed out of Mgwelo Maplot Cemetery on Wednesday. The walkout came the moment a UPND official was called upon to address the gathering.

Both the ruling party and the opposition National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity had contributed toward funeral arrangements for the deceased. UPND gave K400; NRPUP reportedly covered other costs, including transport.

The solemn atmosphere shattered when director of ceremony Goldwin Soko announced that the UPND representative would give remarks. Without warning, a section of mourners rose and left the graveyard in a show of disapproval.

“When funerals are politicised and become battlegrounds, then we have a problem,” Alakwisa Jere, a Chipata-based mourner who witnessed the scene, told The Mast.

The Chipata walkout came barely a day after a similar episode in Mazabuka.

There, District Commissioner Oliver Mulomba was booed by angry residents on Tuesday and forced to abandon his speech. The crowd accused him of campaigning for President Hakainde Hichilema and the UPND at a funeral.

Mr Mulomba had to leave the scene to avoid possible harm.

Jere warned that the Chipata and Mazabuka incidents were a sign of what could unfold as campaigning intensifies in the final stretch before polling day. Leaders from both UPND and opposition parties have since appealed for calm, urging cadres and officials to keep politics out of funerals and other community gatherings.

Separately, Leadership Movement national chairperson David Kalumba accused the Zambia Police Service of failing to act against known perpetrators of political violence.

“Police officers have become spectators of violence,” he said in a statement.

He said his party had campaigned throughout the country encouraging people to reject violence and demand accountability, but that police had “betrayed people it is supposed to protect by failing to stop violence.”

Kalumba said no one should celebrate the destruction of public and private property currently taking place in parts of the country at the hands of political cadres. Zambians, he warned, must reject political violence at all costs, because the aftermath would be difficult to rebuild from.

He stressed that his own party was not a violent movement but a pro-poor organisation focused on building a Zambia with equal job and business opportunities for all.

“Our people have told us that all they want is peace, unity and development, and that is the message we are preaching,” he said.

The Leadership Movement chairman said his party had learnt a great deal on the 2026 campaign trail. Poverty, underdevelopment and lack of opportunity, he said, remain a disease afflicting many communities, particularly in rural areas he accused previous leadership of excluding from the national development agenda.

“Our people in rural areas need development but they cannot see it because previous leadership have excluded them from national development agenda,” Kalumba said.

He pledged that, if voted into office, his party would open access to rural development, working toward better roads, schools, markets, hospitals and clinics for rural communities.

Kalumba said the rural population should remain the main focus for the next five years, noting that the rural vote is larger than the urban vote on the current voter register.

Taken together, the warnings from traditional and religious leaders and the accusations levelled by the Leadership Movement chairman paint a picture of mounting anxiety over the tone of the campaign’s final fortnight. Community leaders are now openly worried that political competition could spill into the kind of bloodshed Zambia has largely avoided in recent electoral cycles.

World.title: Police investigating alleged stealing of 5 months’ baby in Chipata
World.content:
Police in Chipata have launched investigations into the alleged stealing of a 5-month-old baby boy by a 24-year-old woman in Kadiba Village, Chief Chinyaku.

Eastern Province Police Commanding Officer, Robertson Mweemba, confirmed the incident which was reported at Chipata Central Police Station on July 30, 2026 at 19:30hrs.

Mr Mweemba said the incident occurred between 09:00hrs and 15:00hrs on the same day.

“I wish to inform you on the above subject matter which was reported via phone call at Chipata Central Police Station. Occurred today 30th July, 2026 between 09:00hrs and 15:00hrs at Kadiba Village,” he said.

He explained that Mable Daka, aged 50, of Kadiba Village reported on behalf of her neighbor, Mercy Mwanza, aged 16, whose son, Emmanuel, was allegedly taken by Sera Daka, aged 24, of the same village.

According to Mr Mweemba, the suspect is known to the baby’s mother and often visits to play with the child.

“On the material day she went there, played with the baby and asked its mother if she could go and bath and cook for him. Around 09:00hrs, the suspect went with the baby whom she bathed and fed. Around 15:00hrs, the suspect left the village and was seen going to town,” he narrated.

The Commanding Officer said when the suspect did not return the baby, the family tried to call her but she did not pick up and her phone was later switched off, prompting the report to police.

“Investigations have since been launched. No arrest made. More updates to follow as investigations have been instituted. You may wish to take note,” Mr Mweemba said.

World.title: ERB reduces petroleum pump prices
World.content:
The Energy Regulation Board (ERB) has reduced the pump prices of petroleum products for the month of August 2026, citing lower international oil prices despite the depreciation of the Zambian Kwacha against the United States Dollar.

ERB Board Chairperson, James Banda, says the Board had therefore revised the national uniform pump prices downwards, with petrol reduced by K0.86 to K25.29 per liter from K26.15, representing a 3.29 percent decrease.

Mr Banda noted that Diesel has been reduced by K1.25 from K28.11 to K26.86 per litre, representing a 4.45 percent reduction, while kerosene has been reduced by K1.30 from K28.32 to K27.02 per litre, translating into a 4.59 percent decrease.

He noted that the price of Jet A-1 has also been revised downwards to K28.71 per litre respectively.

Mr Banda stated that the revised prices will take effect at midnight – July 31, 2026, and remain in force until the next monthly price review.

He stated that the reduction follows a review of international oil prices, which showed that the average price of petrol declined from US$105.82 per barrel to US$96.92 per barrel, while Kerosene/Jet A-1 dropped from US$158.97 per barrel to US$123.59 per barrel.

Mr Banda explained that the international price of diesel remained relatively stable, rising marginally from US$125.65 per barrel to US$126.58 per barrel.

He however, noted that during the review period, the Kwacha depreciated against major currencies, particularly the United States Dollar from K18.35 to K19.01 per US Dollar, a factor that was also taken into account in determining the new pump prices.

The ERB Board Chairman added that the detailed wholesale and pump price build-ups for August 2026 are available on the Board website.

World.title: Senga Hill residents urged to vote for UPND- Vice President
World.content:
Vice President, Mutale Nalumango, has called on the people of Senga Hill District to vote for the United Party for National Development (UPND) in the August 13 2026 General Elections.

Speaking when she addressed hundreds of people at Mambwe Primary School Ms Nalumango, assured that voting for UPND will ensure continued development in the area.

Mrs Nalumango said Senga Hill District has recorded significant development since the UPND assumed office.

She added that more progress can only be achieved if the people re-elect President Hakainde Hichilema and support UPND candidates.

The Vice President urged citizens to uphold peace before, during and after the elections, saying peace and stability are key to sustaining the country’s development agenda.

She appealed to the electorate to give the UPND another mandate to continue implementing programmes aimed at improving the lives of Zambians.

Mrs Nalumango reaffirmed the government’s commitment to free education, stating that the policy will remain in place to ensure every child has access to quality education.

She added that the government will continue investing in the education sector through the provision of school desks, the School Feeding Programme and the recruitment of more teachers.

Ms Nalumango said the government remains committed to employing more health workers, teachers and other qualified professionals in order to improve service delivery across the country.

The Vice President also encouraged farmers to sell their maize to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA), noting that the government has announced an attractive maize buying price that will enhance household incomes while strengthening national food security.

Ms Nalumango further thanked the people of Senga Hill District for their continued support and further urged them to utilize the increased Constituency Development Fund (CDF) which will accelerate community development projects in the district.

And speaking when she held a meeting with the clergy, Mrs Nalumango called on the church to continue praying for peace and unity in the country.

Speaking on behalf of the clergy, Pastor Wellington Silungwe, encouraged President Hakainde Hichilema and Vice President Mutale Nalumango to remain steadfast in their faith and trust in God regardless of the challenges they face.

Reading from Isaiah 41:10, Pastor Silungwe said God commands his people not to fear or be dismayed because he is always with them.

He said even in the midst of difficulties, trials, or dangerous situations, the President and his Vice should remain courageous, knowing that God will strengthen and protect them.

“Fear should not control lives, God’s presence is greater than any problem or danger that you may encounter,” he said.

Pastor Silungwe further called on the President to continue maintaining a close relationship with God through prayer, obedience, and faith adding that those who remain committed to God will continue to experience his guidance, peace, and strength in every season of life.

While in Senga Hill District the Vice President also held a meeting with Traditional leaders.

Mrs Nalumango has since concluded his 5 days visit of some selected districts in Northern Province with Senga Hill District being the last district to be visited.

World.title: Motorcycle rider attacked and robbed of his motorcycle
World.content:
A 21-year-old motorcycle rider is admitted to Petauke District Hospital after he was allegedly attacked and robbed of his motorcycle by unknown assailant in Petauke District.

Eastern Province Police Commanding Officer, Robertson Mweemba, confirmed the incident to the media saying it occurred on July 31, 2026, around 20:00 hours in Hillside Compound in Chief Kalindawalo’s area.

Mr Mweemba identified the victim as Killion Phiri, 21, of Tasala 10 Compound in Chief Kalindawalo’s area.

He said the matter was reported to Petauke Police Station at about 20:30 hours by the victim, who stated that he was attacked by an unknown man whom he could identify if seen again.

Mr Mweemba explained that the victim, a motorcycle taxi operator, had been hired by the suspect from Petauke Turn-off to Hillside Compound for a fare of K30.

“Upon reaching Hillside Compound, the suspect asked the rider to stop before allegedly striking him on the head several times with a suspected metal bar, “he said.

Mr. Mweemba said the suspect later fled with a black Gatoma motorcycle valued at K25,000. The engine and chassis numbers of the stolen motorcycle have not yet been established.

The Eastern Province Police Chief said the victim sustained multiple cuts to the head but managed to walk to Petauke Police Station, where he reported the matter.

Mr Mweemba said the victim was issued with a police medical report form and rushed to Petauke District Hospital, where he was admitted for treatment.

He added that investigations into the aggravated robbery have been instituted, while efforts to trace the suspect and recover the stolen motorcycle are underway.

World.title: 2026 Kazanga Traditional Ceremony not cancelled-NRE
World.content:
The Nkoya Royal Establishment, (NRE), has dismissed as false reports circulating on social media claiming that the 2026 Kazanga Traditional Ceremony has been cancelled.

NRE Prime Minister, Ntanda Ngwelela, traditionally known as Mwanashihemi said the public should ignore the rumors and treat them as unfounded.

Speaking in an interview to the media in Kaoma today, Mr Ngwelela reaffirmed the Royal Establishment’s commitment to hosting this year’s ceremony as planned.

He said any changes or important developments regarding the event would be communicated through official NRE channels.

“As things stand, the Kazanga Traditional Ceremony will take place as scheduled from 8th to 9th August 2026,” he stated.

The Prime Minister appealed to members of the public, especially those planning to travel to Kaoma, to come and participate in the celebrations.

He expressed concern over the source of the rumors, noting that preparations for the ceremony were progressing smoothly.

The Royal Establishment has since urged the public to rely only on official updates from NRE ahead of the two-day cultural gathering.

Kazanga is the major annual cultural festival of the Nkoya people of Kaoma District in Western Province. The ceremony was revived in 1988 after a period of inactivity.

The event is traditionally a first-fruits harvest ritual and a thanksgiving to God for a bumper harvest.

Historically, Kazanga was also a military occasion used to honour warriors and hunters who distinguished themselves by killing lions and leopards.

World.title: Africa: Africa's Energy Crossroads: What Namibia's Rise and South Africa's Debate Mean for the Continent
World.content:
guest column

Africa stands at one of the most consequential moments in its modern economic history.

From the offshore oil discoveries of Namibia to the natural gas reserves of Mozambique, from Angola's mature petroleum industry to Senegal and Mauritania's emergence as new energy producers, the continent is witnessing the birth of a new energy era. Uganda is advancing towards commercial oil production, Ghana continues to build on its offshore success, while countries such as Kenya, Tanzania and Somalia continue exploring their hydrocarbon potential.

Yet beneath these diverse national stories lies a single continental question: Can Africa convert its abundant natural resources into lasting prosperity?

The answer will depend less on what lies beneath the ground than on what exists above it—strong institutions, sound governance, policy certainty and visionary leadership.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In that context, the contrasting experiences of Namibia and South Africa offer valuable lessons not only for Southern Africa, but for every African nation seeking to attract investment while safeguarding its long-term national interests.

For decades, Namibia and South Africa have shared more than a border. They have shared history, infrastructure, trade and access to one of the world's most promising offshore geological formations—the Orange Basin.

Today, however, their energy trajectories are beginning to diverge.

Namibia is rapidly emerging as one of the world's newest oil-producing nations. Successive offshore discoveries have attracted billions of dollars in investment from international energy companies, transforming the country into one of Africa's most closely watched investment destinations.

Its success is about far more than oil.

It demonstrates that investors are drawn not only to geological potential, but also to countries that provide regulatory clarity, institutional stability, efficient decision-making and confidence that major projects can progress within predictable timeframes.

South Africa, by contrast, possesses considerable offshore hydrocarbon potential and one of Africa's most sophisticated industrial economies. Yet development has progressed more slowly as policymakers, regulators, industry and civil society continue debating the balance between environmental protection, legislative reform and investment certainty.

Neither approach should be caricatured.

Environmental stewardship remains essential. Africa cannot afford development that compromises its oceans, biodiversity or future generations. Equally, prolonged uncertainty can discourage investment, delay economic opportunities and shift capital towards jurisdictions where regulatory pathways are perceived to be more predictable.

This is not simply South Africa's challenge.

It is a policy dilemma confronting governments across Africa.

Whether in Nigeria as it reforms its petroleum sector, Mozambique as it develops its LNG industry, Senegal and Mauritania as they enter production, Uganda as it prepares to export oil, or emerging exploration markets elsewhere on the continent, governments are grappling with the same fundamental question: how can Africa attract investment while ensuring that its natural wealth delivers lasting benefits for its people?

The countries that answer that question successfully will shape Africa's economic future.

Global investment capital is increasingly selective.

Energy companies compare opportunities in Namibia not only with South Africa or Angola, but also with Guyana, Brazil, Suriname, Norway, Qatar and other energy-producing jurisdictions. Investment decisions are influenced by regulatory certainty, governance standards, fiscal stability, infrastructure, local skills and the confidence that projects can move efficiently from discovery to production.

Africa therefore competes not merely within itself—it competes with the world.

That reality should encourage greater continental cooperation rather than rivalry.

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) presents an opportunity to think beyond national borders. Imagine a Southern African energy and industrial corridor connecting Angola's petroleum expertise, Namibia's offshore discoveries, South Africa's financial and manufacturing capabilities, Mozambique's natural gas resources, Botswana's logistics strengths and the engineering talent found across the region.

Such integration could stimulate local manufacturing, strengthen African supply chains, develop world-class technical skills, increase regional value addition and create hundreds of thousands of high-quality jobs.

Instead of exporting raw resources and importing finished products, Africa could increasingly build, process, manufacture and innovate at home.

This is ultimately the continent's greatest opportunity.

Oil and gas should not be viewed as ends in themselves. They are catalysts that can finance economic diversification, renewable energy, scientific research, education, healthcare, infrastructure and industrial development.

History offers Africa both inspiration and warning.

Some resource-rich nations transformed natural wealth into broad-based prosperity through sound governance and long-term planning. Others became cautionary examples of missed opportunity, institutional weakness and overdependence on commodity exports.

The choice remains Africa's to make.

Namibia's emergence deserves celebration because it demonstrates what is possible when natural opportunity is matched by policy confidence and institutional credibility. South Africa's experience equally offers valuable lessons about the importance of balancing environmental responsibility with regulatory efficiency and investment certainty.

Neither country represents the entire African story.

Together, however, they illuminate choices confronting governments from Dakar to Dar es Salaam, from Kampala to Windhoek, from Accra to Maputo.

Ultimately, Africa's future will not be determined by the quantity of oil beneath its seabed or minerals beneath its soil.

Close 

It will be determined by the quality of its institutions, the consistency of its policies, the transparency of its governance and the courage of leaders willing to make decisions that balance today's opportunities with tomorrow's responsibilities.

The race for Africa's energy future has already begun.

Those nations that embrace cooperation over competition, certainty over indecision and long-term national vision over short-term political calculation will not simply attract investment—they will help define Africa's next chapter of economic transformation.

The question is no longer whether Africa possesses the resources to prosper.

The question is whether Africa will build the institutions capable of turning those resources into a lasting legacy for generations to come.

------------------

Daniel Makokera is a renowed media personality who has worked as journalist, television anchor, producer and conference presenter for over 20 years. Throughout his career as presenter and anchor, he has travelled widely across the continent and held exclusive interviews with some of Africa's most illustrious leaders. These include former UN Secretary General Kofi Annan, former South African presidents Nelson Mandela and Thabo Mbeki, former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, Zimbabwean Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai and presidents Robert Mugabe of Zimbabwe and Joseph Kabila of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. He currently is the CEO of Pamuzinda Productions based in South Africa.

World.title: Uganda: HIV Injection Is Not a Vaccine, Experts Warn
World.content:
Kampala — Experts have urged those who already received their first injection of the twice-yearly HIV preventing drug Lenacapavir to consider using combination prevention options, warning that the game changer injection is not a vaccine.

The initial recipients of the drug that has since had a lot of demand countrywide are set to receive their second dose in October and Dr Vincent Bagambe, the Policy Planning and Strategic Manager at the Uganda AIDS Commission says for those who access it, they should be keen on receiving their next dose on the prescribed dates if they are to maintain optimal drug levels in their blood.

Bagambe says that with the injection now part of the prevention tools in the country, they hope to cut the 37,000 new infections recorded yearly to less than 10,000 by 2030, which will all depend on how compliant people be to maintain the required drug levels in their blood to guarantee protection.

At the launch of the prevention option in April, Uganda had received 19,200 doses supplied across 103 health facilities across the country. The main clients targeted for the drug include people at highest risk of infection such as sex workers, couples in discordant relationships, fisherfolk and pregnant women engaging in risky behavior among others. But reports by the Ministry of Health show that the drug was accessed by those not listed as high risk as demand surpassed available supplies.



Asked about supplies for those who will soon need the second dose, Dr Herbert Kadama who coordinates Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) at the Ministry of Health said sixty - percent of the facilities that received the first batch have now received second batches.

Kadama explains that the facilities received the second batches earlier than scheduled because the doses were running out in two to three weeks and yet at the beginning, they had thought they would be supplying every two months.

Meanwhile, the country expects a top-up consignment of another 19,200 doses donation.

In an earlier interview with URN, Dr Peter Mudiope who heads HIV Prevention in the ministry this consignment was initially expected to arrive in the country in June only to be informed by the manufacturer Gilead Sciences that this couldn't happen due to shortages of a tablet that complements the injection, also called the loading dose.

Mudiope says that as calls for more doses continue and the valid need for people to comply on the prevention treatment, government cannot do much to avail the game changer drug for now. He says the current price of Lenacapivir is still too high to be afforded by the government. At 28,000 dollars per dose, the official says Uganda can for now only count on more donations expected from Global Fund and the American government to guarantee availability.

Close 

With supplies not yet guaranteed, Mudiope says the public should continue relying on other prevention options such as condoms, Pre and Post Exposure Prophylaxis tablets and being faithful as they are equally scientifically tested and confirmed to prevent HIV infection.

However, a study conducted by Makerere University School of Public Health in which they assessed access to HIV prevention services found use of key prevention options low.

According to results of this study which were released on Wednesday, researchers found only 24 percent of female sex workers and injection drug users, who are also a high at-risk group used PEP in the last three months. Seventy-six percent reported to have not used the prevention option despite knowledge of where to access it.

In terms prevalence, while national prevalence currently stands at 4.9 percent, among sex workers and injection drug users, HIV prevalence is high at 30 percent and 17 percent respectively.

Ideally, Kadama says such groups are the ones targeted as a top priority for Lenacapavir.

World.title: East Africa: U.S. Senators Urge Rubio to Address Impact of Ebola Outbreak on Women
World.content:
press release

WASHINGTON — Yesterday, U.S. Senators Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging the State Department to take swift action to protect women and infants from the deadly impact of the Ebola outbreak in eastern Africa. The Senators called on the Trump Administration to promptly use congressionally appropriated funds for voluntary family planning programming to distribute already purchased family planning commodities and back the UN Population Fund’s (UNFPA) health clinics operating in the region.

In the letter, the Senators emphasized the catastrophic toll of Ebola on pregnant women and warned that conflict and displacement in Ituri and North Kivu—in addition to increases in gender-based and sexual violence and transactional and survival sex—are exacerbating the outbreak.

“Ebola during pregnancy is catastrophic, with a nearly 100 percent fetal loss rate and catastrophic maternal mortality risk due to severe hemorrhaging. By providing women with the option to voluntarily prevent unplanned pregnancies and to protect themselves from transmission of the virus and have access to clinics, the United States can prevent further deaths of women and the cruel and certain death of any fetus exposed to the virus,” wrote the Senators.

“The inclusion of family planning in the U.S. response to the Ebola virus, including condoms and hormonal contraceptive methods, post-rape care and lifesaving anti-hemorrhage maternal health medicines is paramount. Congress, on a bipartisan basis, supports voluntary family planning programs because such programs support families and reduce maternal and infant death rates. In East Africa right now, access to family planning is essential to protecting women and babies and to reducing viral transmission,” continued the Senators.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

“The rapid spread of the virus, with more than 2,000 confirmed cases and 796 confirmed deaths as of this week in the DRC, leaves no time for delay in providing all possible interventions to save lives and prevent the transmission of the virus. The cost of United States response is approaching $1 billion. Investment now in voluntary family planning is fiscally rational in addition to being morally urgent,” concluded the Senators.

Full text of the letter is available HERE and provided below.

Dear Secretary Rubio,

We write to urge the State Department to take swift action to address the devastating impact of the Ebola outbreak in eastern Africa on women and infants by utilizing funding provided by Congress for voluntary family planning programming, to distribute already purchased family planning commodities and supporting the UN Population Fund’s (UNFPA) health clinics in the region.

Ebola during pregnancy is catastrophic, with a nearly 100 percent fetal loss rate and catastrophic material mortality risk due to severe hemorrhaging. By providing women with the option to voluntarily prevent unplanned pregnancies and to protect themselves from transmission of the virus and have access to clinics, the United States can prevent further deaths of women and the cruel and certain death of any fetus exposed to the virus.

During the Ebola outbreak in West Africa from 2014-2016, maternal mortality rose an estimated 75%. The staggering increase in maternal mortality was a result of the Ebola virus, as well as pregnant women forgoing antenatal and attended delivery care because of fear of contracting the virus at health clinics.

Currently, conflict and displacement are exacerbating the Ebola outbreak with spikes in gender-based and sexual violence in Ituri and North Kivu, as well as an increase in transactional and survival sex. Access to voluntary family planning counseling and supplies is critical to protect the lives of women and babies and to control the spread of the virus.

The inclusion of family planning in the U.S. response to the Ebola virus, including condoms and hormonal contraceptive methods, post-rape care and lifesaving anti-hemorrhage maternal health medicines is paramount. Congress, on a bipartisan basis, supports voluntary family planning programs because such programs support families and reduce maternal and infant death rates. In East Africa right now, access to family planning is essential to protecting women and babies and to reducing viral transmission. We urge you to utilize the $608 million in international family planning funding included in the Fiscal Year 2026 Appropriations bill and to distribute the remaining $1.7 million in already purchased family planning commodities in storage in Geel, Belgium which we understand will otherwise be destroyed.

Close 

We also ask that you issue a humanitarian exemption to support UNFPA's sexual and reproductive health programming in affected areas. UNFPA is already operational across 29 health zones in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and in Uganda; emergency contributions would be deployed immediately through an existing, proven delivery system with no ramp-up delay. Providing sexual and reproductive health support to women is not a parallel track alongside the Ebola response: it is the Ebola response for the 642,000 women of reproductive age - including an estimated 37,820 pregnant women - in the affected areas.

The rapid spread of the virus, with more than 2,000 confirmed cases and 796 confirmed deaths as of this week in the DRC, leaves no time for delay in providing all possible interventions to save lives and prevent the transmission of the virus. The cost of United States response is approaching $1 billion. Investment now in voluntary family planning is fiscally rational in addition to being morally urgent.

World.title: Africa: AHEFT Prize Launched to Recognise African Universities Leading Higher Education Transformation
World.content:
interview

Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — As Africa grapples with shrinking international development funding and rising pressure to create jobs for its rapidly growing youth population, the Mastercard Foundation is making one of the continent's biggest long-term investments in higher education, committing US$500 million over the next decade to transform African universities.

In an interview with AllAfrica's Melody Chironda, Dr. John Nkengasong, Executive Director for Higher Education, Collaboratives and Strategic Initiatives at the Mastercard Foundation, said the Foundation views universities as critical engines for developing the talent, innovation, and leadership needed to drive Africa's economic transformation. He argued that strategic investment in higher education has helped countries around the world build knowledge-based economies. He said African institutions have the potential to play the same role by preparing young people for dignified work while advancing research, entrepreneurship, and inclusive development.

Nkengasong, a Cameroonian-American virologist, was the inaugural Director of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and served as the U.S. Global AIDS Coordinator in the Biden administration and the World Health Organization Special Envoy for Africa during the COVID-19 pandemic,

$500 million over a decade is a significant bet on higher education specifically, at a moment when many donors are pulling back from Africa. Why did the Foundation choose universities as the lever, rather than, say, direct scholarships or workforce programs?



Human capital investment, through higher education, is at the centre of every story of national economic transformation around the world. Through strategic investments in higher education for human capital development, many countries around the world have successfully transformed from resource-scarce nations into advanced, knowledge-based economies with sustained GDP growth. With strategic investments in higher education, Africa can generate the necessary talent that can propel the continent towards economic growth and sustained livelihoods for its young people.

The Mastercard Foundation is committed to a world where every young person has the opportunity to learn and prosper. Our Young Africa Works strategy aims to enable 30 million young people to access dignified and fulfilling work by 2030. Through the Africa Higher Education for Transformation (AHEFT) Prize, the Foundation is strengthening Africa's higher education system as a catalyst for talent development, expanded opportunities for young people, and inclusive socio-economic growth. Building on two decades of experience supporting African institutions to reimagine higher education, the AHEFT Prize converts proven success into sustained momentum through a decade-long commitment to advancing homegrown excellence and driving system-wide transformation across the continent.

The Prize talks about 'systemic, institution-wide transformation' rather than individual achievement. How do you actually measure that a university has transformed, as opposed to simply having a strong department or a few good graduates?

The AHEFT Prize is not intended to rank institutions, departments, or graduates. Instead, it aims to establish a benchmark for transformational impact in African higher education. All applications were assessed against a common set of criteria, including transformational impact, alignment with Africa's development priorities, community engagement, inclusion and access, student experience, and collaboration. Through their applications, African institutions are defining what transformation looks like by sharing their own stories of innovation, impact, and measurable change.

The Prize focused on institution-wide transformation rather than isolated excellence. It assessed whether change is embedded across the university's core functions, including teaching and learning, research, entrepreneurship, and transitions to employment and whether that change delivers measurable outcomes for students, communities, and society.

The inaugural winners exemplified this wide-ranging transformation in different ways. From creating effective pathways from learning to earning, to advancing applied research and innovation, strengthening health systems, influencing national development priorities, and expanding regional and continental impact. Together, they demonstrate that transformational universities do more than excel in a single department; they become engines of opportunity, innovation, and socio-economic progress.

What insights did this inaugural cycle provide, and how will those lessons inform the Prize as it expands to universities across the continent?

The inaugural cycle reinforced the critical role of African higher education institutions as drivers of human capital development and socio-economic progress, showcasing diverse models of transformational impact across the continent. It also validated the importance of assessing universities holistically and in context, examining how leadership, systems, partnerships, teaching, research, and student outcomes work together to create lasting change. These insights will help strengthen future cycles of the Prize as we identify, recognize, and elevate a broader range of institutions delivering institution-wide transformation and measurable impact for young people and society.

Every winning institution has a genuinely different story, from refugee employment in Uganda to health workforce training in Rwanda. Is there a common thread the jury was really looking for, or is 'transformation' being defined differently in each context?

Every application was assessed against the same standardized criteria: transformational impact, relevance to Africa's development priorities, community engagement and service, inclusion and access, student experience, and collaboration and partnerships. We see this diversity as a strength.

The winning institutions demonstrated the breadth of transformational impact being driven by African higher education institutions. Across diverse contexts, they are strengthening pathways from education to employment and entrepreneurship, advancing applied research and innovation to address societal challenges, transforming health systems through workforce development and clinical excellence, and embedding industry-relevant, experiential learning. Beyond their campuses, these institutions are influencing policy, contributing to national and regional development, fostering strategic partnerships, and building resilient, sustainable models that position higher education as a catalyst for human capital development, innovation, and inclusive socio-economic growth across Africa.

How does the Foundation think about supporting these institutions to keep the momentum going after the initial $3 million grant?

Beyond the financial award, the AHEFT Prize will provide programmatic support to help winning institutions scale their transformation initiatives. We will also bring winners together to share learning, foster collaboration, and amplify their work to create ripple effects across institutions and ecosystems. The inaugural Higher Education for Transformation Convening, scheduled for September 22 in Accra, marks the beginning of this journey.

Leveraging the Foundation's network of more than 200 African higher education institutions, the goal is to create a platform through which institutions can access the support, partnerships, and connections needed to sustain and scale their transformative work.

You've committed to at least 150 institutions over ten years, but Africa has thousands of higher education institutions. How do you think about the trade-off between depth of impact at a few flagship universities versus breadth across the continent's weaker systems?

The Prize is designed to achieve both depth and scale. First, it strengthens high-performing institutions so their impact in teaching and learning, research, entrepreneurship, and transitions to employment can reach more young people. Second, it seeks to catalyze broader system-wide change by demonstrating what transformative higher education can look like and encouraging governments, funders, and institutions to invest in and adopt similar approaches. This is an ambitious goal that the Foundation cannot achieve alone. We recognize that we are one of many stakeholders working toward the same objective.

Beyond the Prize itself, the Foundation advances systemic transformation through Higher Education Collaboratives- multi-stakeholder partnerships across sectors with significant potential for job creation and social impact, including health, agriculture, climate resilience, digital transformation, and education. For example, the Africa Higher Education Health Collaborative brings together universities across the continent to strengthen health workforce development and health entrepreneurship, extending impact far beyond individual institutions.

Close 

Africa's graduate unemployment and brain drain numbers remain stark. Where does this Prize actually move the needle on young people finding dignified work at home, versus simply making strong universities stronger?

Supporting universities and improving employment outcomes for young people are linked and aligned to our Young Africa Works strategy, which aims to enable 30 million young people to access dignified and fulfilling work by 2030. Through the AHEFT Prize, the Foundation is strengthening Africa's higher education system as critical human capital and talent infrastructure, enabling institutions to deliver quality, inclusive, and industry-relevant education that prepares young people for dignified and meaningful work. This is why transitions to employment is one of the Prize's four core thematic areas, alongside teaching and learning, research, and entrepreneurship.

The AHEFT Prize launches as some traditional donors are stepping back from the continent. Do you see the AHEFT Prize as the Foundation stepping into a gap left by others, and does that change how much responsibility philanthropic capital should carry for Africa's education systems?

For more than 20 years, the Mastercard Foundation has partnered with African institutions and witnessed their ability to redefine what higher education can deliver. Rather than responding to changes in the funding landscape, the AHEFT Prize builds on this experience, transforming proven success into momentum through a long-term commitment to recognize, elevate, and scale African-led excellence. By strengthening universities and the broader higher education ecosystem, the Prize aims to advance talent development, innovation, and leadership, enabling institutions across the continent to become powerful engines of opportunity and socio-economic transformation for millions of young people.

World.title: Nigeria: FG to End Electricity Subsidy From 2027
World.content:
The Federal Government has announced plans to phase out electricity subsidy payments from 2027 as part of efforts to address mounting debts in the power sector.

Minister of Power Joseph Tegbe disclosed the plan during a media interactive session on Friday, saying the subsidy would be removed gradually and consumers would not lose access to electricity services.

"We have the mandate of Mr President to clear the legacy debt and come up with sustainable structures to make sure this doesn't pile up any more," Tegbe said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"I promise you, next year, by God's grace, we will put a stop to this so-called subsidy in the power sector. Mr President, we will not deprive Nigeria of anything. We'll make sure Nigerian consumers continue to have power and improve power services."

The minister also said there is no immediate plan to increase electricity tariffs.

The announcement aligns with recommendations by the International Monetary Fund for Nigeria to gradually remove electricity subsidies.

The government has previously put the subsidy burden at about N3 trillion as of February 2024, while the Association of Power Generation Companies says GenCos are owed roughly N6.5 trillion.

Tegbe's comments come amid ongoing efforts to clear legacy debts in the sector. President Bola Tinubu recently approved a N4 trillion bond programme for debt settlement.

In January, the government issued a N501 billion inaugural bond under the Presidential Power Sector Debt Reduction Programme. On July 20, it announced a second tranche worth about N729 billion to settle verified debts owed to power generation companies.

Earlier this year, Tinubu also directed ministries, departments and agencies to use existing electricity laws to determine how subsidy costs should be shared among the federal, state and local governments in the 2026 budget.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigerian Police Deploy New CP to Oversee Osun Governorship Poll
World.content:
The deployment comes after months of controversies sourrounding the conduct of the Osun State Police command led by former CP Ibrahim Gotan and calls for his redeployment by the state government.

The Nigeria Police Force has deployed a new Commissioner of Police (CP), Samuel Erale, to oversee the forthcoming 15 August governorship election in Osun State.

This comes after months of persistent calls from the state government for the removal of CP Ibrahim Gotan amid controversies his alleged partisanship and poor handling of election-related security.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Police Public Relations Officer in Osun, Abiodun Ojelabi, a deputy suprintendent of police, confirmed Mr Erale's deployment to replace Mr Gotan on Friday.

However, it appears Mr Erale will only be in charge of the police in the state for the time being, pending the conclusion of the forthcoming election.

"What we have is that election CP is being deployed to Osun State. Although he is yet to report or assume office," Mr Ojelabi told PREMIUM TIMES via a phone call.

Although the police have yet to officially announce the reason for the redeployment, the development follows sustained criticism of Mr Gotan's leadership, particularly over the command's handling of politically sensitive incidents and election-related violence in the state.

Sahara Reporter reported that Mr Gotan has been redeployed to serve under the Commissioner of Police in charge of Communications Operations at the Force Headquarters, Abuja, on a special duty assignment.

The redeployment comes barely 24 hours after the police released the Osun State Secretary to the State Government (SSG), Teslim Igbalaye, who was arrested alongside five others during a controversial raid on his residence on Wednesday over allegations of vote-buying and harbouring a wanted suspect.

The operation generated widespread political reactions, with the Osun State Government and the ruling Accord Party accusing the police of targeting senior government officials for political reasons.

Pressure before replacement

Pressure on the former commissioner, Mr Gotan had intensified in recent months as political actors and civil society organisations questioned the neutrality of the state police command ahead of the governorship election.

PREMIUM TIMES reported in June that a coalition of civil society organisations staged a protest in Osogbo, demanding Mr Gotan's redeployment over alleged bias in the handling of election-related violence and politically sensitive security matters.

The ruling Accord Party on Thursday also petitioned President Bola Tinubu and Inspector-General of Police, accusing the commissioner of partiality in responding to attacks on its members. The party alleged that Mr Gotan targeted officials of Governor Ademola Adeleke's administration.

The criticism escalated after police officers raided the residence of the SSG, claiming to have recovered N4.8 million cash, two permanent voter cards, voter registers, and other items during an investigation into alleged electoral offences.

While the police defended the operation as a lawful investigation, the state government described it as politically motivated, alleging that security agencies were being used to intimidate government officials ahead of the election.

Redeployment of CP not the first ahead of Osun election

Mr Gotan's replacement continues a familiar pattern in Osun State, where a police commissioner has come under intense political pressure during governorship election, and later replaced with a new commissioner.

Ahead of the 2022 governorship election in the state, civil groups and supporters of the then Minister of Interior, Rauf Aregbesola, demanded the removal of then Police Commissioner Olawale Olokode after attacks on campaign offices and allegations that the command was not acting impartially.

Close 

The then Inspector-General of Police, Usman Alkali, subsequently redeployed Mr Olokode before the election to the Force headquarters in Abuja, and replaced him with Julius Okoro as commissioner that supervised the Osun election.

Political observers say the recurring redeployment of police commissioners during election seasons reflects persistent concerns about the neutrality of security agencies in one of Nigeria's most politically competitive states.

The new commissioner assumes duty at a time when Osun has witnessed a rise in politically linked violence, arrests and accusations among rival political parties ahead of the August 15 governorship election.

The election is expected to be keenly contested by incumbent Governor Ademola Adeleke of the Accord Party and Bola Oyebamiji of the All Progressives Congress (APC), alongside candidates of 12 other political parties.

World.title: Somalia: Somalia's President Arrives in Uganda Ahead of Aussom Summit, Holds Talks With Museveni
World.content:
Kampala — Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud arrived in Uganda's capital Kampala on Friday, where he held bilateral talks with Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni ahead of a summit expected to shape the future of the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM).

The two leaders discussed strengthening long-standing ties between Somalia and Uganda, with talks focusing on security cooperation, counterterrorism efforts, state-building and regional collaboration to promote lasting peace and stability in the Horn of Africa.

They also exchanged views on the upcoming summit of leaders from countries contributing troops to AUSSOM, which is expected to address the future of the African Union-led mission, continued international support for Somalia's security sector and the gradual transfer of security responsibilities to Somali forces.

The meeting comes at a critical time for Somalia, which is facing mounting security, political and economic challenges.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Somali government continues military operations against the Islamist militant group Al-Shabaab while seeking international backing to sustain security gains as uncertainty grows over the future funding and mandate of AUSSOM.

Political tensions have also persisted over electoral reforms and constitutional amendments, with disagreements between the federal government and opposition figures complicating efforts to build political consensus.

At the same time, Somalia faces increasing financial pressures, including the need for sustained international funding to support its security forces, government institutions and development programmes. Financing for AUSSOM has become a key concern after the United States announced it would end its support for the mission when current arrangements expire at the end of 2026.

Uganda remains the largest troop contributor to AUSSOM and has played a central role in African Union peace operations in Somalia for nearly two decades. As host of the Kampala summit, Uganda is expected to play a leading role in discussions on the mission's future, including its mandate, funding mechanisms and support for Somalia's transition toward assuming full responsibility for national security.

The summit follows a meeting of defence ministers from AUSSOM troop-contributing countries, who called for the United Nations Security Council to extend the mission's mandate by 18 to 24 months to prevent a security vacuum while Somali forces continue to build their operational capabilities.

World.title: Nicole 'Snooki' Polizzi undergoes major surgery six months after her cervical cancer diagnosis
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Nicole "Snooki" Polizzi is giving fans an update on her health, six months after sharing her cancer diagnosis.

In an emotional Instagram video shared on Saturday, the 38-year-old reality star revealed she underwent a hysterectomy six months after she was diagnosed with cervical cancer.

The video started off with clips of Polizzi arriving at the hospital and getting ready for surgery as she narrated what was going on via voice-over, before transitioning to her speaking directly to the camera following the procedure.

"I told you guys in general I’m not good with pain, and I’ve really been trying to be tough, but it’s not great," Polizzi said. "And the reason is because we did that C-section cut, and he obviously ended up taking out the uterus, my cervix and then some parts of my vagina just to make sure we get everything. So that was crazy. The fallopian tubes, all of it. We kept my ovaries so I don’t go into pre-menopause, which is nice."

VANESSA TRUMP REVEALS BREAST CANCER DIAGNOSIS IN EMOTIONAL STATEMENT: 'I AM STAYING FOCUSED AND HOPEFUL'

The "Jersey Shore" star then cut the camera as she got emotional, telling viewers, "Sorry, it’s just been a lot," but that she is "trying to stay in good spirits."

She later shared her frame of mind prior to the surgery, explaining that the process involved hooking her up to machines, "put[ting] iodine in my nose. I had to scrub my body with this wipe, which left her feeling "nervous and anxious."

"I was starting to get nervous and anxious, getting checked in and stuff, and then they wheel me in where they’re doing the procedure," she said. "And I’m like, ‘Stay positive, it’s gonna be fine, don’t freak yourself out.’ My heart’s starting to race, I’m getting anxiety, and I’m getting the shakes. And then right when I go in, it’s just like, ‘Oh my god, like it hit me, like holy s---. I’m going under surgery. I’m losing my uterus and my cervix, fallopian tubes, half my vagina, like holy s---.’"

As she continued, she got emotional, recalling how she "start[ed] hysterically bawling" as she was "so scared," feeling like, "I don’t know what’s gonna happen."

CLICK HERE TO 

"I don’t wanna feel pain," she said. "It’s very scary. But I got on the table and the nurses are great. They’re saying I’m gonna do fine. The doctors are great, so I lay down, and I’m like, ‘F---, it’s happening,’ and then they give me something in my IV to calm me down. And I’m like, What the f--- couldn’t you give me this 20 minutes ago so I could calm down?

Polizzi also shared a lighter moment in which she felt determined to "set the record" for how long she could hold out before passing out from the anesthesia after doctors told her most people only make it to three seconds, proudly telling her followers she counted to 10.

In addition to getting a hysterectomy, Polizzi shared that the doctors also treated her for diastasis recti, with the reality star saying, "Obviously, I’ve had three kids, so when you have kids, sometimes your abs, they disconnect."

When it comes to why she chose to share her health journey with her followers, she explained, "It’s a scary thing and a lot of us women deal with it, and no one really talks about it. So I’m here to give that platform for all of us ladies."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"And I read a lot of your comments that some of you are going to get surgery next week, you’re doing the same thing, so I’m here to show you what’s up and it’s scary, and it’s okay to be scared," she continued. "But now it’s over. It’s over. I just have to deal with the pain. It’s just like any surgery. You have pain, you gotta manage it, manage it, get the pain meds, and in a couple of days, you’ll feel brand spanking new, no more periods. I don’t have to take birth control anymore. Hopefully I’ll be cancer free, and that’s it."

She ended her post by thanking her followers and encouraging them to "get your Pap smears, okay?"

Polizzi first shared that she was diagnosed with Stage 1 cervical cancer in February, saying at the time that "I’m gonna probably get the hysterectomy."

World.title: Lynx coach defends trans athletes ahead of big game vs Fever with Sophie Cunningham rally scheduled outside
World.content:
Minnesota Lynx head coach Cheryl Reeve defended the right of "Save Women’s Sports" demonstrators to gather outside Sunday’s game against the Indiana Fever, even as she rejected their argument.

Reeve said that the scenario of "biological men" in girls' locker rooms is "not the case."

"It is not the case that we have 'biological men' in girls' locker rooms. The way it's being phrased, the innuendo there that transgender women are predators of some kind in the locker room. There's a lot of narrative that is problematic that we need to address," she said.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM RALLY ROCKS WNBA GAME AS 'SAVE WOMEN'S SPORTS' ACTIVISTS FACE COUNTERPROTEST

Fever star Sophie Cunningham recently said that she took a stand on the issue because, "I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

Reeve's remarks came before a rally dubbed "Sophie Night," which XX-XY Athletics founder Jennifer Sey plans to hold outside Target Center in support of Cunningham, ahead of the Lynx game against the Fever.

Reeve suggested she is not concerned about any safety issues as a result of the rally.

"I don’t think we should feel like our safe space is being threatened," Reeve told reporters on Saturday. "I don’t think these demonstrators are not being peaceful, not that I’ve seen. I haven’t seen all of it. I haven’t heard everything that’s happening. But everyone has a right to peacefully assemble, whether you agree with them or not."

Similar demonstrations followed the Fever to Seattle on Tuesday and Portland on Friday this past week. The Seattle game erupted into controversy when two teenage Cunningham supporters alleged that Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton cursed at them courtside. The WNBA fined Keaton and barred her from Seattle’s next five home games.

Reeve said the league must protect players and fans who feel threatened or discriminated against while preserving the WNBA’s culture of inclusion.

"The commissioner and the league have a responsibility to ensure that any topic that could be problematic for players, or they perceive to be unsafe or threatened in any way or discriminated against, I think that’s something that’s fair for our leadership," Reeve said. "And I’m quite sure that they have eyes on and ears on to make sure that it’s a safe space for everyone. And that’s what makes our league beautiful."

STORM CO-OWNER SUSPENDED AFTER INCIDENT WITH SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM FANS AS STAR BREAKS SILENCE ON CONTROVERSY

But Reeve also argued that transgender participation has been presented as a larger threat to women’s sports than it is.

"In terms of, you know, my views, since I said last week, I come from a space of inclusion. And the narrative that I think that is problematic is to suggest that, um, number one, that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports. And I, I think this is what's bothersome is that there's a faction of people in our country that are making this, uh, a massive issue," she said.

However, she acknowledged that questions become more complicated after puberty and at elite levels where championships and scholarships are at stake.

"Every kid has the right to access," Reeve said. "Now, what gets nuanced is when you’re beyond puberty, when you’re an Olympic sport, when you’re looking at scholarships and that sort of thing. That’s where I say that common-sense people get together and you find common ground to find a way to be inclusive. The answer isn’t no."

Reeve said she previously encouraged league officials to establish a policy before such a situation arises.

"I encouraged the WNBA leadership years ago: What’s our stance? What are we going to do when this occurs? Are we going to be ready? Are we going to be reactionary?" Reeve said. "It would make sense for our league to be leaders in this space."

The debate has reached the WNBA after other major sports institutions moved toward sex-based eligibility. The NCAA limits women’s competition to biological females, while the International Olympic Committee will impose biological eligibility rules and genetic screening for women’s events beginning with the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

The Supreme Court also upheld state laws protecting female school sports in June. The justices ruled 6-3 on the constitutional questions, while all nine agreed Title IX does not require states to make exceptions allowing transgender athletes into female competition.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Reeve nevertheless maintained that transgender participation is not the greatest obstacle facing female athletes, pointing instead to disparities in facilities, uniforms, locker rooms and institutional investment.

"This is an issue that I think we can thoughtfully work through," Reeve said. "You can voice your opinion, have a strong opinion, but it’s a safe space for everyone regardless of whether or not we agree."

Reeve revealed her stance on the issue on July 17, days before Cunningham revealed hers. Reeve was asked that day about the recent Supreme Court ruling that protects state laws that ban males from women's sports.

"The attacks on trans people, the attacks that they’ve gone through… it seems like it’s got way more aggressive, it’s sort of sickening when the issues they are trying to tackle are really not issues, the number of transgender athletes they are now making laws for and creating a problem, to get elected," Reeve said.

"What I’m hopeful for is that people have gotten themselves more educated and they understand that, that’s not actually a problem… exclusion is never the answer, separate isn’t equal, and trans lives matter, so to take away something that’s so valuable that sports brings to young people in particular and what it does, as I have a youngster, encourages you to be part of a team and what it gives you in terms of teamwork, leadership, competitiveness, all the things, they have every right to that as well"

Now, Reeve will lead a marquee matchup showdown against Cunningham, Clark and the Fever with what is expected to be the biggest Cunningham rally to date raging outside on Sunday.

World.title: State Department raises travel warning for part of Spain as migrant surge sparks military deployment
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The State Department on Saturday raised its Travel Advisory for Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta to Level 3: Reconsider Travel after tens of thousands of migrants surged into the Spanish territory from neighboring Morocco, prompting a major security response.

The updated advisory warns that the "massive and uncontrolled arrival of migrants from Morocco to Ceuta may lead to unpredictable and dangerous security situations."

"Spain has deployed the Spanish military, Spanish National Police, and Guardia Civil as a result of this serious situation," the advisory states. "Americans should reconsider travel to the area given the risks posed to their safety and security."

SPAIN DEPLOYS MILITARY AFTER THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS OVERWHELM BORDER ENCLAVE, AT LEAST 18 DEAD

The advisory applies only to Ceuta, an autonomous Spanish city on the northern coast of Africa that borders Morocco. The rest of Spain remains under its existing travel advisory level.

Spanish officials have scrambled to respond after tens of thousands of migrants crossed into Ceuta this week. Ceuta President Juan Jesús Vivas said Friday that about 60,000 migrants entered the enclave over a 24-hour period, while Spain's Interior Ministry later estimated roughly 50,000 arrivals since Thursday. Authorities said thousands have since returned to Morocco.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said Spain would boost the presence of security forces in Ceuta, deploy a physical sea barrier to help facilitate repatriations and continue working with Moroccan authorities to combat human trafficking networks.

TRUMP BLASTS SPAIN MIGRANT SURGE AS 'CATASTROPHE,' WARNS US COULD FACE WORSE IF DEMOCRATS REGAIN POWER

Authorities have linked the migrant surge to a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling involving migrants arriving by sea. Sánchez said human trafficking organizations misrepresented the decision, triggering the influx.

The crisis also drew comments from President Donald Trump during a Cabinet meeting Friday at Camp David.

"You know, I saw Spain yesterday, and I watched the catastrophe that took place. It looks like an invasion of a country by hundreds of thousands of people. And that same thing is going to happen to us if the Republicans don't get elected," Trump said.

World.title: Sophie Cunningham shares touching moment with young Fever fan after game against Portland
World.content:
There was a lot of intensity in the building when the Indiana Fever paid a visit to the Portland Fire on Friday night.

Most of that intensity came from leftist fans who were upset that Fever star Sophie Cunningham voiced her support for keeping biological men out of women's sports. A stance you'd think is universal among female athletes and fans of women's athletics in general... but here we are.

However, Cunningham didn't let that get to her; in fact, she did the exact opposite, and it was summed up nicely in a heartwarming moment with a young fan after the game.

FEVER SHUT DOWN SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM QUESTIONS, ABRUPTLY END PRESS CONFERENCE

Cunningham was welcomed onto the court in Portland with boos and fans waving transgender flags, and she quickly shut them up by burying a three-pointer and sending a quick message of her own.

Cunningham finished the night with 13 points and 3 assists, and the Fever went on to win 112-98 thanks in large part to a triple-double from Caitlin Clark.

But after the game, Cunningham showed that she practices what she preaches.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

In the ESPN profile that sparked the events of the past week, Cunningham talked about wanting to "protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

So, after what had to be one of the more intense games of her WNBA career, Cunningham had an incredible moment with a young fan in which she gave her one of her game-used shoes.

Hang on to that shoe, young lady; those things are tough to find these days.

What a moment, and one that the young girl will never forget. You can also see that Cunningham's willingness to support women and girls is being felt, and in this case very much appreciated.

As Riley Gaines recently pointed out, the WNBA is at a crossroads where it must decide whether its priority is growing the next generation of girls who will one day join its ranks or political activism.

I think this is a pretty good example of why the former is the right choice.

Yeah... okay.

World.title: How often are married people having sex? What to know about the intimacy standard in America
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

New survey data offers a snapshot of how often married Americans are having sex, while researchers say the findings challenge common assumptions about relationship health.

National demographic studies suggest that lower sexual frequency is often a normal part of aging and long-term relationships, and that there may be a "sweet spot" associated with marital satisfaction.

Data from the General Social Survey, conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago, found that married Americans report a wide range of sexual frequency.

WEIGHT-LOSS MEDICATIONS COULD IMPACT SEXUAL HEALTH IN UNEXPECTED WAYS

The survey asked how often couples have had sex during the last 12 months. Among the 1,893 married respondents surveyed in 2024, the responses were as follows.

32.5% said not at all

11.3% said once or twice during the year

11.7% said about once a month

15.3% said two or three times a month

12.9% said about once a week

12.2% said two or three times a week

4.1% said more than three times a week

The average American adult has sex 53 times a year — or a little more than once per week, according to research by the telehealth platform Hims.

While marriage is often associated with less frequent sex, research has found the difference to be relatively small. A 2014 study found that married people had sex about 55 times a year, compared with 59 times a year among their unmarried peers.

"There’s no ‘perfect statistic’ or ideal amount of sex."

"Experts aren’t sure precisely why this difference exists or why what used to be an advantage has become a disadvantage, but some believe it may be related to the increasing age at which most people get married," Hims wrote in a medically reviewed article.

"There’s no ‘perfect statistic’ or ideal amount of sex. In other words: You like what you like, and that’s perfectly OK."

CLICK HERE TO 

Clinical data suggests that aiming for a daily or high-volume sexual quota does not actually improve relationship quality.

A study published in Social Psychological and Personality Science in 2015 evaluated more than 30,000 individuals over four decades and discovered a drop-off in additional benefits.

While overall happiness increased as physical intimacy moved from monthly to weekly, couples who had sex two, three or four times a week experienced no additional statistical boost in marital satisfaction compared to those hitting the weekly threshold.

Experts emphasize that sexual desire naturally fluctuates as couples navigate career demands, parenthood and biological aging.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Despite some research suggesting a slowdown with age, intimacy remains an important factor in healthy aging, linked to improved physical and emotional well-being.

AARP survey data indicates that physical connection remains routine for many older Americans, with roughly 17% of adults aged 70 and older engaging in sexual activity on a weekly basis.

Reasons for declining intimacy

When a couple experiences an intimacy dry spell, medical professionals recommend evaluating physiological factors rather than jumping to conclusions about incompatibility.

Educational resources from the International Society for Sexual Medicine note that the following physical conditions can influence libido.

World.title: State Department urges Americans to consider leaving Middle East as regional conflict escalates
World.content:
The State Department on Saturday urged Americans across the Middle East to consider leaving the region or be prepared to depart on short notice, warning of flight disruptions and security risks as the conflict with Iran escalates.

President Donald Trump has threatened Iran with additional attacks, saying Friday that the U.S. will be “hitting them very hard,” while Iran has vowed to “punish” the U.S. and both nations traded what some U.S. officials described as “heavy” strikes.

“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions,” the State Department said Saturday. “Some airlines in the region have postponed resumption of earlier flight schedules; others have cancelled some routes. Americans in the region should consider departing, or be prepared to depart should there be escalation.”

The State Department also urged Americans to reconsider travel bans to or through the region.

Residents inspect the damage caused by Israeli airstrikes last night on residential buildings in the Safatawi area of Gaza on Aug. 1. Ahmad Hasaballah / Getty Images

The warning was distributed through U.S. embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar and Saudi Arabia.

The agency posted a nearly identical statement earlier this month, but that bulletin did not urge Americans to prepare to leave the Middle East or to reconsider upcoming trips, reflecting Washington’s growing concern that the conflict could widen.

On Saturday, the Kuwait Army said its air defense systems intercepted drone attacks from Iran.

“Kuwaiti air defenses are currently engaging hostile drone attacks following the Iranian aggression. The General Staff of the Army notes that any explosions heard are a result of air defense systems intercepting the hostile attacks,” the army said.

Two days ago, the U.S. military confirmed it had executed a “heavy wave of strikes” on Iran, hours after Fox News reported that the president in a phone call had vowed to “beat the f-----g s--- out of” the country.

Trump has grown increasingly exasperated with the state of the war, one Trump ally told NBC News.

Displaced Palestinians inspect the destruction following an Israeli airstrike that targeted the central Gaza Strip on Aug. 1. Majdi Fathi / NurPhoto via Getty Images

“There was not a real strategy for how long or what they should do to get to the endpoint,” the ally said.

The conflict has now entered its sixth month, despite Trump’s repeated early predictions that the war would resolve itself “shortly.”

The protracted conflict has led to soaring oil prices globally and rising gas prices in the U.S.

There was a brief reprieve from fighting in June when the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding outlining the process for talks to end the war.

But in early July, Trump declared a ceasefire to be “over” and the countries resumed striking targets in the Middle East.
