"That's where you pop it up on a screen and it hits you, you know, right in the face," Hoge says.

The FDA said it would not review Moderna's application for its mRNA flu shot, effectively rejecting it.

It was a shock. "We had talked to the FDA at every step along the way, including prior to filing," he says. "And they had said, you can go forward and submit and we will conduct a review."

An FDA decision that reverberated

Moderna went public with what happened. The news shook the pharmaceutical industry. There was an outcry over the FDA's backtracking.

A little over a week later, the agency reconsidered and agreed to review the vaccine after Moderna promised to add a confirmatory study of the vaccine if it makes it to market. In June, a panel of advisers to the FDA recommended that the agency approve the vaccine.

The agency has a Wednesday deadline to make a decision. If the FDA gives it the green light, the Moderna vaccine would be the first mRNA-based flu shot to make it to market. But the FDA's flip-flop in February has already had a chilling effect.

Rena Conti, a health economist at Boston University, says the industry and its investors will be watching closely because the U.S. market is where they make most of their money. They depend on the FDA to be consistent and fair.

Sponsor Message

"They don't want to spend money if they don't think there's going to be a way to actually make money on the other end," she says.

What's more, the Department of Health and Human Services canceled nearly $500 million in mRNA vaccine research funding last summer.

In response to NPR's questions about the administration's actions on experimental mRNA vaccines, an HHS spokesman provided the following statement: "Under Secretary Kennedy's leadership, HHS is advancing President Trump's commitment to strengthen public health through gold-standard science, and FDA will continue applying rigorous, evidence-based standards to every product it reviews while supporting innovation that meets those standards."

Investors in mRNA research are wary

But Hoge says Moderna is holding off on some planned mRNA research until the company knows how things will shake out.

In the world of mRNA, Moderna is a big fish and most of the rest are tiny biotechs with 20 or 30 employees, says Jeff Coller, a professor at Johns Hopkins University who has studied mRNA technology for decades.

"When you see the FDA rejecting a product that comes from Moderna, why is it that my little company would be able to push through?" he says.

Coller says the FDA's actions combined with the HHS funding cuts spooked the venture capital firms that backed many of the smaller biotechs working on mRNA therapies for conditions ranging from Lyme disease to rare cancers.

That matters to people like 69-year-old Janusz Racz, a retired computer scientist who lives in London. When his doctors found inoperable Stage 3 lung cancer two years ago, it was a surprise.

He's a runner and sailor and had no symptoms, but the tumor was the size of a golf ball. If he did nothing, his doctors told him he would be dead in a matter of months.

Racz got into a clinical trial in London, where he lives, that made him the first person in the U.K. to receive an mRNA vaccine made by BioNTech, Pfizer's partner on the first vaccine against COVID-19.

Sponsor Message

"I decided just to participate because I saw that was a big chance." he says. "And also, as a scientist ... I wanted to participate in such a program to give other patients a hope."

After a year of regular vaccinations, the cancer is gone. He's making plans for the future while the study continues for other patients.

But he's watched as the Trump administration and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have taken aim at mRNA vaccines.

Racz is a U.S. citizen, so he says he wrote Kennedy a letter.

"I told him my story," he says. "And this is a new hope for people, for millions of people. And they cut off the hope."

He says Kennedy never wrote back.

World.title: Lebanese who fled the Israeli invasion visit to see what's left
World.content:
Lebanese who fled the Israeli invasion visit to see what's left

toggle caption Diego Ibarra Sánchez for NPR

NABATIYEH, Lebanon — Past the shattered glass of the balcony doors of Najib Ayyad's damaged apartment in southern Lebanon, he can see a historic local landmark — now occupied by Israeli forces.

"You see the castle?" he asks. Beaufort Castle, a crusader-era fortress, was seized in May by Israeli forces who have now gone far beyond what the Israeli government describes as a "security zone" in southern Lebanon.

"They can see us clearly from there," he says. "Even if my apartment weren't damaged I couldn't stay."

On the day we visit in June, smoke is rising from an Israeli artillery strike near Nabatiyeh, a small city that is a hub in the south of the country. The sound of Israeli drones is a constant backdrop in a city devastated by war, but which still shows tentative signs of residents trying to rebuild their lives here.

toggle caption Diego Ibarra Sánchez for NPR

Ayyad, a parliamentary office worker, has come back only to salvage some belongings from the apartment. He used to commute to work from here to the parliament member's office near Sidon, a short drive away. With no money to rent another apartment, he is staying with his daughter in her flat in Beirut.

Sponsor Message

It's a struggle to even get to his apartment. Broken chunks of concrete cover the building's entranceway while the staircase is littered in rubble and broken glass. Israeli air strikes have knocked out electricity throughout the city.

toggle caption Diego Ibarra Sánchez for NPR

Three floors up, shafts of light from empty windows with jagged frames illuminate piles of broken furniture.

On the street outside, most homes have been destroyed or heavily damaged. One elegant multi-story villa set back behind metal gates appears intact but the back of the building has been heavily damaged.

A long history

toggle caption Diego Ibarra Sánchez for NPR

Nabatiyeh is an administrative center for the Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah, whose fighters and infrastructure Israel now says it is targeting. But Hezbollah is also a political party and a provider of social services, and as in other towns and cities in the south, much of the damage and many of the casualties are civilian.

Lebanese health officials say at least 4,200 people have been killed since the war began on March 2. At least one in five of the dead are women or children, they say. Israel says 37 of its soldiers and one military contractor, along with two civilians, have been killed by Hezbollah attacks.

For hundreds of years, Nabatiyeh's covered market was a thriving commercial center — first on a transit route between Jerusalem, Damascus and Mecca and then as an important Ottoman-era town. In 1982, invading Israeli forces occupied the city, withdrawing three years later.

toggle caption Diego Ibarra Sánchez for NPR

Its covered market with red-tiled roofs and stone arches featured farm produce, clothing and handicrafts — much of it now in rubble from Israeli attacks.

Sponsor Message

"We are telling people to wait to come back," says Mayor Abbas Fakhreddin pointing out damage to the historic market. "Not only because of the security situation but also because we don't have the necessities of life. There is a huge amount of work to be done here."

Fakhreddin and residents here say the extensive damage appears to show Israel's aim of halting the city's commercial life.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said in July that Israeli forces further south had demolished more than 15,000 homes in border villages to prevent residents from returning. Those villages are in what Israel calls a "buffer zone" that it says is aimed at preventing Hezbollah from launching more rockets or other attacks across the border.

Bodies still under the rubble

toggle caption Diego Ibarra Sánchez for NPR

Just around the corner from the Nabatiyeh covered market is Hanan Hamadi's tiny convenience store. It is far less grand than the historic shops, but a vivid illustration that residents are determined to overcome the destruction of this latest war with Israel.

"When we arrived we found the shop completely damaged," says Hamadi, who returned with her mother from Beirut, where they had taken refuge. She and her mother threw out damaged goods, restocked, put the framed photo of her late father back on the wall and re-opened for business. A plastic sheet substitutes for the broken door.

A little boy comes in to ask the price of a candy bar. Hamadi tells him whatever he has is enough and later explains that the child's father was injured in an attack.

The shop's wares include canned goods, yogurt, plastic bags of flat bread, batteries and – in a sign of optimism that life could someday be normal again – birthday candles.

"God willing we will rebuild the market better than ever and everyone will come back," says her mother Salwa Hachouch.

Sponsor Message

But for now it's hard to imagine. Two months after some of the most devastating airstrikes, there are still bodies buried under the rubble.

Hamadi says the Basma family, who lived just across a lane from them in a neighborhood called the Nuns' Quarter, was killed in an airstrike in March — the parents along with all four of their children. The impact collapsed the house on top of them and two of the children — ages around 8 and 11 — are still under the rubble, she says.

"Now when I look at the neighborhood they are the only ones I can think about," she says.

She says in a quiet area full of older people, the family's four children brought life to the neighborhood. "They were the ones who made all the noise and activity," she says.

Hammadi says she used to drink coffee with the mother, who was in her late 30s. She would talk about waiting for her children to grow up.

"They were wonderful people," she says. "Now there's no one left from the family."

Amnesty International investigated the March 31 airstrike that killed the family, saying there were no apparent military targets nearby and calling it a potential war crime. Another neighbor was also killed in the airstrike.

The human rights group said the family had stayed despite the danger because they had no money to leave. The father was an unemployed house painter. The children were between the ages of seven and 16.

Israel told Amnesty last month it was investigating but provided no further information. It refused to provide an update on the case in response to an NPR query, repeating that it takes precautions to mitigate harm to civilians. It did not answer what the precautions were or why they resulted in the deaths of the family with no apparent military target nearby.

Sponsor Message

Resilience, tested to the limit

Hamadi, who is 40, says she and her mother stayed in Nabatiyeh during the war with Israel two years ago and every conflict before that.

"Before we were able to withstand the strikes. This time we couldn't," she says. "In this war they are not distinguishing between civilians and others," she says referring to the Israeli military. "Whoever dies, dies."

Hamadi took leave from her job with a non-governmental organization to help her mother. She says there is so much damage she often doesn't recognize once-familiar streets. Death and destruction have hollowed out the city she grew up in.

"Now when we look at the neighborhood, or the houses where people used to be we ask ourselves – 'Where are the children? Where are the people?' There's nobody," she says.

"The difference between us and others is that we are very resilient," she says of people in the south. "But at the same time we have reached a stage where we are tired."

Exhausted first responders

toggle caption Diego Ibarra Sánchez for NPR

On the edge of Nabatiyeh, a house turned into a center for first responders buzzes with the intense camaraderie of bonds forged in dangerous environments. Some of the young men joke and drink coffee as they watch black smoke rise from artillery strikes in the distance. Others prepare food to be distributed to families in town.

Israeli air strikes have killed at least 130 Lebanese first responders, including three from this all-volunteer unit of the Nabatiyeh Emergency Medical Services They include Jude Sleiman, the16-year-old son of the unit commander Mohammad Sleiman. The boy, wearing a paramedic uniform, was killed along with a 23-year-old colleague while on a motorcycle delivering food to civilians.

toggle caption Scott Peterson/Getty Images

Ali Rida, who develops software embedded in devices such as smartwatches, gave up his job three years ago to volunteer as a paramedic. He has worked in Qatar, Thailand and Turkey. But it's here in his hometown of Nabatiyeh where he got the full-sleeve tattoo depicting characters from the movie The Godfather and the Statue of Liberty.

toggle caption Diego Ibarra Sánchez for NPR

"One of my dreams is to spend Christmas in New York," he says, a longing fostered by the Home Alone movies. "Probably I can't get a visa to the U.S. but still it's a dream."

Sponsor Message

"This is our duty," he says. "Whenever the country needs us we must be there."

Mohammad Sleiman says this war with its toll on civilians is unlike any others he has encountered. Some of the paramedics have died in follow-up strikes that killed them as they responded to calls to help the wounded.

toggle caption Diego Ibarra Sánchez for NPR

"This is creating a lot of psychological pressure but the guys insist on doing this job despite the danger," he says.

Nabatiyeh, he says, was once a city full of life. Even during the previous war with Israel two years ago, he says residents would come and go and the paramedics could go and see their families. Now, he says they spend weeks without going home.

"We are sitting here, waiting for the airstrikes," he says.

World.title: WestJet flight cancellations rise as Sunday strike deadline approaches
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WestJet passengers are anxiously watching the clock as flight attendants move closer to a Sunday strike deadline. Canada's second largest airline already began cancelling dozens of flights on Saturday, and travellers at Toronto Pearson Airport say they've been frustrated trying to get help from the airline amid the uncertainty.

Some travellers are heading into the long weekend on edge, as WestJet begins its first round of cancellations ahead of a possible strike by flight attendants.

The airline announced that a total of 279 flights have been cancelled as of Saturday evening. The company says the move is meant to prevent crew and passengers from getting stranded, and travellers should check their flight status before leaving for the airport.

"This action is in response to the union’s notice to strike and the inability to reach an agreement. WestJet’s most recent proposal was designed to be a transformative, industry-leading agreement for WestJet's cabin crew, and directly addressed the key issues the union identified as its priorities," a WestJet spokesperson said in a statement.

The union representing the flight attendants has said the proposal didn't address all of their concerns.

If a deal is not reached by Sunday morning, either side could begin a work stoppage that would cancel hundreds of flights during a long weekend for much of the country.

WestJet says it is continuing to bargain with the Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE), which represents 4,400 flight attendants, in the hope of reaching an agreement on a new contract.

The union triggered a 72-hour strike notice that ends just after midnight Sunday in Calgary, where WestJet is headquartered, and the airline responded with a lockout notice on the same timeline.

People check in at Vancouver International Airport in Richmond, B.C., on Friday. (Ethan Cairns/CBC)

That strike notice doesn't commit flight attendants to taking job action but has proved worrisome for passengers who are left in limbo, unsure whether or not their flights will take off this weekend.

In emails obtained by CBC News, WestJet said it had put forward what it believes is the best agreement it could responsibly offer.

That includes what the company claims is a union proposal "for compensation before and after flights through duty premium payments," which would be included in what WestJet describes as a cumulative wage increase of about 36 per cent over four years.

The company also says it offered scheduling improvements and better provisions for things like travel and hotels while flight attendants are away from home, according to one of the internal WestJet emails viewed by CBC News.

The union representing flight attendants told CBC News that the proposals don't go far enough.

"We aren’t just bargaining a few things, we are seeking a comprehensive contract that reflects the priorities of our members," CUPE WestJet Component president Alia Hussain said in an email.

WATCH | Former WestJet flight attendant speaks with CBC News Network: Former flight attendant on why she quit the industry | Duration 5:10 Calleigh Gingras is a former flight attendant who has been a vocal critic on social media about issues within the airline industry. She says she is not shocked by news of a possible strike by WestJet flight attendants and that despite loving the job, the pay for the working conditions, including many hours of unpaid work, was 'not sustainable' for her.

Hussain said while some progress has been made toward reaching a deal, there are issues remaining that "need to be resolved at the table."

"We are hopeful that we can still avoid a strike and remain committed to resolving this there."

Patty Hajdu, federal minister of jobs and families, said in an emailed statement to CBC News that she has met with the two parties as they mediate in Calgary.

"Our government has always maintained that the best deals are reached at the bargaining table," Hajdu said.

"With federal mediators supporting negotiations since May, the parties can and should reach a deal. Canadians are counting on it.”

The Calgary Chamber of Commerce said in a statement it hopes the dispute will be resolved soon, noting a labour disruption will affect both tourism and supply chains.

"Businesses and travellers need air transportation that is predictable and reliable," the group said.

"Maintaining this confidence is essential to supporting economic growth and ensuring Calgary remains connected to markets within the country and around the world."

LISTEN | WestJet is parking its jets and there's still no deal: Your World Tonight 28:00 WestJet uncertainty, migrants return from Ceuta, sports equipment libraries, and more

What happens to affected travellers?

As cancellations begin, the airline has said travellers should check the status of their flights ahead of their trips.

Ahead of the potential strike, WestJet has been allowing passengers travelling between July 30 and Aug. 4 to make a one-time change or cancellation with no fees.

But only passengers with certain kinds of bookings can get a refund back to their original form of payment if they take advantage of the one-time cancellation offer. Those who booked PremiumFlex and BusinessFlex flights, or premium and business passengers travelling between Canada and Asia, can get their cash back, and others will get a refund in the form of a travel credit.

If a customer decides to keep their WestJet booking, and delays or cancellations still occur, the airline said affected passengers will be refunded or re-accommodated as applicable. Under Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations, affected customers should be rescheduled on a flight with WestJet or one of its partners within 48 hours, or they can receive a refund instead of a travel credit.

If the airline cannot reschedule customers within 48 hours, it is obligated to try to reschedule them on a competitor's flight if necessary, but that can be at another airport.

The airline said travellers who booked with WestJet directly will be notified of any changes through the contact information provided in their booking, and those who booked through a third party such as a travel agent will have to make changes through the third party.

One such traveller who's trying to change bookings without much luck is Edmonton's Gani Suleman.

He told CBC News that his trip from Alberta to Scotland to attend his sister's wedding had been planned for months, but he has spent the last few weeks in a holding pattern as his tries to confirm with WestJet and a third-party travel agency, from which he bought his tickets, that his flight is still leaving as scheduled.

When he asked the travel agency if he could change his flight as per WestJet's announcement, Suleman said the agency told him that it was not informed about any such option.

"We're just waiting," he said. "The worst thing is that every single day, if I'm looking at alternative prices, they're just escalating ... but there's nothing we can do."

WATCH | Taking labour issues into consideration when booking flights: How can air passengers take labour issues into consideration when booking flights? | Duration 2:10 Talks continue this morning between WestJet and the union representing its flight attendants. CUPE 8125 issued a 72-hour strike notice yesterday. And WestJet responded with a 72-hour lockout notice. The workers will be in a legal strike position late Saturday night Pacific time

At Toronto's Pearson International Airport, meanwhile, anxiety was high.

Alyesha Singh told The Canadian Press that she was worried she would miss her 15-person family reunion in the Dominican Republic. She hasn't seen some family members in years and is thrilled to get everyone in one place.

Her parents planned their trip and have been keeping a close eye on cancellation updates, Singh said at the airline's baggage drop-off station.

"We just hope everything comes to a conclusion before we get back."

What is this dispute all about?

Compensation for work done on the ground remains a key stumbling block in the talks, less than a year after the same issue sparked a work stoppage by Air Canada flight attendants. They ultimately won compensation increases.

The union has characterized certain ground duties as unpaid, but WestJet describes it differently.

WestJet's current "credit hour" system combines flight time, ground duties, delays and other labour into a "single, higher rate of pay" that is then credited across the workday, the company says on its website.

The pay rate ranges between $28.88 and $53.61 per credit hour, the company says. At 80 credit hours a month — considered full-time work — that adds up to between $2,300 and $4,300.

Many airlines operate under a similar structure, but Delta Air Lines spearheaded reforms in 2022 when it became the first carrier in North America to pay flight attendants specifically for work done on the ground. American Airlines and Alaska Airlines followed suit with boarding pay of 50 per cent of regular rates.

Suleman, the traveller from Edmonton, said he sympathizes with the cabin crews, noting he himself would not do any extra work if he wasn't paid for it.

"They've gone out of their way," he said of their ground duties. "I think it's now WestJet's turn."

World.title: New HIV infections in Canada are rising. Advocates say years of progress are at risk
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

New federal data shows HIV cases in Canada rose 23 per cent in 2024 compared with 2022, with more cases appearing in small communities that lack adequate healthcare. Experts worry U.S. cuts to international AIDS funding could trigger more resurgence of HIV/AIDS around the world.

Dr. Julio Montaner has spent decades in the fight against HIV but says he feels years of progress slipping away.

“I am very worried about what's coming our way,” said Montaner, executive director and physician-in-chief at the BC Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS in Vancouver, the largest HIV/AIDS research and treatment facility in Canada.

He says new cases of the virus are popping up in British Columbia every week — a reality reflected in health data from across the country, sparking calls from advocates and health experts for Canada to address the growing issue.

New modelling data from the Public Health Agency of Canada shows there was a 22.8 per cent increase in new HIV infections between 2022 and 2024.

In 2024, an estimated 2,517 new infections occurred compared with the 2,050 infections recorded two years earlier.

Dr. Julio Montaner delivers a speech at the 18th International AIDS Conference in this file photo from July 23, 2010. He was head of the International AIDS Society between 2008 and 2010. (Samuel Kubani/AFP/Getty Images)

In 2019, B.C. declared an end to the HIV epidemic after new AIDS cases had declined by 90 per cent and new infections were at a record low. But since then, Montaner says infection numbers have been moving in the other direction.

In May, Manitoba's public health minister declared HIV a public health emergency after HIV rates rose sharply, becoming 3.5 times higher than the national rate. Earlier this year, Saskatchewan reported infection rates just under Manitoba's, making theirs the second-highest rates in Canada.

“What we're seeing is a resurgence of HIV, both new infections and AIDS, which was until two or three years ago, persistently declining — because the strategy was working,” Montaner said.

Canada below key HIV targets

Montaner's research into highly active antiretroviral therapy in the mid '90s helped prove HIV infection could be effectively managed by using a combination of drugs. The world renowned physician and professor went on to be the lead architect behind the strategy "treatment as prevention," introduced in 2006 at the International AIDS Conference in Toronto.

The approach was adopted by the United Nations in 2014 in an effort to end the AIDS pandemic by 2030. A majority of UN member states, including Canada, endorsed and committed to the strategy in 2016, and reaffirmed those commitments this past June.

The strategy asks countries to aim for three targets: 95 per cent of people with HIV to be diagnosed, 95 per cent to be on treatment and 95 per cent to have a suppressed viral load.

But Canada has so far only reached one of the three goals.

“The most important number, at the end of the day, is the number of people that are virologically suppressed because you don't get sick, your disease doesn't progress, you lead a normal life — and you don't transmit HIV,” Montaner said.

Other countries have succeeded.

A new report from UNAIDS , the UN body that leads the global effort against the spread of AIDS, says 11 countries — seven of which are in eastern and southern Africa — have reached the threshold required to eliminate AIDS as a public health threat.

Globally, new HIV infections and deaths from the disease are at the lowest levels in 30 years, the report says.

According to UNAIDS, since 2010, the estimated number of new HIV infections fell by 42 per cent globally while deaths decreased by 57 per cent. In 2025, there were 1.2 million new infections and 570,000 deaths.

However, the same report says 21 countries have seen a rise in infections.

Cuts, slow tracking undermine future progress

This week, global health leaders at the International AIDS conference in Rio de Janeiro warned that major foreign aid cuts , mostly from the United States and other high-income countries — including Canada — could unravel years of progress.

UNAIDS says, in 2025, international funding for HIV testing and treatment initiatives in low- and middle-income nations plummeted by 18 per cent.

A new report from the United Nations AIDS agency, whose logo is pictured in Geneva, says while deaths and new infections are the lowest they've been in decades, more than 20 countries are reporting a rise in new infections. (Denis Balibouse/Reuters)

Montaner says Canada should restore its funding of global initiatives but says the resurgence of HIV cases at home also needs attention and investment from Ottawa.

“We are reporting every two years and we're reporting four years behind,” Montaner said. “We cannot adequately take steps to alleviate what's in front of us if we keep on looking backward.”

He says he’s been asking the federal government to report on national HIV infections quarterly, not every two years, and to make sure treatment is accessible.

Antiretroviral drugs have come a long way, Montaner says, with lower costs and many that are a single daily pill. There’s also oral and injectable medications such as pre-exposure prophylaxis, known as PrEP, and post-exposure prophylaxis, known as PEP, that significantly lower the risk of getting HIV.

Montaner says not everyone can afford deductibles and co-payments, and these medications should be free through Canada’s national pharmacare program.

The changing face of HIV

Jody Jollimore, an executive director for the Canadian AIDS Treatment Information Exchange (CATIE) agrees that more can be done.

Jollimore says despite Canada’s commitment in 2016 to eliminate HIV, investment in the HIV and Hepatitis C Community Action Fund that supports programs, like CATIE, has mostly been stagnant.

Public Health Agency of Canada says funding through the HIV and Hepatitis C Community Action Fund and the Harm Reduction Fund amounts to $33.4 million annually and is "tailored to reach key populations and the regions of the country most affected by HIV, hepatitis C" and other sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections.

“A dollar does not go as far as it used to,” Jollimore said.

Canada approved the sale of over-the-counter, rapid-oral HIV self-tests, like this one, earlier this year. (Eduardo Lima/The Canadian Press)

Jollimore says the face of HIV is changing in Canada. He says when the AIDS crisis began in the 1980s it was centered in big cities, mostly affecting gay men, but today, it is showing up in rural and remote communities without adequate health infrastructure and resources. He says more investment is needed to reach those people.

“These communities have little infrastructure," Jollimore said. "They almost certainly do not have an HIV organization supporting the work. And in fact, many don't even have a clinic or a health-care provider available to them.”

The Public Health Agency of Canada estimates 70,900 people are living with HIV in Canada. The agency says over half identify as gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men. More than a quarter are female and about 12.6 per cent are people who have injected drugs.

“It tends to thrive in pockets where there's the least connection to care,” Jollimore said. “In those communities where stigma or discrimination or racism may prevent someone from coming forth to get tested or treated.”

Darryl Jordan is a harm-reduction navigator at the non-profit Persons Living with AIDS Network in Saskatoon. The organization provides support and education for people living with HIV/AIDS. (Travis Reddaway/CBC)

Reconnecting to care

Those are just some of the barriers Darryl Jordan is working to address.

His father died from AIDS in 1994. Then in 2010, Jordan himself was diagnosed with HIV. Today, he works as a harm-reduction navigator in Saskatoon for a local Indigenous organization called Persons Living with AIDS Network.

Its program helps people get tested and connected to HIV treatment, but Jordan says that work has been affected by provincial funding cuts to harm reduction initiatives.

He says stigma around HIV is one of the many reasons people may not want to get tested. But there are other challenges, like substance use, mental health and poverty that have created barriers to getting people help.

“A lot of people have lost connection with their care,” Jordan said. “They're not taking their medication. I mean, in order to take care of yourself, you got to have a roof over your head.”

Jordan says rapid HIV oral tests have made it easier for people to find out their status.

“Once you're tested you can be treated and once you're treated you're going to live a normal life.”

World.title: Kids' birthday parties are getting more expensive. Should guests help pay for them?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Kids' birthday parties are a big business these days pretty much any way you go about it.

At best, there's the price of food, cake and balloons. Maybe you rented a bouncy castle to keep the kids entertained, or hired Elsa to sing Let it Go, or paid for the reptile zoo to come to you.

Perhaps, at worst, you booked a party package at the soft play/arcade/ball pit/laser tag/loud indoor theme park. Or maybe you're taking six pre-teens for manicures, or a dozen kids to make splatter art and friendship bracelets at your local pottery studio/craft shop/artisan sandwich cafe that — did you hear?! — just started booking birthday parties.

Big or small, the costs add up. But does this mean the hosts should ask other parents to help cover the expense?

That's the debate currently raging across the internet amid reports some parents are asking guests for tips. And we don't mean advice. We mean cash in a jar, a contribution, or paying to attend.

"Have you seen this on an invitation yet? I bet you will," a cake decorator said in a viral TikTok video last year. In the video, she claims at least three families she'd worked with included requests for tips on their party invitations to help cover costs.

"If you are inviting my children to your child's birthday and you asked me to pay for them to come, nine out of 10 times they're probably not going to be attending," a U.K. parent and financial advisor recently posted.

"I've seen it … the mom invoiced people," a parenting podcaster said in a video posted in March.

In the comments online, most people argue you shouldn't be throwing a party you can't afford, while others defended the practice given costs for everything are skyrocketing.

But it also opened up a bigger conversation: when did the expectations for kid parties get so, well, bananas?

"When it's financially difficult for families to do this to the extent they have to ask other families to pitch in, we are really getting out of hand," Vanessa Lapointe, a parenting consultant based in Surrey, B.C., told CBC News.

An Instagram post from Kim Kardashian from May 14 shares details of her son's Pokemon birthday party. (@kimkardashian/Instagram)

'The pressure is real'

According to recent media reports, the average parent spends at least $445 for a party, at least one in five parents spend more than $700, and a third of parents go into debt for it. Event planners have described wealthy parents willing to spend upward of $42,000 to throw extravagant parties for their children.

Other reports have suggested over two-thirds of parents polled think planning their kid's birthday party is more stressful than their day job. And nearly half of a thousand U.K. parents polled last year admitted they felt competition with other parents to throw the best party.

Meanwhile, parenting blogs and websites encourage "enchanted garden" party themes (complete with fairy doors and pixie dust) and advise that "farmcore" parties — in which the children churn their own butter — are trending. Elsewhere, celebrities like Kim Kardashian are posting photos of their children's bashes, including, in her case, a giant Pikachu.

"There’s definitely a pressure to make sure your kid has a memorable party," Ottawa mom Gaelan Jaffray told CBC News.

"You’re measuring yourself against what you’re seeing on social media and what your friends are doing and you don’t want to be the one with the lame party. The pressure is real and mostly self-inflicted."

Gaelan Jaffray's son opens a present at a dinosaur-themed party she hosted in Ottawa that she jokingly says was 'Pinterest-worthy.' (Gaelan Jaffray)

It's also incredibly expensive no matter which route you take, Jaffray says. She estimates parties for her son, 10-year-old Everett, average about $400, and even hosting at home becomes pricey once you factor in food, cake, decorations, entertainment and loot bags.

For instance, five years ago, Jaffray threw Everett a dinosaur-themed party at home that she jokingly describes as "Pinterest-worthy." There was a balloon arch, a mural, custom cupcakes, a dinosaur bouncy castle and a loot bag for each guest.

"That said, I don’t think the rising cost of hosting justifies asking invited guests to subsidize the party," Jaffray said.

"To me, bringing a gift is already the guest’s contribution."

Warning over 'culture of comparison'

Expectations for modern parenting have become so all-consuming that researchers now have a term for it: the intensification of parenting.

Even the U.S. surgeon general has acknowledged these pressures, issuing a public health advisory in 2024 about the impact on parents' mental health. Part of modern parenting's unique struggles are what he called our "culture of comparison," propagated by influencers and online trends that create unrealistic expectations.

You know, like ombre balloon arches, professionally designed cakes and loot bags that could rival the swag bags at the Oscars.

"Comparison is the thief of joy," said Lapointe, the parenting consultant.

And it's not like the quality of a birthday party is going to make or break their childhood, she added. Kids will look back on the experience and how they felt, not how splashy it was.

Still, said Jaffray, as kids get older and start having specific requests, it's hard to say no.

"It’s the only time they’re going to turn that age," she said. "You want it to be special."

World.title: Canada could add billions to its economy by processing more food. Here's what it's trying
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Inside their demonstration plant in Benmiller, Ont., Martin VanderLoo and Graham Markham are working to prove a point: Canada can generate a big economic boost and strengthen its food sovereignty by processing more food at home.

The two men are focused on soybeans, a legume that Canada grows millions of tonnes of each year. Their company, New Protein International, aims to produce soy protein isolate, which is used in products like baby formulas, protein bars and nutrition shakes.

"The demand for plant-based protein just continues to increase dramatically," VanderLoo said.

Indeed, according to the U.S. Foreign Agricultural Service , global production of soybeans has risen from 350.8 million tonnes in 2016 to 429.4 million tonnes in 2025.

The issue, according to VanderLoo and Markham, is that Canada is leaving money on the table by sending a sizable chunk of its agricultural products outside of the country for processing, then importing them back for consumption.

Graham Markham, left, is the chief development officer at New Protein International, and Martin VanderLoo is the CEO. The two men are working to create a commercial facility that can process Canadian soybeans into soy protein isolate, which is used in products like baby formulas, protein bars and specific beverages. (Submitted by Graham Markham and Martin Vanderloo)

"We will forever become a servant state of the other countries where they will continue to build more manufacturing facilities and buy our stuff and process it there," Markham said.

"Let's make it here."

According to Soy Canada, a national association that represents groups involved in the development, transportation and processing of soybeans, more than 70 per cent of Canada's production is shipped abroad.

The federal government's recently-released national food security strategy notes that "despite its current size, Canada does not process nearly as much of the food that is grown or harvested in Canada as it could."

"Instead, this food is exported to other countries to be processed. This decreases our food sovereignty, and it also means that we lose out on potential economic gains of processing the food in Canada," the strategy says.

Some groups, like Protein Industries Canada, estimate Canada could unlock $25 billion in annual GDP growth with the right investments, infrastructure and policy support for its plant-based ingredient manufacturing and food processing sector.

VanderLoo and Markham are hoping to seize on that opportunity. Their demonstration plant uses a unique process to extract the protein without using hexane, a petrochemical. Their goal is to create Canada's first large-scale facility in the near future.

A panoramic shot of Markham and Vanderloo's demonstration plant. According to the two men, the commercial facility would use 70,000 metric tonnes of soybeans to produce enough soy protein isolate to fill several million large-size protein powder tubs. (Submitted by Graham Markham)

According to VanderLoo, the commercial facility would use 70,000 metric tonnes of soybeans, and it's expected to produce 17,500 tonnes of soybean protein isolate — several million large-size protein powder tubs.

Canada in a pickle

Dan Froese, who works with seven of his siblings on their family farm in Vienna, Ont., to grow cucumbers and peppers, described how the family used to ship their crops to Canadian plants owned by pickle brands like Bick's and Heinz.

WATCH | Bick’s pickles no longer stocked in some stores due to ‘tariff impacts': Bick’s pickles no longer stocked in some stores due to ‘tariff impacts’ | Duration 2:13 Bick’s, a popular Canadian pickle brand assembled in the U.S., is facing a 25 per cent Canadian retaliatory tariff, making its pickles pricier and harder to find. Experts say companies dealing with complex cross-border supply chains have been hit especially hard by the trade war.

Those plants have since closed, Froese said, so his crops are now shipped to the U.S. for processing. The issue is that upon return they're viewed by Canadians as American-made — despite the raw ingredients being fully Canadian.

"It hurt our industry hugely for this year," he said. "The contracts for this year were literally smaller toward the farmers because Canadian people stopped buying Bick's pickles to a large extent."

Henry Voth works for Hartung Brothers, a U.S.-based company that purchases cucumbers from farms, including Froese's, and delivers them to companies for processing.

"Everyone's gone to the U.S.," he said, and companies are enticed to move operations there because regulations are less cumbersome and, accordingly, less expensive.

From left to right: Jaime Froeze, Henry Voth, Dan Froese and Neil Reimer at Froese Vegetables in Vienna, Ont. on Thursday, July 30, 2026. (Derek Vanderwyk/CBC)

"Food safety is a great place but can be overdone. ... I'm not saying it's not important, there are definitely important pieces there, but we're overregulated in that."

Froese's brother Jamie concurred.

"The tax burden in Ontario is just astronomical," he said.

"If you want to look for solutions, you're going to have to have tax incentives or reduce taxes. But it seems as long as we have a Liberal government, it's just going to keep skyrocketing."

What Canada's doing, and needs to do

Ottawa's food security strategy pledges hundreds of millions of dollars to strengthen Canada's food processing sector, with a goal of increasing the proportion of domestically-processed food consumed in Canada from 70 to 80 per cent, though there's no specific deadline.

Markham, with New Protein International, said the goal is realistic but requires ambition.

The federal government's recently-released national food security strategy notes that 'despite its current size, Canada does not process nearly as much of the food that is grown or harvested in Canada as it could.' (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

Arlene Dickinson, founder of District Ventures Capital and star of CBC's Dragon's Den, has been vocal about the decline of Canadian food processing. She told The House on Thursday that Canada has long considered itself a commodity-driven nation.

Dickinson also said Canada's food manufacturing and agri-food space employs more people than its auto sector. According to the federal government, in 2024 the food and beverage processing industry employed 318,000 Canadians.

"It is the largest employer of manufacturing in the nation," Dickinson said.

For too long, she said investors have been chasing the high returns of the tech sector, while the food sector is steadier.

"We have to start thinking differently. We have to stop thinking about it in terms of only the profile of the return — which by the way is very good in the food space — but also think about it in terms of food sovereignty."

Arlene Dickinson, star of Dragon's Den, says Canada will need a campaign to tout the value of its processed food to change its image for investors and other nations. (Blair Gable/Reuters)

Dickinson said the federal strategy is "a start to what we need to begin to do here" and Canada must be focused on the last mile of commercialization.

"In order to do that, we have to put capital to work. People have to invest in processing plants, manufacturing plants and finishing plants," Dickinson said. "We need more capital to be deployed against this really important sector."

As for whether the Canadian government can achieve its goal of strengthening its food sector in time to capture more value, Dickinson said she thinks it will.

"I now see growth funds that are putting money towards agriculture. … I'm a big believer in Canada. I know we've got opportunity in front of us. I believe we're gonna make it work."

World.title: Weather conditions expected to spark new wildfires, accelerate fire growth, B.C. Wildfire Service says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS) warns an approaching cold front could spark new wildfires and cause existing fires to spread rapidly because of strong winds and possible lightning.

"The existing fires on the landscape this weekend are going to experience more challenging conditions," said Aydan Coray, a fire information officer at the Provincial Wildfire Coordination Centre.

"Any new fire starts that come from incoming convective activity such as lightning starts will likely spread quite quickly and have rapid rates of growth."

As of 1 p.m. local time on Saturday, there were 35 active evacuation orders and 31 alerts across the province, affecting 2,900 and 2,800 properties respectively, according to the Ministry of Emergency Management and Climate Readiness.

New evacuation orders issued

The Fraser Valley Regional District (FVRD) issued an evacuation order effective at 9 a.m. PT Saturday, due to the Brunswick Creek Complex and the Ainslie Creek wildfire.

"The previously issued evacuation alert for the Alexandra Lodge to the Alexandra Bridge area has been upgraded to an evacuation order," said the FVRD in a news release.

In an email to CBC News, FVRD said there are active evacuation orders across the district affecting 495 properties. It said 279 properties are currently on evacuation alert in the area from Sawmill Creek to Dogwood Valley.

The district says anyone in areas under an evacuation order must leave immediately.

The Spuzzum First Nation says on its social media page that all Spuzzum First Nation reserve lands are also under an evacuation order as of Saturday morning.

Residents are being told to go south on Highway 1 toward Hope.

Just after 11 a.m. Saturday, the Regional District North Okanagan (RDNO) issued an evacuation alert for 22 properties on Six Mile Creek Road due to a wildfire in the area.

The Okanagan Indian Band issued an evacuation order at 3:44 p.m. on Saturday for all properties north of Marys Emerald Bay Road to Simla Road, due to the Bradley Creek Wildfire. Emergency services are conducting a tactical evacuation for residents on Pebble Park Lane.

The band's registered population is over 2,600.

MLA calls for state of emergency

In a post to Facebook Friday night, Cariboo-Chilcotin MLA Lorne Doerkson said a "very serious situation continues to develop in the South Cariboo."

"We need help and we need it right now."

Smoke can be seen in the distance in this photo from the B.C. Wildfire Service's Aug. 1 operational update on the Big Bar Complex, which includes the Pear Lake wildfire. (B.C. Wildfire Service)

He said residents have been calling for the provincial government to declare a state of emergency, and he is "joining them in that plea."

"There are hundreds of people fighting these fires right now, but the fires continue to advance in massive ways," he explained.

Doerkson noted the rate at which the Pear Lake wildfire is growing, from under 750 square kilometres to 905 square kilometres — its listed size Saturday morning — in a single day.

As of 10 a.m. PT, there were more than 100 active wildfires in B.C., including 46 classified as out of control, 44 under control and 18 being held.

The BCWS dashboard also showed 16 fires declared out and three new fires discovered during the same reporting period.

Coray said lightning starts aren't uncommon during this time of year, but what's more unusual is it being paired with high winds and "the intensity that this weather front is going to bring."

"The Cariboo Kamloops and Southeast Fire Centre in particular, are expected to have that increased activity this weekend."

Forests Minister Ravi Parmar told CBC News that crews are doing everything they can to protect homes.

"What we are seeing from the Pear Lake fire is extreme fire behaviour," he said.

“I have a duty as does the B.C. Wildfire Service leadership to ensure we are not putting our wildland firefighters, our aerial equipment at risk, their safety and the safety of residents is our utmost priority."

World.title: Bombing near upscale Moscow restaurant kills 3 people, wounds at least 21
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A homemade bomb carried by a woman killed three people and injured at least 21 in ​an explosion near an upscale restaurant in central ​Moscow on Saturday evening, authorities said.

The explosion occurred just before 8 p.m. local time close to an upscale Italian restaurant ​located in one of Moscow's seven Stalin-era skyscrapers at Kudrinskaya ⁠Square, the police said.

Russia's ⁠Anti-Terrorism Committee said an unidentified woman ‌had tried to get into the restaurant but was stopped by a security guard, the state RIA news agency reported.

It said the woman, the security guard and a customer at ⁠the Balzi Rossi Italian restaurant had been killed in the blast that followed. Those injured received wounds of varying seriousness, the police said.

The RIA news agency released ‌video of heavily armed law enforcement officers at the scene, which had been closed off to the public.

Law enforcement officers and emergency crews work at the site of an explosion outside a restaurant in Moscow. The explosion took place just before 8 p.m. local time on Saturday. (Anastasia Barashkova/Reuters)

The authorities did not name those killed or injured, nor did they say who they thought ​might have been responsible.

More than four years ​into a full-scale war with Ukraine, Russia's FSB security service said earlier this year that authorities would step up ⁠protection for high-ranking military officials after a series of assassinations and attempted killings ⁠it blamed on Ukraine.

The Kommersant daily newspaper cited its own sources ⁠as saying ⁠that the bomb had ​been intended to maim and kill guests who were enjoying themselves on the ​restaurant's summer terrace outside.

It suggested ⁠that the bomb had been set off by someone else remotely and that the woman carrying it may not have known that it was an explosive device.

The restaurant's website said the venue had been closed on Saturday for a ⁠private event.

World.title: The mystery of the 'Great Wall' of Hant’s Harbour
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Step into the woods above Hant’s Harbour, and you’ll find something out of a fairytale: a maze of moss-covered stone walls stretching off into the trees.

The largest section is a metre high, almost two metres wide, and over 20 metres long, and, though the local nickname “The Great Wall” may be tongue-in-cheek, it does reflect the intensive labour that must have gone into building these structures.

“The Great Wall really has a bit of an air of speculation and mystery about it that I think really gets people’s imaginations going,” said Marlayne Hardy, chair of the Willow Tree Heritage Society, a group that aims to preserve the history of Hant's Harbour.

The Great Wall is one of the sights on the society’s new audio walking tour of the area, but it’s been a favourite local landmark for years.

“When I have people that come to visit Hant’s Harbour,” said Hardy, “the Great Wall is one of the walks that we do because I want them to see it. It’s one of the highlights.”

The question is: who built the wall, and why?

Archaeological evidence suggests the walls were built in the 19th century by European settlers to support local agriculture and roadwork. (Submitted by Marlayne Hardy)

Though it’s survived centuries, the wall wasn’t secured with mortar.

Some sections were built over natural features of the landscape that were bolstered with stones using a technique called nogging. Others were assembled in a rubble pattern, with larger rocks laid first and pebbles inserted into the gaps between them for stability.

This second construction method allows stones to shift independently of one another so a structure can better withstand the movements caused by settling and the freeze-thaw cycle. Water can drain through the openings in the wall, and individual stones can fall out without setting off a progressive collapse.

Some of the boulders used in the Great Wall are so large they couldn’t have been carried, and the site suggests either generations of effort or strenuous work by a large group of people.

The origin of the wall has been a subject of local debate for years.

Some speculate that it may have been built as a caribou fence by pre-contact Indigenous people or that it was part of a hideaway for pirates like Peter Easton and his crew, who really did build a fort at Harbour Grace on the opposite side of the Bay de Verde Peninsula around 1612.

A report submitted to the Provincial Archaeology Office by Gerald Penney Associates in 2014, though, determined that the wall is more recent. Their investigation of the site uncovered ceramic sherds and a fragment of a green glass bottle dating to the mid-1800s.

At that time, Hant’s Harbour was a prosperous fishing port and a trade centre for nearby communities on the eastern shore of Trinity Bay.

Newfoundland fishing families relied on subsistence farming to supplement their diet, but the region’s rocky hillsides would have been challenging to cultivate.

Parts of the Great Wall might have been retaining barriers, intended to shore up the land into terraces for gardening. Or they could have been field walls, created from stones that were rooted out to ready the soil for planting and dumped at the edge of the clearing.

The Great Wall is the third stop on an audio walking tour of Hant’s Harbour released in June by the Willow Tree Heritage Society. (Submitted by Marlayne Hardy)

That the Great Wall runs so close to a hiking trail suggests a third possibility.

This coastal path follows an old road that once connected communities along the shore.

Parts of the trail are still paved with flat stones that were probably meant to keep carts from getting bogged down in mud.

In the late 1820s, during an economic slump caused by the Napoleonic wars, the colonial government began to invest in road upgrades in rural areas. These projects were intended to encourage agriculture by giving farmers better access to land, supplies and markets.

Footpaths were expanded to bridle paths wide enough for a horse and rider, then to roads broad enough for a wagon.

Two men from Hant’s Harbour requested money from the government in 1840 to complete a road between Hant’s Harbour and Seal Cove (now New Chelsea) about three-and-a-half kilometres to its northeast.

Teams of men would have been hired for this construction work, and they could have built the Great Wall from stones they cleared to smooth the roadway. Using wheeled carts, groups of three to four people would have been able to move even the larger boulders found in the structure today.

More mounds to mull

The Great Wall isn’t the only mysterious monument on the eastern shore of Trinity Bay.

Other mounds and platforms of rock are clustered along the old road northeast of Hant’s Harbour.

Where their purpose can be identified, the Gerald Penney Associates report concludes they were associated with 19-century agriculture, fishing and roadwork.

The Willow Tree Walk self-guided tour is intended to transport visitors back to those early days of settlement in the region. At each stop, including the Great Wall, visitors can listen to a story inspired by local history and read by a Hant’s Harbour resident, from Mayor Korri Power to actor Andy Jones.

The audio tour and map can be downloaded here.

“When you walk through, you think, what was life like in the mid-nineteenth century?” said Hardy. “What was that like for people trying to garden and trying to farm?”

An overgrown wall in the shadowy woods is bound to spark the imagination, but, in this case, the reality may be just as thought-provoking as the fantasy.

World.title: Whales are dying in B.C. waters. Here's how 2 groups are trying to save them
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Whales are dying in British Columbia waters — some struck by vessels, others unable to find food because of ship noise.

In May, video captured a person driving a Sea-Doo strike a grey whale off Vancouver, as witnesses watched in horror. Last October a humpback whale was struck by a whale-watching boat. A dead whale washed up dead days later, in the same area. A month earlier, a humpback was struck by a B.C. Ferries vessel, and a whale was found dead the following day.

It's become something of a growing trend, and could happen more often as ferry traffic increases and Canada pushes to ship more goods to Asia, across those very waters.

That's why t wo B.C. groups are trying to help.

One of them is a pilot project out of Simon Fraser University called HALLO — Humans and Algorithms Listening for Orcas , which aims to reduce ship noise to allow the endangered southern resident killer whales to find food.

“[The whales] are just a major part of this ecosystem that we want to protect,” said Lauren Laturnus, a masters student in biology at SFU.

Using a piece of surveying equipment, she tracks whales in the Salish Sea while also monitoring vessel traffic from East Point on Saturna Island, between Vancouver Island and the Lower Mainland.

Lauren Laturnus will spend the summer on Saturna Island visually monitoring and logging whales in the Salish Sea, as well as vessel traffic. (Dillon Hodgin/CBC)

“We're trying to see how often they're here at same time as these big vessels,” said Laturnus.

When she spots a whale she sends a report to the Ocean Wise Whale Alert System , which provides real-time notifications to commercial mariners to allow them to slow down or alter course.

About 100 volunteer citizen scientists have also been trained to monitor whale movements around Saturna, Pender and Mayne Islands and report what they see to the Whale Alert System.

“When a whale gets hit we all feel a little helpless, and being able to collect the information that could inform those vessels is, it feels good,” said Maureen Welton.

Maureen Welton, who lives on Saturna Island, is part of a group of citizen scientists who have been trained to monitor whale movements in the Salish Sea and report what they see. (Dillon Hodgin/CBC)

HALLO’s aim is to create an environment that allows southern resident killer whales to feed in peace.

“They rely on sound to essentially see their surroundings,” said Laturnus. “This noise from vessels interferes with that.”

Southern resident orcas are one of the most critically endangered marine mammals in Canada, according to the federal government's Species at Risk Act, and the Centre for Whale Research says there are about 74 left in British Columbia’s waters — as well as a new calf not included in their numbers. Their main food source is the declining chinook salmon, primarily located in the Salish Sea, one of the busiest shipping corridors in North America.

Push for increased protections

HALLO has partnered with the W̱SÁNEĆ Marine Guardians, an Indigenous-led monitoring and conservation initiative in the Salish Sea.

The Marine Guardians say by restoring the sacred bond between First Nations people and the whales, they can ensure their survival and protect ecosystems.

Biologist Rachel Fairfield Checko analyzes hydrophone recordings from underwater microphones to determine the whale species heard. That information, combined with First Nations knowledge, is used to advocate to the federal government for better whale protections.

Biologist Rachel Fairfield Checko. (Dillon Hodgin/CBC)

She says the W̱SÁNEĆ people successfully fought for increased protections in the Tumbo Channel, between Tumbo and Saturna islands, resulting in a voluntary slow down zone from June 1 to November 30, 2026.

“The southern resident killer whales are, they're here all year so what we have been asking the Government of Canada is why aren't these vessel restricted zones in place all year?” said Fairfield Checko.

The Government of Canada recently increased the distance vessels can be near the southern resident orcas from 200 metres to 1000 metres.

Protections for humpbacks also needed, say experts

An estimated 20,000 whales are killed worldwide by vessel strikes each year, according to the International Marine Mammal Project . It says large whales like humpbacks, grey, blue and fin whales are most often victims.

“There’s nothing in their evolutionary history that makes them even aware that there can be such a creature out there as a ship that they need to be careful about,” said Andrew Trites, professor and director at the UBC Marine Mammal Research Unit.

He said orcas, seals and sea lions have been able to coexist with vessels, but humpback whales have not.

WATCH | Watch how two groups try to save whales from dying in BC waters: Whales vs. massive ships: making B.C.’s Salish Sea safer for marine life | Duration 4:37 B.C.’s Salish Sea is home to a variety of marine mammals, including the critically endangered southern resident killer whale. For The National, CBC’s Caroline Barghout takes a closer look at the fight to protect marine life in one of North America’s busiest shipping corridors.

Glenn Jones, founder of Reach Technologies Inc. thinks he can help.

"We've developed an optical technology that will distinguish basically any object that penetrates the surface of the the water," said Jones.

The 360-degree rotating multispectral camera system was initially designed for the Canadian Department of National Defence to detect objects piercing the surface of the water and prevent damage to military ships. Jones has since discovered it also works for whales.

“The whole idea is to automatically detect whales around the vessel along with other objects of interest and put them on the chart plotter for the skipper so they can avoid the whales and stay out of their way,” said Jones.

He says the camera can identify whales 700 to 1,000 metres away, which should give large vessels more lead time to slow down or change course.

Glenn Jones' company Reach Technologies originally developed a 360-degree multispectral camera for the Canadian military to detect debris in the water. He has since discovered it also works well for tracking whales. (Dillon Hodgin/CBC)

Jones hope s his technology gets on commercial vessels and ferries to quickly identify whales. Eventually, he wants to pinpoint highly travelled routes so vessels can stay away.

“The whales are coming back in larger and larger numbers and we get more and more ships and we have to be able to stay out of their way and respect each other's space."
