World.title: When legacy media’s hypocrisy gets called out: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
I am increasingly finding myself analyzing the Mexico narrative as it’s told by different media outlets. Just this past week brought us another ludicrous example with The Atlantic magazine publishing an article titled “A Planeload of Informants” with the subtitle: “The United States is intensifying its hunt for narcos within the Mexican government. Is this all prelude to an attack?”

I guess The Atlantic was feeling left out of the party by other large media outlets writing breathtakingly sensationalist articles about Mexico. If you remember, leading up to the World Cup, The Economist magazine informed its readers that: “The World Cup will test Mexico’s control over its territory.” The Wall Street Journal told us that the “World Cup puts Mexico’s Cartel Crisis on the Global Stage.” And the New York Times has written at length of experts confidently predicting Mexico would enter a period of increasing violence after the February government operation against CJNG leader Mencho.

But they have all been wrong. Totally wrong. The post-Mencho spiral of violence? It didn’t happen. In fact, Mexico has seen its homicide rates hitting lows not seen in over a decade. The “World Cup test” of Mexico against the cartels? There was no test. The world watched with envy as foreigners partied alongside Mexicans across the country. Not a single article has been written acknowledging getting things so wrong. And so now we have the media moving on to the next big story: A potential attack by the United States on Mexico.

Let’s be clear about the history here: Mexico has, for decades, genuinely struggled with cartel violence, and I am not arguing otherwise. But what these outlets consistently omit is the context of the last year. Cooperation between the U.S. and Mexico against cartels is, in the words of officials on both sides, at unprecedented levels — a shift I’ve tracked in real time (see my columns on the World Cup coverage and Mexico’s business community). The result of that cooperation isn’t more violence; it’s homicides down by almost 50% this year. Apparently good news doesn’t sell subscriptions.

Which brings me to two personal anecdotes from this past week that I want to share:

Cancelling a 30-year subscription

The first took place at a friend’s dinner party in Mexico City. A few hours into some good conversation, he (quite randomly) asked me: “Do you still read The Economist magazine?” To which I responded that I do. He then said: “I have been a loyal subscriber for over 30 years, but I am about to cancel it. I am done with them.” His reasoning was enlightening: “I am tired of the narrative of their coverage. By cancelling my subscription with them, I am choosing to not pay attention to the reality that they are presenting.” He went on: “The predictive power of their writers and editors has changed … and as a result they are just flat out wrong on many topics.”

The words stuck with me as I have been increasingly feeling the same about The Economist. In just the past few months, I have actually written twice about how intellectually lazy, disingenuous and downright wrong their coverage has been regarding Mexico. Increasingly, as I read their coverage on the country, I have found myself wondering, “Why am I reading this? It’s not accurate. It’s sensationalist. And it doesn’t represent reality. Why am I paying to read something that I think is just plain wrong?”

As my friend’s cancellation shows, his decision reflects a broader pattern I’m seeing: As irresponsible coverage piles up, readers simply stop trusting — and stop paying for — outlets they once considered essential.

The conversation went further with others at the party explaining that, in contrast, they read Mexico News Daily precisely because it “provides optimism by showing me the Mexico that I want to believe exists today and believe can exist in the future.” The comment wasn’t made out of ignorance or a lack of information, but rather in a way that reinforced the optimism they have for Mexico. Said differently, they are choosing to align with a narrative of informed optimism versus colonialist click-bait pessimism. It’s unfortunate to increasingly see people tuning out of legacy media, but it’s easy to understand why they are doing it. As many outlets increasingly present a pessimistic, dystopian, doom-and-gloom view of much of the world — one that increasingly is out of touch with reality — many people are choosing to tune out.

The Economist’s Elon Musk interview

The second anecdote came earlier this week when I watched The Economist’s editor-in-chief, Zanny Minton Beddoes, interview Tesla/SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. The nearly 90-minute-long interview went on fine for the first hour, but then turned decidedly testy. Ms. Beddoes at one point begins to take issue with Musk’s assessment of the current state of the U.K. (where The Economist is based and where she lives). She questioned his motives, repeatedly said he was incorrect, accused him of supporting “fringe” and “far right” parties and questioned when he had last visited the U.K. To be clear, the point here is not whether Musk’s take on the U.K. is right or wrong, that’s a separate debate entirely.

Here you have the head of The Economist, the British publication that has increasingly misconstrued, misrepresented and irresponsibly presented other countries around the world, getting extremely defensive about someone questioning the U.K. She repeatedly took offense to any of Musk’s critiques of her own country, claiming “People say that you’re racist,” “people loathe you,” “What is the motivation for [participating in tribalism]?” It was quite shocking to see the head of a publication that for decades has portrayed much of the rest of the world as dangerous, backwards and corrupt take so much offense to someone questioning the current state and future direction of her own country.

As she waged increasingly personal attacks against Musk, he finally had enough and responded with a dagger: “A lot more people hate you, the media — more than you realize. Do you realize the media is despised? Do you realize … the favorable view of journalists is like 15%? … They hate you.” It was a striking moment. Her defensiveness made her and her publication feel small, out of touch, aloof. It was a moment where I found myself even further questioning the true motives of The Economist.

Musk’s jab about journalism’s approval rating isn’t just a soundbite — it’s the direct consequence of the pattern I described above. When outlets choose sensationalism over accuracy, they erode trust in journalism broadly, pushing people toward sources — credible or not — that at least feel honest to them.

Is The Economist really trying to live by its founding mission from 179 years ago of taking part “in a severe contest between intelligence, which presses forward, and an unworthy, timid ignorance obstructing our progress”? Or are they more likely contributing to the obstruction of progress with increasingly ignorant and biased journalism? If the latter is in fact the case, as I sadly suspect it is, they will likely experience more people like my friend moving on.

I strongly believe that the role of the media is more important than ever. But we in the media also needs to work harder than ever to earn your trust and respect — and many outlets seem to have forgotten that.

Thank you for reading and supporting MND.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: After a young girl’s death, Mexico shuts down all militarized grade schools
World.content:
Following the death of a female student, the Education Ministry (SEP) ordered all so-called “military schools” shuttered by Aug. 31.

Furthermore, Education Minister Mario Delgado said such schools must immediately reimburse payments made for outstanding educational services, such as re-enrollment fees, school supplies and uniforms.

President Claudia Sheinbaum praised Delgado’s decision, while lamenting the 13-year-old girl’s death. “What happened in Tamaulipas is very sad,” she said. “Abuses occurring under the pretext of discipline cannot be allowed.”

The SEP resolution comes after the July 16 death of Dafne Zapata, who died during a summer camp at Marina Doenitz Military Academy in the state of Tamaulipas.

Dafne’s death prompted immediate demands for justice from family and friends, eventually leading to the arrest of three alleged perpetrators.

That day, Dafne’s mother was informed that her daughter was suffering from a cough and dehydration, only to be told minutes later that she had died.

An autopsy refuted the academy’s conflicting claims about Dafne’s death — sudden circulatory failure and accidental death were cited — indicating that she died from drowning.

Medical examiners also found bruises and signs of recent physical abuse, prompting the authorities to rule out natural causes and classify the case as femicide.

Soon thereafter, prosecutors arrested Jorge Luis Ponce Ortega, the school’s director, Estrellita Mora Díaz, a supervisor, and 18-year-old Danna Yanina, a teaching assistant.

Former students of the academy criticized the arrest of Yanina, staging a protest while proclaiming that she was another victim who was forced to carry out “disciplinary measures.”

The SEP has ordered a comprehensive review of all 31 military-style academies in the country, with Delgado saying, “There can be no true educational transformation if expressions of violence are permitted.”

The edict requires all 32 state education ministries to thoroughly review the authorizations, permits and Official Recognition of Studies they’ve granted and shutter all military-style schools and institutions.

Additionally, Delgado instructed local education authorities to order the immediate delivery of school documentation to students affected by this measure, including full or partial certificates of studies to guarantee the continuity of their education and to facilitate their incorporation into other educational institutions.

Dafne’s mother, Alejandra Quintos, this week proposed legislation to address security and safety issues at military-style institutions. The so-called Dafne Law would establish controls, security protocols and oversight mechanisms for military academies, summer camps and other such organizations, whether public or private.

With reports from El País, El Economista, La Jornada and Animal Político

World.title: Cookie craze hits CDMX: Crumbl opens first Mexico location
World.content:
The viral global cookie phenomenon known as Crumbl has arrived in Mexico.

Famous for its large gourmet cookies, weekly rotating menu and signature pink boxes, the U.S. bakery chain opened a store in the chic Mexico City neighborhood of Roma Norte on Tuesday.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Crumbl Mexico (@crumbl.mx)

It did not go unnoticed.

El Universal newspaper described Tuesday’s opening day as a “frenzy,” reporting that dozens of people arrived early in hopes of “being among the first to try the famous viral cookies” and “a line of approximately 800 people snaked around the block.”

The event attracted content creators and influencers to the shop at Calle Durango 225. They busily documented the atmosphere and shared images of the event on various digital platforms.

Crumbl’s approach breaks with traditional baking. Its menu isn’t fixed; it has over 270 recipes in its catalogue, but offers 3 or 4 new flavors each week.

The brand — founded in Logan, Utah, in 2017 — produces weekly Sunday night flavor reveals across platforms such as TikTok and Instagram to drive hype. The strategy has attracted long customer lines at its outlets in the U.S., Canada and Puerto Rico.

The limited edition cookies available in Mexico City through Saturday — the shop is closed on Sundays — are Tres Leches Cake, Confetti Cake and a S’mores Cookie.

Crumbl typically offers several other items on a Classic Cookies list. This week, there were four on the menu: Cookies and Cream, Pink Sugar, Milk Chocolate Chip Cookie and Chocolate Chip Cookie Thins.

The cookies come with a hefty price tag, however: One cookie costs 89 pesos; a pack of 4 costs 315 pesos; a pack of 6 costs 450 pesos; a package of 12 costs 885 pesos; and a monthly subscription (5 cookies shipped to your house) is available for 990 pesos.

Award-winning fast-casual restaurant enjoys solid first two months in Yucatán

Though not matching the ballyhoo produced by the Crumbl opening, Dog Haus opened its first restaurant in Mérida in June, its first permanent international restaurant.

The fast-casual gourmet restaurant — also known as Dog Haus Biergarten — is a hot dog, sausage and burger chain headquartered in Pasadena, California. It is known for its use of Black Angus beef and King’s Hawaiian rolls, earning recognition as a Menu Trendsetter by Nation’s Restaurant News.

The Mérida location is the first of three Dog Haus locations planned for Mexico in 2026, with openings planned for Mexico City and Tijuana.

With reports from El Universal, Animal Gourmet, Food and Travel México and Expansión

World.title: Opinion: Is China Claudia Sheinbaum’s surveillance model for Mexico?
World.content:
Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, elected in 2024 with nearly 60% of the vote, has continued many of her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s policies while placing emphasis on clean energy, public-private investment, and aggressive mass digitalization. Her flagship Llave MX platform, run by the new Digital Transformation and Telecoms Agency, aims to unify citizen data for easier access to government services and health records.

Central to this effort is República Sana (Healthy Nation) program, which seeks to integrate Mexico’s major public health institutions and advance toward universal healthcare. Enrollment will require a biometric digital identity card under the Unique Population Registry Code (CURP) system, including photos, fingerprints and possibly iris scans, with ambitious goals for broad coverage by 2030. The president argues that centralized biometrics will reduce bureaucracy and petty corruption.

However, critics such as R3D (Digital Rights Defense Network) caution that linking every government transaction, tax payment, medical visit and benefit to a single biometric identity could enable greater surveillance and data vulnerabilities. In a country where roughly 55% of the workforce operates in the informal economy, the system could also help formalize tax collections but at the potential cost of privacy and potential misuse.

The China precedent

China provides a clear cautionary reference point. By combining centralized digital identities with extensive surveillance cameras, it has developed tools for tracking, behavioral scoring and social control. Although Sheinbaum has pledged that her government will not spy on citizens, the infrastructure being built in Mexico — centralized databases tied to biometrics — has prompted concerns about possible function creep and future authoritarian risks.

The Chinese system developed gradually. It began with a national ID program in the 1980s, expanded to biometric collection in the 2000s, and was later integrated with facial recognition, financial records and other data. In Xinjiang, advanced tracking tools have been used for ethnic targeting. The broader lesson is that systems initially justified for efficiency and public safety can, in combination, expand in unintended ways. Mexico is unlikely to replicate China’s model, but the architecture merits careful scrutiny. Biometric collection is also mandatory for non-citizens at U.S. borders but widely applied on a “voluntary” basis for U.S. citizens, also raising serious concerns of potential function creep.

The surveillance infrastructure

Mexico’s digital agenda already connects with a large camera network. As mayor of Mexico City from 2018 to 2023, Sheinbaum expanded the city’s cameras significantly. Under current Mayor Clara Brugada, the Ojos que te cuidan (Eyes that protect you) program has added another 30,400 high-resolution units, bringing the total above 113,000 — the largest urban video surveillance system in the Americas, with plans to have 150,000 installed by 2030.

When combined with Llave MX’s national biometric registry and the Central Intelligence Platform, this network could support automated facial recognition and real-time tracking. Anthropologist Esteban Salmón’s research points to practical downsides in Mexico City, including false positives, issues with evidence handling and over-reliance on video in some prosecutions.

Similar systems elsewhere have shown higher error rates for darker-skinned individuals and women in facial recognition. In Mexico, this could disproportionately affect Indigenous and mestizo populations. Without strong safeguards, such tools risk unintended consequences for justice and civil liberties.

Oversight, security reforms, and implementation challenges

These issues are compounded by changes to independent institutions. The Sheinbaum administration has moved regulatory authority over telecommunications under the executive following the abolition of the independent Federal Telecommunications Institute.

In June and July 2025, the government passed the Investigation and Intelligence Law and the National Public Security System Law. These measures grant the Ministry of Security and Citizen Protection (SSPC) and the military-controlled National Guard broader access to biometric, telephone, vehicle, tax and property records. The new Central Intelligence Platform aims to interconnect these databases across government levels to help prevent and investigate violent crimes.

Critics including R3D and Article 19 have expressed concerns about limited judicial oversight and further militarization of security functions. This builds on earlier debates, including the Supreme Court’s 2021-2022 decision striking down a biometric phone registry on privacy grounds. Mexico’s history of data breaches also highlights risks associated with greater centralization.

Significant implementation challenges remain. Large segments of the rural population and many elderly Mexicans face barriers related to Internet access, devices and digital literacy. Without adequate support, digitalization efforts risk creating new forms of exclusion.

Mexico’s big tech and digital push

The Mexican government’s digital push has fostered significant relationships with global technology companies such as Nvidia, Microsoft, Palantir, and others for investments in data centers, AI infrastructure, manufacturing partnerships and talent development. Although there is no confirmed contract between the Sheinbaum administration and Palantir for core intelligence or biometric systems, the U.S. firm recently expanded its presence in Mexico through a major deal with GNP Seguros, the country’s largest insurer. Palantir’s Foundry and Artificial Intelligence Platforms are being used for fraud detection, risk monitoring and data integration.

Because these platforms also excel at mass surveillance, profiling and other operations with human rights implications, the company’s aggressive expansion in Latin America has raised questions about how private-sector AI tools could eventually feed into government surveillance architectures. The Sheinbaum administration also has agreements with Google, Meta and TikTok ostensibly focused on combating digital violence, but critics worry that broad partnerships with global tech giants could accelerate the centralization of citizen data.

What can be done

The system is still under development, which offers an important window for civil society to shape its direction. Mexico’s Supreme Court has previously pushed back against biometric overreach. That precedent, along with input from organizations like R3D and Article 19, can help strengthen oversight of the new Central Intelligence Platform. International standards from the Inter-American Court of Human Rights and the IACHR offer additional leverage. Immediate attention should focus on implementing regulations for the Investigation and Intelligence Law. Concerned legislators and privacy advocates can seek provisions for judicial oversight, data minimization, independent audits and penalties for misuse.

Broader engagement is also important. Trade unions, Indigenous communities, digital rights groups and others can advocate for greater transparency around Llave MX and the República Sana program, including independent oversight mechanisms particularly in relation to arrangements with global AI powerhouses.

Sheinbaum’s digital agenda is ambitious and officially presented as a way to improve efficiency, reduce corruption and expand access to services. At the same time, it assembles key elements of centralized data systems: biometric identities, integrated intelligence platforms, extensive camera networks and shifts in regulatory oversight. Its long-term character will depend on whether robust transparency safeguards, independent review and legal protections are incorporated from the outset. Getting the balance right between security, efficiency and rights will be essential — not just for Mexico, but for the broader struggle against digital authoritarianism in Latin America.

This article was written by It was originally published by Foreign Policy in Focus.

World.title: Mexican soccer officials break ranks with US and Canada by not rejecting FIFA’s World Cup privatization plan
World.content:
The Mexican Football Federation (FMF) is breaking ranks with its fellow soccer federations in the United States and Canada by refusing — for now — to reject FIFA’s plan to bring private investors into the World Cup’s commercial rights.

While the plan being pushed by FIFA President Gianni Infantino has drawn ire worldwide, the FMF said on social media it is undertaking a “process of study and analysis to make the decision that best suits the development of Mexican soccer,” without endorsing Concacaf’s swift rejection.

VIDEO | ⚽️ Infantino asegura que la creación de la filial comercial (FFE) es “una oportunidad para crecer” que podría elevar hasta 40M$ la ayuda a cada federación. pic.twitter.com/f7fLnCt91N — EFE Deportes (@EFEdeportes) July 30, 2026

Concacaf, the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football, held an urgent meeting this week in which the presidents of its 41 member associations “rejected the proposal” and voiced “deep concerns” about “the lack of due process” and an “artificially short deadline.”

Concacaf includes Mexico, the U.S. and Canada, the co-hosts of the recently completed 2026 FIFA World Cup. The rejection of the proposal was supported by the U.S. and Canada.

The regional confederation questioned why private equity is needed after “the most profitable FIFA World Cup in history” and pointed to FIFA’s “billions of dollars in reserves and no debt.”

The project Infantino is promoting calls for the creation of FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a commercial subsidiary that would run events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup and sell minority, non‑controlling stakes to outside investors on a $20 billion valuation.

FIFA says FFE would raise up to $4.2 billion by working with J.P. Morgan and long‑term investors including Thrive Capital, an investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, brother of President Donald Trump’s son‑in‑law Jared Kushner.

The 211 member federations are being offered a one‑time $20 million payment plus a jump in regular FIFA Forward development funding from $8 million to $20 million for the 2027‑30 cycle, with further increases later.

FIFA says the additional money would support infrastructure, coaching, national teams, competitions, and women’s and grassroots soccer.

In a clarification posted on X, FIFA said “nobody is selling football” and argued that FFE would remain fully owned and controlled by FIFA, with governance and the global match calendar unchanged.

The backlash has been swift. The 55 member associations of the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) voted unanimously to boycott the World Cup and all FIFA competitions if the project goes ahead.

UEFA said football “is not FIFA’s to sell” and warned that “the soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially.”

In its vote Thursday, Concacaf cited the absence of any review by FIFA’s own governance bodies, but stopped short of threatening a boycott.

It tasked its FIFA Council members with pushing FIFA to tap existing reserves instead and to run any future plan through proper procedures under the FIFA statutes.

FIFA has promised to open working groups so federations can review more details before a Sept. 19 deadline, leaving Mexico to weigh whether to join with its confederation’s stance or support the proposal.

On Friday, the story took some more turns. Infantino’s senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned, saying “I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup” and calling the $20 billion commercial subsidiary “a bad deal for soccer.”

In a separate statement, FIFA chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff had been “deceived” by Infantino’s lack of openness and argued the plan is “the project of one person” that “must not go ahead.”

With reports from Mediotiempo, ESPN Deportes, TUDN, Proceso and Associated Press

World.title: Harry Styles concerts will boost Mexico City’s economy by 2 billion pesos
World.content:
Six Mexico City shows by pop mega-star Harry Styles, starting Friday and running through August 10, will inject more than 2 billion pesos (US $120 million) into the economy, according to the local chapter of the National Chamber of Commerce (Canaco CDMX).

Canaco says ticket sales will account for more than 80% of the economic windfall, with the rest coming from lodging, food, transportation and other services.

According to Canaco, the hospitality industry is expected to be among the main beneficiaries, with revenue from lodging projected to exceed 299.7 million pesos (US $17.2 million), as visitors arrive from across Mexico and abroad.

The food service sector is also expected to get a significant boost, with spending at restaurants, cafés and other establishments near the venue projected at 156 million pesos (US $9.0 million).

Ticketmaster Mexico estimates that around 60% of attendees at the GNP Stadium will travel to Mexico City for the shows, staying an average of two to three nights. The influx will significantly move the economic performance needle of the capital’s tourism sector and related industries.

Head of Canaco CDMX Vicente Gutiérrez Camposeco confirmed the figures in a statement, adding that the benefits from an event like the Styles concerts extend beyond the entertainment industry.

“It’s not just the event organizers who benefit,” he said. “Hotels, restaurants, shops, tourism services, transportation, ride-hailing platforms, travel agencies, suppliers, and thousands of small and medium-sized businesses that participate directly or indirectly in serving visitors also benefit.”

Mexico City is one of seven cities worldwide chosen by Styles to host a 2026 residency, and the one with the most concerts in the region, concert promoter Ocesa said. The soft rocker and One Direction graduate’s six GNP Stadium dates are likely to attract more than 400,000 fans.

Some 60% of them will be women, while 35% will be under 25 years old, according to Ocesa.

The Styles concert phenomenon reinforces Mexico City’s position as one of Latin America’s leading entertainment tourism destinations, providing not just culture and entertainment, but also, as Ocesa puts it, “acting as engines for economic development, job creation, tourism promotion, and the strengthening of the cultural industry.”

With reports from EFE and Excélsior

World.title: Costa Rica Immigration Outage Hits San Jose Airport a Second Time
World.content:
If you are flying out of San José today, leave for the airport far earlier than you normally would. A failure in the judicial branch computer systems that immigration officers depend on has forced the San Jose Airport into manual passport processing, and the backlog has already cost travelers their flights.

The Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería confirmed on Saturday afternoon that the disruption forced the outright cancellation of one flight. A further 36 passengers missed a JetBlue departure. The problem was first reported around midday and worsened as the afternoon went on, with long lines forming inside the terminal while officers fell back on the physical entry and exit card protocol.

In case you are wondering, here is why that slows everything down. When you pass through immigration on your way in or out of Costa Rica, the officer does not simply stamp your passport. Your details are run against databases held by the Poder Judicial, which flag court-ordered travel bans, alerts, and cases where a child cannot legally leave without authorization. Those checks cannot be waived, so when the electronic link fails, officers have to do the same work by hand on paper. A process that normally takes seconds per passenger stretches into minutes, and the queue backs up fast.

The Poder Judicial press office said scheduled maintenance on its internet links is underway and is causing internal disruption that is spilling over into immigration service. It added that its own servers and the links Migración draws on have been reviewed and are functioning normally, and that technical staff from its information technology division are working alongside Migración technicians to pin down exactly where the failure lies.

This is the second time in under a month that the same dependency has broken down. A similar outage on July 12 produced long lines at the airport after the immigration query system supplied by the judiciary went down. Migración has formally raised its concern with the Poder Judicial over the repeated interruptions, warning that the failures are affecting the movement of people through Juan Santamaría and other entry and exit points.

If you have a flight this weekend, plan for a slower airport than usual. Four hours ahead of an international departure is a reasonable target while manual processing continues, rather than the usual three. Check your flight status directly with your airline before you leave, and again once you arrive, because a delay at the immigration counter can hold a departure even when the aircraft itself is ready. Have your passport and any residency or entry documents out and open before you reach the counter, since anything that adds a second look adds time for everyone behind you.

Getting to the terminal is its own problem today. The annual Romería pilgrimage to Cartago is at its peak, with road closures in place and heavy traffic across the Central Valley, so the drive to Alajuela may take considerably longer than your map application suggests. Build that into your timing rather than assuming the delay begins at the terminal door.

If you do miss a flight because of the queues, speak to your airline at the counter rather than waiting to sort it out later. Rebooking options thin out quickly on a Saturday in high season, and passengers already at the desk tend to be handled first.

Two failures of the same system in three weeks raise a question that goes beyond one bad afternoon at the airport. Border processing at our busiest airport currently depends on an information technology link maintained by a separate branch of government, and when that link fails there is no electronic fallback, only paper. Until that changes, any traveler passing through San Jose is exposed to the same risk, and the cost lands on people holding boarding passes.

World.title: Chris Hemsworth Shares Terrifying Costa Rica Flight
World.content:
Chris Hemsworth has shared frightening footage from a small-plane flight during his family vacation in Costa Rica, showing lightning flashing outside the aircraft as heavy turbulence shakes the cabin. The sequence appears in a five-minute video posted on the Australian actor’s YouTube channel. Hemsworth films the cockpit and dark storm clouds before several large flashes illuminate the sky around the aircraft.

He then turns the camera toward himself with a visibly alarmed expression. Text added to the video describes the experience as a “life-threatening plane ride,” while Hemsworth called it a “crazy plane ride through the lightning” in the video description. The aircraft landed safely, and no injuries were reported. Hemsworth did not identify the airline, flight operator, route or type of aircraft involved.

The footage also does not make clear whether his wife, Spanish actress Elsa Pataky, or their three children were aboard during the stormy flight. They appear throughout the rest of the vacation video. Hemsworth and his family spent much of their Costa Rica visit surfing, fishing, riding ATVs, climbing rocks, jumping from cliffs and exploring waterfalls. The actor described the vacation as one of the best trips the family had taken together.

The family was spotted in early July around Santa Teresa and Montezuma on the Nicoya Peninsula.. Hemsworth was photographed surfing, exercising with a Costa Rican trainer and posing with fans during the trip. The frightening flight footage has drawn particular attention because Hemsworth is best known for playing Thor, Marvel’s god of thunder. Several viewers joked that the actor appeared far less comfortable around real lightning than his superhero character.

Although several reports have described the aircraft as being struck by lightning, the publicly available footage only clearly shows flashes around the plane. It does not establish whether lightning directly hit the aircraft. The flight also appears to have been a domestic trip within Costa Rica rather than the family’s international journey into the country.

The remainder of the video returns to the family’s outdoor adventures, including deep-sea fishing, surfing and waterfall visits. Hemsworth ends the video on a considerably calmer note, describing Costa Rica as the setting for one of the family’s most memorable vacations.

World.title: Whale Watching Season Returns to Costa Rica’s Golfo Dulce
World.content:
Humpback whales are back in Costa Rica’s South Pacific, and if you want to see them, the next four months are your window. Whales from the Southern Hemisphere reach Costa Rican waters between July and November, arriving to breed and to give birth in some of the calmest, warmest water they will find anywhere on their route north. Golfo Dulce, the sheltered gulf tucked between the Osa Peninsula and the mainland, is where many of them end up.

Costa Rica is unusual in that it gets two separate humpback populations in the same calendar year. The southern whales come between July and November. Northern Hemisphere whales, traveling down from Alaska and the west coast of North America, arrive between December and March. Almost nowhere else on the planet hosts both, which is why Costa Rica is often described as having the longest humpback season in the world. For a visitor, that means you are far less locked into a single narrow travel window than you would be in most whale destinations.

Golfo Dulce became the first Whale Heritage Area in Latin America in 2023, a designation given to places where whale watching is run responsibly and where local communities are actively involved in protecting the animals. The gulf covers roughly 750 square kilometers (about 290 square miles) and is one of only four tropical fjords in the world. Its depth, its calm surface, and the freshwater and nutrients flowing in from surrounding rivers create protected conditions where mothers can rest and nurse their calves without fighting open-ocean swell. That is the whole reason the whales choose it, and it is also why sightings here tend to be closer to shore and less punishing on the stomach than offshore trips elsewhere.

More than 30 cetacean species have been recorded in Costa Rican waters, and seven turn up regularly in Golfo Dulce. Alongside humpbacks, you can expect bottlenose dolphins, pantropical spotted dolphins and false killer whales, with orcas and Bryde’s whales appearing occasionally. The gulf also supports one of the most significant resident bottlenose dolphin populations in the Eastern Tropical Pacific, which means dolphins are around year-round even outside whale season. Researchers use the same resident groups to track long-term health of the gulf, so a tour here is often feeding into ongoing science whether you notice it or not.

Before you book, it helps to know the rules your captain is working under, because they shape what the trip will actually look like. Boats have to stay at least 100 meters (about 330 feet) from whales and 50 meters (about 165 feet) from dolphins. Any single encounter is capped at 30 minutes.

No more than two boats may watch the same group at once. Getting in the water with whales or dolphins is not allowed at all. Those distances exist because engine noise and crowding push mothers and calves away from resting areas and can separate a calf from its mother, which in the worst case is fatal. If a captain offers to get you closer than that, or offers a swim, you are being sold a trip that breaks the rules and stresses the animals. Walk away and find another operator. A good guide will explain the distance before you leave the dock rather than after you complain about it.

Set your expectations accordingly. You will see blows, backs, tails and, with luck, a breach, usually through binoculars or a long lens rather than from directly overhead. September and October are generally the strongest weeks of the southern season. Mornings are calmer than afternoons on the water. Bring sun protection, water and something for motion sickness if you are prone to it, and book with an operator that carries certified guides.

The season matters economically as much as ecologically. Whale watching has grown from a niche add-on into one of the anchors of sustainable tourism in the South Pacific, and it feeds hotels, restaurants, marinas, transport services and certified guides across Golfito, Osa and surrounding communities during months that would otherwise be quiet. Tour operators, community groups and business associations have spent years professionalizing the sector through training, operating protocols and public education.

“We want every whale-watching experience to be an opportunity to learn, inspire conservation and demonstrate that tourism can coexist with environmental protection,” said Ana González, general manager of Marina Bahía Golfito.

The timing lines up with a strong stretch for Costa Rican tourism generally. Costa Rica recorded 959,738 air arrivals in the first quarter of 2026, a 12.9 percent increase over the same period a year earlier and the highest first-quarter figure on record, according to the Instituto Costarricense de Turismo (ICT). Demand has skewed heavily toward nature-based travel, and the South Pacific has drawn an unusual amount of international attention this year.

If you are already heading south for the whales, the gulf pairs easily with other things. Boats leaving from Marina Bahía Golfito also run sport fishing, kayaking and birdwatching trips, and the marina connects to Piedras Blancas National Park, the Osa Peninsula and Corcovado National Park. Most visitors build two or three days around the region rather than treating the whale trip as a standalone outing.

Getting there has become easier. Golfito sits roughly six to seven hours by road from San José, and domestic flights to Golfito and Puerto Jiménez cut that to under an hour. Book flights, lodging and tours well ahead if you are traveling in September or October, when the peninsula fills up.

World.title: Pura Vida and Property: How Costa Rica’s Traditional Way of Selling Homes Is Entering the Digital Age
World.content:
When people think about buying or selling property in Costa Rica today, they often picture property portals, real estate agents, Realtors and international buyers searching online for their dream home.

But that isn’t how Costa Rica built its property market.

For generations, Costa Ricans sold property through their communities. A simple “Se Vende” sign outside the gate. A conversation with a neighbour. A recommendation from a friend. Trusted lawyers handling the legal side of the sale. It wasn’t unusual. It was simply the Costa Rican way.

As Costa Rica became one of the world’s most desirable places to live, retire and invest, the property market naturally evolved. International buyers needed guidance through an unfamiliar legal process, language and culture, and real estate agents and Realtors became an important part of helping people buy property in Costa Rica with confidence.

For many homeowners, that remains exactly the right choice.

But somewhere along the way, one long-standing Costa Rican tradition quietly lost its place.

The professional private seller.

“Living in Costa Rica changed the way I looked at property,” says Wayne Johnson, founder of Slide’N Doors.

“I’d bought and sold property before, but Costa Rica felt different. There was a real sense of community. People trusted each other. Neighbours helped neighbours. That independent spirit is part of what makes this country so special.”

Wayne says he often met homeowners who weren’t trying to avoid real estate professionals. They simply wanted another option.

“Some people genuinely enjoy showing buyers around their home. They know every room, every fruit tree, every sunset from the terrace and every reason they fell in love with the property.

They weren’t asking how to avoid commission. They were asking why choosing to sell privately meant having fewer professional ways to market one of the biggest investments of their lives.”

That simple question stayed with him. Not as a business plan, but as an idea that refused to go away.

About a year ago, he decided to stop thinking about it and start building something.

“People often think the only alternative to using a Realtor is Facebook Marketplace,” Wayne says. “Facebook is brilliant at connecting people, and it proves there’s huge demand for private property sales. But selling a home there can feel a bit like selling a luxury watch at a busy flea market. The right buyer might be there, but your property is surrounded by sofas, bicycles and children’s toys. One of the biggest financial decisions of your life deserves a platform built specifically for property.”

For Wayne, that became the mission behind Slide’N Doors.

Not to replace real estate agents, but to stand alongside them by giving homeowners another professional option.

“The choice shouldn’t be whether your property gets seen,” he says. “It should simply be about choosing the way you want to sell your home.”

As our conversation continued, Wayne explained that the inspiration behind Slide’N Doors wasn’t technology.

It was Costa Rica.

“The longer I lived here, the more I realised Pura Vida isn’t just a saying. It’s a way of thinking. It’s about community, trust, independence and people looking after one another.

As Costa Rica grows, many people naturally worry about losing some of the traditions and culture that make this country so unique.

I didn’t build Slide’N Doors to change the Costa Rican way of selling property.

I built it because I was inspired by it.

I wanted to create a modern platform that reflects those same values. A business that puts people and choice at its heart. Technology that supports communities rather than replaces them. Giving homeowners more choice while continuing to respect the important role that real estate professionals play.”

Progress doesn’t have to mean leaving tradition behind. Sometimes the best ideas are simply old Costa Rican values, given the tools to thrive in a modern world.

Every day, buyers from around the world search for Costa Rica homes for sale, investment opportunities, retirement properties and beachfront homes. Wayne believes they should be able to discover professionally presented private listings alongside properties represented by experienced Realtors, giving buyers more choice while allowing homeowners to decide how they wish to sell.

As our conversation came to an end, one final question seemed obvious.

Is Slide’N Doors trying to change the way Costa Rica sells property?

Wayne smiles.

“No.

Costa Rica has always understood the value of community, trust and doing things your own way. Those values inspired every decision we made while building Slide’N Doors.

Technology should never replace a country’s culture.

It should help preserve it.

If people see Slide’N Doors as a modern expression of the values Costa Rica has believed in all along—people first, community first and always Pura Vida—then I’ll know we’ve built something worthwhile.”

Thinking of Buying or Selling Property in Costa Rica?

Whether you’re looking to buy a home, sell your own property or invest in Costa Rican real estate, Slide’N Doors brings private sellers and real estate professionals together on one platform.

• List your property in under 10 minutes.

• Reach buyers around the world.

• Pay zero commission if you find your own buyer.

Learn more at www.slidendoors.com

World.title: What the Judicial Coup Fight in Costa Rica is Actually About
World.content:
President Fernández accused four justices of the Constitutional Chamber of staging a coup d’état on Friday and announced that the governing-party legislative bench will file a criminal complaint against them on Monday over a ruling that provisionally extended the appointments of the court’s substitute justices.

The announcement was delivered in a video recorded at Casa Presidencial, where Fernández appeared alongside Legislative Assembly president Yara Jiménez and deputies of the governing Partido Pueblo Soberano. Fernández said the Chamber’s decision to extend appointments that expired on December 16, 2025 was illegal and unconstitutional, and that the power to appoint, remove or extend the terms of justices belongs exclusively to the Legislative Assembly. She cited articles 9, 11, 121, 154, 157, 158 and 164 of the Constitution in support of that position.

Jiménez said the complaint will be filed before the Secretariat of the full Supreme Court and will allege the offense of prevaricato against justices Fernando Cruz Castro, Paul Rueda Leal, Ingrid Hess Herrera and Jorge Araya García, the four who formed the majority. The Chamber rejected the coup characterization the same day, defending the ruling as grounded in law and describing the Executive’s statements as disproportionate.

What the Constitutional Chamber ruled

The ruling, adopted Thursday by a vote of four to three, resolved an appeal brought by a private citizen who argued that his cases had stalled because sitting justices had recused themselves and the court could not be properly constituted without substitutes to replace them.

The Chamber provisionally extended the appointments of the substitute justices whose terms ended last December and held that the extension remains in force until deputies elect replacements. It voided the Legislative Assembly’s agreement returning the candidate list to the Supreme Court and ordered Jiménez to bring the matter to a vote using the existing list of 18 candidates, from which at least nine substitutes must be chosen. The Supreme Court had sent that list to the Assembly, and the governing bench had returned it twice without voting.

Voting with the majority were Cruz, Rueda, Araya and Hess. Justices Fernando Castillo, Luis Fernando Salazar and Anamari Garro dissented and would have rejected the appeal.

What a substitute justice does

The Constitutional Chamber, known here more commonly as Sala IV, is made up of seven sitting justices. Substitute justices are elected by the Legislative Assembly to step in when a sitting justice is absent, disqualified or recused from a particular case. Recusal is routine rather than exceptional, and it occurs whenever a justice has a prior connection to a matter that would compromise impartiality.

Without a pool of substitutes, a case in which one or more sitting justices have recused themselves cannot be assigned a full bench, and it simply waits. That is the mechanical problem the ruling addresses. At the time of the decision, 123 case files were reported to be stalled for that reason, including claims involving pensions and access to health care. The Chamber described the extension as a transitional measure adopted to prevent the court from seizing up entirely.

What Prevaricato means under Costa Rican law

Prevaricato is an offense in the Costa Rican Penal Code that applies to judicial and administrative officials who issue rulings contrary to the law, or who base rulings on facts they know to be false. It is not a charge of simple legal error. It turns on knowledge and intent, which is what makes it both a serious accusation against a judge and a difficult one to prove.

The government’s filing takes the form of a querella rather than a denuncia. A denuncia routes an accusation through the Public Ministry, which decides whether to pursue it. A querella is a private criminal action advanced by the accusing party itself. Constitutional lawyer Marvin Carvajal noted that any official with decision-making authority can be accused of prevaricato, but said that filing an accusation does not establish that an offense occurred, and that the choice of a querella suggests the accusing side does not expect prosecutors to find a crime here.

Carvajal also said the complaint does not suspend the ruling. The order directing the Assembly to vote remains in effect while any complaint proceeds.

How the Chamber and legal scholars responded

In a written statement, the Constitutional Chamber said its decision responded exclusively to the constitutional mandate to protect citizens from the consequences of having no substitute justices available, and that its rulings are properly founded in legal norms and principles. It called the Executive’s remarks disproportionate and inconsistent with the respect that should prevail among branches of government, and said it would continue to act with firmness and independence.

Constitutional lawyer Hubert May said the ruling neither disregards nor violates the separation of powers, arguing that an invasion of powers occurs when one branch usurps the functions of another, and that the Chamber had instead ordered another branch to exercise a function it already holds. Rubén Hernández said the justices were correct to adopt an exceptional extension, describing extension as a general principle of law used to preserve continuity of service. Constitutional lawyer Manrique Jiménez also rejected the government’s characterization of the ruling.

Opposition figures backed the court. Deputy Claudia Dobles, who served as first lady between 2018 and 2022, said the Assembly is the body that has failed to meet its obligation to elect substitutes. Former president Luis Guillermo Solís described the government’s accusations as extremely serious.

What happens next

The querella is expected to be presented on Monday. Separately, the Assembly remains under the Chamber’s order to vote on substitute justices using the list of 18 candidates already in its hands, an instruction the governing bench has resisted for roughly seven months.

The confrontation continues a pattern that began under the previous administration, and it now places two branches of government in open dispute over which of them controls the composition of the highest constitutional court. How that dispute is resolved will say a good deal about where the boundary between them actually sits.

World.title: Costa Rica Pressed to Improve Conditions for Indigenous Coffee Workers
World.content:
More than 500 people and organizations, among them three former presidents of Costa Rica and Panama, have signed a public statement demanding that the Costa Rican state guarantee decent living, working and social protection conditions for the Ngäbe-Buglé workers who pick coffee each year.

The Kioscos Socioambientales program at the University of Costa Rica, which coordinated the effort, reported 512 signatures in all. They include roughly a hundred Indigenous, labor, community, feminist, coastal, environmental and social organizations from Costa Rica and Panama, along with academics, artists and professionals.

Former Costa Rican presidents Abel Pacheco de la Espriella and Laura Chinchilla Miranda signed, as did former Panamanian president Ricardo de la Espriella Toral, who governed from 1982 to 1984. Writer Ana Cristina Rossi Lara, musician Manuel Obregón López and the bands Malpaís, Sonámbulo Psicotropical and Un Rojo Reggae Band are also among the signatories.

The statement was presented publicly on July 21, roughly four months before the main harvest opens in November and while coffee regions prepare for seasonal labor arrives.

It responds to a February internal report written by Randy Ramírez Coto, acting chief of the Judicial Investigation Agency’s Los Santos Regional Unit, and addressed to the OIJ press office. Ramírez wrote that his purpose was to make visible what he described as the dehumanization of the Ngäbe-Buglé population in Los Santos, the coffee-growing region south of San José that supplies a substantial share of national production. The report linked the conditions he described to barriers in health care access, an absence of institutional follow-up and the deaths of children.

Between January 1, 2020 and February 11, 2026, the report recorded 19 deaths of Ngäbe-Buglé minors from Panama in the Los Santos area. Bronchopneumonia was the registered cause in 10 cases. The document also listed two suicides, one death during childbirth, one caused by parasitic infection and five cases awaiting forensic autopsy.

According to the report, the cases shared health-related circumstances that included births in inadequate settings, untreated respiratory illness and missing vaccinations. The document stated that all of the deaths could have been prevented, tying that assessment to the absence of timely preventive public health care, vaccination and epidemiological reporting. An initial review of child deaths across the region identified 17 cases; a subsequent review focused specifically on the Ngäbe-Buglé population raised the count to 19.

The Los Santos harvest generally runs from November through late February. The report noted that the work historically depended on Costa Rican and Nicaraguan labor, but in recent years has fallen mainly to Ngäbe-Buglé workers from Panama, many of them from Bocas del Toro, Chiriquí and Veraguas.

On housing, the report described workers being placed in temporary lodgings known locally as baches, with conditions that varied sharply. Some sit near canton centers with access to basic services. Others are in remote mountain areas among the coffee plantations, where residents depend on transport provided by farm owners. The report questioned whether those spaces are subject to regular oversight, stating that the regional unit’s inquiry found no evidence of follow-up visits during the period some of the lodgings were in operation.

The document also raised a registration gap. Costa Rica manages seasonal agricultural migration through the Migrant Labor Traceability System, known as SITLAM and administered by the Ministry of Labor and Social Security. In the deaths reviewed by the Los Santos unit, the report stated, SITLAM did not appear actively connected to the people involved, a difficulty the document placed in the context of irregular entry through mountainous sectors of the border with Panama.

The Ministry of Health has said it carries out physical and sanitary assessments of the lodgings used by coffee workers, both before and during the season, to verify sanitary requirements and habitability. On the deaths recorded by the OIJ, the ministry said the people involved had entered the country irregularly, which complicates the traceability and follow-up built into official registration and migration control mechanisms. The ministry added that irregular entry does not restrict access to health services, and that these workers retain the right to care under existing regulations and the country’s public health principles.

The Coffee Institute of Costa Rica, ICAFE, has said it takes part in working groups aimed at regularizing pickers’ migration status, promoting adequate hiring conditions and circulating information among producers and farm managers. The institute noted that enforcement of labor, migration, sanitary and housing rules falls to the competent authorities in each area, and said that everyone working in the coffee sector should do so in dignified and safe conditions consistent with Costa Rican law.

ICAFE reported that 39,608 pickers received temporary coverage through the Costa Rican Social Security Fund and a work-risk policy from the National Insurance Institute during the 2025–2026 harvest. Separately, ICAFE board president Fernando Naranjo Retana wrote in mid-July that 14,400 migrant pickers entered the country for that same season, and that the National Coffee Sustainability Fund invests between ₡600 million and ₡700 million a year — roughly $1.3 million to $1.5 million at the Central Bank reference rate — in primary health care for pickers and their families.

He also wrote that the Casas de la Alegría program, which provides childcare, meals and health monitoring for pickers’ children while their parents work, served more than 3,000 children across the country’s seven coffee regions last season. The statement asks authorities to investigate the circumstances surrounding the children’s deaths and determine institutional responsibility; to strengthen primary care, vaccination, epidemiological monitoring and maternal and child health services throughout the coffee season; and to carry out periodic, effective inspections of housing, transport, hiring and working conditions on all farms and in all lodgings used during the harvest.

It calls for full compliance with labor, sanitary, migration and social security law as it applies to migrant Indigenous workers, and for permanent coordination between public institutions, Ngäbe-Buglé organizations, host communities, coffee companies and human rights groups.

It further asks that information on health, work, housing and rights protection be published regularly, that coffee companies and every actor in the commercial chain assume responsibility for the rights of the workers who sustain the industry, and that the Labor Ministry build a permanent map of the coffee value chain — identifying principal companies, contractors and intermediaries, and geolocating their farms and lodgings — to monitor legal compliance and assign responsibility.

The organizers noted that in August 2020, more than a hundred social organizations issued a similar warning about conditions facing Ngäbe-Buglé workers during the harvest. Six years later, the statement argues, those concerns remain unresolved and their consequences have reached an unacceptable severity. Costa Rica’s General Protocol for the Attention of Labor Migration during harvest seasons was last updated in May 2024; the signatories contend that the gap lies between the rules on paper and their application on the ground.

The document was presented by Kioscos Socioambientales together with the Environmental Human Rights Clinic of the Institute of Latin American Studies at the National University, the Center for Research in Culture and Development at the State Distance University, and the Labor Relations Observatory at the University of Costa Rica’s law school. Speakers included Zeidy Brukwä Rodríguez, a Ngäbe-Buglé leader and member of the National Front of Indigenous Peoples; Rosibel Víquez Abarca of the State Distance University; Sharon López Céspedes of the National University; and Mauricio Álvarez Mora of the University of Costa Rica.

Days before the statement was released, the health ministries of Costa Rica and Panama signed a memorandum of understanding creating a Binational Health Card for Ngäbe-Buglé workers who move between the two countries for temporary agricultural work. Costa Rican Health Minister Alexander Sánchez Cabo and his Panamanian counterpart, Fernando Boyd Galindo, signed the agreement in San José in the presence of First Vice President Douglas Soto.

The physical card will be issued each July and remain valid for six months, a window that matches the period of heaviest cross-border movement. Panama’s health ministry designated the Bugaba intermediate care post in Chiriquí as the main issuing and renewal point. Boyd Galindo said the card would carry vaccination histories and other clinical information, and would help stop children from receiving repeat immunizations because their records were unavailable.

The Ministry of Labor and Social Security declined to say what action it had taken on the matter, indicating that it would not comment because the OIJ report is an internal document. The ministry has changed hands twice in recent weeks: Roy Thompson Chacón resigned on June 30, and President Laura Fernández Delgado named attorney Mercedes Flores Badilla as minister on July 20.

The harvest that prompted the statement begins in November. Whether the inspections, health coverage and registration the signatories are demanding will be in place by then is the question now sitting with the institutions named in the document.

World.title: High Court affirms Firearms and Ammunition Control Board’s regulatory authority; Dismisses claim of being political biased and discriminatory
World.content:
High Court affirms Firearms and Ammunition Control Board’s regulatory authority; Dismisses claim of being political biased and discriminatory

By Jose Luis Cruz: Belmopan, Belize: The High Court of Belize issued a landmark judgment in late July, 2026, reaffirming the statutory authority of the Firearms and Ammunition Control Board (FACB) in the administration and regulation of firearms licensing under the Firearms Act.

The decision arose from judicial review proceedings brought by Abner Murillo and Lock N Loaded Guns and Ammunition Belmopan Limited against the FACB and the Attorney General, in Claim No. 823 of 2024, challenging several licensing decisions and administrative actions taken by the Board.

In its judgment, the Court upheld the FACB’s authority to administer the Firearms Act following the legislative transfer of licensing powers from the Commissioner of Police to the Board. The Court confirmed that licences issued after that statutory transfer by the Commissioner of Police were legally invalid because the authority to issue such licences had already been vested in the FACB.

The Court also dismissed allegations that the FACB acted with political bias or discriminated against the claimants. Applying the legal test for apparent bias, the Court found there was no evidence that the Board’s decisions were influenced by the Minister of Home Affairs or any improper consideration. Similarly, the constitutional claim alleging unequal treatment under section 6(1) of the Constitution was rejected.

In recognizing the nature of firearms regulation, the Court emphasized that the licensing of firearms, firearms dealers, instructors, and shooting ranges involves significant public safety considerations. The judgment acknowledged that the FACB is entitled to carefully scrutinize applications, verify supporting documentation, and ensure compliance with statutory requirements before granting licences.

While the Court made limited findings on certain procedural aspects of the Board’s administration, it largely upheld the FACB’s statutory mandate and dismissed the principal claims challenging the Board’s independence and regulatory authority. The Court awarded the claimants nominal constitutional damages of BZ$5,000 each, reflecting the limited nature of the findings, while declining to grant the broader constitutional relief sought.

The decision represents an important precedent for firearms regulation in Belize. By confirming the FACB’s legal authority, rejecting allegations of bias and unequal treatment, and recognizing the Board’s responsibility to regulate firearms in the interest of public safety, the High Court has reinforced the FACB’s role as Belize’s independent firearms licensing authority.

Former inaugural Chair of the Firearms and Ammunition Control Board and former CEO of the Ministry of Home Affairs, Sharole Carr-Saldivar, welcomed the Court’s decision, describing it as an important affirmation of the Board’s statutory role. “When the Firearms and Ammunition Control Board was established, it began with no dedicated staff or institutional infrastructure. Every policy, procedure, and licensing framework had to be developed while simultaneously assuming responsibility for a completely new regulatory regime. The Court’s decision confirms that the Board acted within its legal mandate on the principal issues before it and reinforces the importance of maintaining an independent firearms regulator committed to public safety.”

World.title: Horse found dead in Lord’s Bank as resident alleges ongoing animal cruelty
World.content:
Horse found dead in Lord’s Bank as resident alleges ongoing animal cruelty

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Warning: images accompanying this story may be disturbing to some readers.

A resident of Lord’s Bank Village is calling for action after a horse was found dead in the BDF housing area along Nim Li Punit Street, in what the resident alleges is part of a troubling pattern of animal abuse in the community.

According to the resident, who contacted Breaking Belize News on Saturday morning, young men in the area have been taking people’s horses and abusing them. The resident alleges the animal found dead was mistreated until it died overnight, and photographs shared with this newsroom show the horse lying in a grassy area with severe visible injuries.

The allegations have not been independently verified, no official cause of death has been determined, and no individuals have been identified in connection with the animal’s death.

Cruelty to animals is an offence under Belizean law, and the death of a working animal is also a real economic loss for families who depend on horses for transport and labour. The circumstances described, if accurate, would warrant investigation by police and the Belize Agricultural Health Authority, which also has a role where carcass disposal raises public health concerns for nearby residents.

Anyone with information about this incident is asked to contact the nearest police station. Information can also be shared confidentially with Breaking Belize News and will be passed to the relevant authorities.

World.title: International News: El Salvador has new direct flight to Madrid, Spain
World.content:
International News: El Salvador has new direct flight to Madrid, Spain

By Zoila Palma: Today, President of El Salvador Nayib Bukele participated in the signing of the agreement formalizing Air Europa’s integration into the country’s connectivity network.

Air Europa added a new direct route between San Salvador and Madrid that will begin this December.

“This agreement is a commitment to further positioning El Salvador on the world stage, bringing us closer to Europe and opening the doors to more airlines, more visitors, and more investment,” a statement from the Government of El Salvador said.

The flights will be operated with Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner aircraft, offering greater efficiency and an experience aligned with the airline’s international standards.

Air Europa has been operating since 1986 and flies to more than 55 destinations worldwide.

World.title: “We are still mental slaves and true emancipation remains elusive” – Are we equally to blame?
World.content:
“We are still mental slaves and true emancipation remains elusive” – Are we equally to blame?

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Hugh O’Brien, San Ignacio, Cayo: Being the son of a wise black man, being married to a black woman, having black children, living amongst and interacting with black people, organizing, coaching and playing football at various levels, including semi-pro, with my black brothers, teaching black brothers and sisters at the Belize College of Agriculture and then Galen University, watching my black brothers hate on each other, seeing how we are full of envy especially against our own family, against our black neighbours, and watching our black brothers killing each other over red and blue colors, petty grievances, drugs, turf, etc., I have come to realize that a large majority of my BLACK PEOPLE ARE STILL MENTAL SLAVES…AND TRUE EMANCIPATION REMAINS ELUSIVE TO MOST OF US.

My father, George O’Brien, was a smart black man who married a wise Mestizo woman, named Romelia O’Brien nee Cruz. Together they raised seven (7) well educated, successful, independent and loving children. We are a close knit, loving family. My dad was very emancipated mentally but not fully emancipated. He transmitted the ethics of seeking peace, hard work and education to all of us, he believed in his capabilities and transmitted much of these to his children. However, he had two flaws he tried to transmit to me, which I never accepted. I can write a whole article about my dad, his experiences, what a great school teacher he was, and all the attributes he had, but today, I want to focus on the two flaws as they are crucial elements for the focus of this article.

One of the flaws my dad tried to transmit was to discourage me from studying agriculture as he wanted me to be a professional, an educated person who works for someone, a doctor or a lawyer or like profession. He said agriculture is hard work, and is not for the black man. This mentality prevails amongst most of us black people. Because our forefathers were slaves and were forced to work in the fields, we do not want to work the land. Even when we inherit land, the first thing that comes to most of our minds is to sell it. We have lost our connection to the land, and to some extent we also do not value hard work as the foundation for success. We will go as far as to say “Nobody wa work me like wa slave” to show how much we associate hard work with slavery.

The second flaw was to encourage me to marry someone that is fairer than me, in order to improve the color of my skin, he said, and to better the chances for my children’s success. My dad had essentially resigned himself to the idea that being black, you cannot succeed, or will have a hard time succeeding in Belize. I did not follow his advice and I married black, l love black, empowered my black children and will help to do the same to my grandchildren. I will not turn back on believing that black is beautiful, powerful and talented. Am saying all this, even though am fully aware that a large percent of my black brothers and sisters in Belize are still mental slaves, avoid farming and hard work, prefer the easy “Big Chill” life while other cultures around us are advancing.

Four hundred years ago, we ‘blacks’ lived as tribes in Africa, capturing our brothers from other tribes, and we sold them as slaves to the British and the French as their ships sailed by. The British put us in chains and shipped us across the Atlantic to the Caribbean and Belize where we were placed in the bondage of slavery. While we cast all the blame on the Europeans for our past as slaves and labeling us as ‘Chattels’, our black tribe forefathers are equally to blame as we sold our captured black brothers from other tribes as cheap ‘Chattels’.

Less than 200 years ago, we ‘blacks’ were still slaves in British Honduras working in mahogany and logwood camps, and we and our children were owned by white slave masters from a foreign land.

The history of our slavery and colonialism, have affected us significantly, and in a negative way. But should we continue to focus on the evils of the past, the enslavement of our forefathers and the slavery abuse of us blacks by our white slave masters?

It is my view that we must reflect on our slavery past to understand why we are where we are, but we must take responsibility for our future from now on. Rather than continue to blame and hate the white man, we need to accept that our black forefathers who captured us and sold us into slavery are to blame or are responsible as well. We need to move next to FORGIVENESS – forgive both the white man and our black forefathers for the evils of the past and focus more on the opportunities that emancipation, freedom and the future can offer. We must be like the Jews and the Israelites, who have the mentality that because they were enslaved in the biblical days, that they must never be slaves again. That because they were subjected to mass persecution and genocide during World War 2, that they must try to rule instead of be ruled. Their focus is to be their brothers keepers and protect their ‘peoples’ anywhere they are, to be progressive wherever they live, and to be rulers of the world in business and in politics.

In Belize, our black and ‘Kriol’ population appears to be the most challenged, and is the group that is not making full use of the opportunities around us. The state of affairs, particularly the mental state, of our black population can change. We all know too well that the leaders of the UDP or the PUP, whether Black, Arab or Spanish are not the solution…in fact, they have become part of the problem. In their own selfish or ‘unaware’ ways these leaders continue to promote dependency, political tribalism and deep down are content that we are a poor, dependent people, one that they can easily buy with some groceries and a few dollars.

Based on the scenario presented above, are we truly emancipated? Are we not still mental slaves? And is it not true emancipation remains elusive to most of us?

And to end on a positive note, do we want to remain where we are? If not, we gotta start thinking like the Jews and the Israelites. We gotta get rid of the ‘crab mentality’ and be more united and work together like the Mennonites.

I will follow up this article later today with some ideas on how to help get us out of mental slavery. It is time to talk about where we will go and how we can get there. In order to move forward, we have to develop the right mindset to overcome mental slavery and get rid of the dependency syndrome.

If we start to follow this plan as individuals, as families, as communities and as a people in general, the state of affairs for ‘black’ people in Belize will move towards positivity, growth and development, and from within the ranks of those who have changed will emerge real leaders…who will assist in breaking us out of the chains of mental slavery and pave the way towards true emancipation.

World.title: Beloved health advocate Milagro Garel in critical condition following stroke
World.content:
Beloved health advocate Milagro Garel in critical condition following stroke

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): For twenty years, Milagro Garel has been the person Belizean families turned to when a sick child needed care beyond our borders. Today, she is the one who needs help reaching it.

Garel, Country Director for World Pediatrics in Belize, suffered a stroke on July 28 caused by a ruptured brain aneurysm. Because the specialized neurosurgical care she urgently requires is not available in Belize, she was transported to Guatemala, where she remains in critical condition.

The news comes barely a week after World Pediatrics celebrated her extraordinary 20 years of service as Country Director, honoring the countless children and families whose lives she has touched. In its message sharing news of her condition, the organization wrote that Garel “has spent decades moving mountains to help children access lifesaving care,” and that it is now standing with its beloved colleague as she faces an unimaginable medical crisis.

Her family and friends have created a GoFundMe campaign, titled Support Milagro Garel’s Emergency Medical Care, to help cover her transportation, surgery, intensive care and hospitalization. World Pediatrics notes that the fundraiser is independently organized by Garel’s family and friends, and that the organization is sharing it in support but is not involved in collecting or managing donations.

Members of the public who wish to contribute can find the campaign on GoFundMe under her name, and are encouraged to donate, share, and keep Milagro and her family in their thoughts.

Few Belizeans have done more, more quietly, for the country’s sick children. Now the country has a chance to return the kindness.
