World.title: International News: Universities in U.S. developing programs aimed at preparing “Influencers” and “Content creators”
World.content:
International News: Universities in U.S. developing programs aimed at preparing “Influencers” and “Content creators”

By Zoila Palma: Influencing is emerging as a dream career for a growing number of young Americans, prompting universities to develop programs aimed at preparing students for the booming creator economy.

Arizona State University recently announced a bachelor’s degree in content creation, while Syracuse University is launching an interdisciplinary minor focused on content creation, digital entrepreneurship and online businesses, CNN reports.

The programs come as younger Americans face a changing job market, rising concerns over the cost of higher education and the growing impact of artificial intelligence on traditional white-collar careers.

Goldman Sachs has estimated that the global creator economy could be worth nearly $500 billion by 2027, while ASU’s program will cover areas including brand storytelling and podcasting, with courses such as “How to Become an Influencer.”

Experts say college campuses have become fertile ground for aspiring creators, with students turning their daily lives, talents and interests into online content.

Ryan Schram of Syracuse University’s Center for the Creator Economy said many students are interested in careers in the creator economy, even if they do not necessarily want to be the person in front of the camera. Social media skills and personal branding are also increasingly becoming part of traditional career paths.

World.title: International News: US ICE detains Johns Hopkins researcher as airport immigration arrests rise
World.content:
International News: US ICE detains Johns Hopkins researcher as airport immigration arrests rise

By Zoila Palma: U.S. immigration agents have arrested a Johns Hopkins University researcher at Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport, amid reports of a surge in immigration enforcement at U.S. airports.

Fatima Ameaka, a Cameroonian national and employee of the university’s Bloomberg School of Public Health, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) while preparing to board a domestic flight.

The Department of Homeland Security said Ameaka had overstayed her visa, which authorized her to remain in the United States until June 2024.

She will remain in ICE custody while removal proceedings are underway, Reuters report.

Johns Hopkins described Ameaka as a “respected member” of its community and said the university was working to provide her with support.

Immigration lawyers say there has been an increase in arrests at airports in recent weeks, with authorities reportedly targeting foreign nationals who have overstayed temporary visas.

World.title: Belize Police Department opens new Teakettle Sub-station
World.content:
Belize Police Department opens new Teakettle Sub-station

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Belize Police Department announced the opening of a new Teakettle Police Substation.

The substation is led by Office in Charge Sgt. Shane Casimiro and manned by 13 officers.

“This substation is critical for crime prevention and law enforcement, and is a collaboration between the BPD, the Cayo South Committee, the Ministry of Infrastructure Development and Housing and the people of Teakettle,” the Belize Police Department said.

“We are always willing and ready to assist with any project which benefits our people, and this station will serve our people well,” MIDH expressed.

World.title: US embassies urge citizens to consider departing Middle East
World.content:
Smoke rises from Israeli bombardment near the village of Kfar Tibnit as seen from nearby Marjayoun (Marjeyoun) in southern Lebanon on June 14, 2026. Israel struck Beirut's southern suburbs on June 14, killing three people, in response to what it said was Hezbollah fire at northern Israel, while its military also carried out broader strikes on southern Lebanon. The latest escalation came amid expectations that a deal between the US and Iran to end the Middle East war could be imminent, but Iranian chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said there was "no point" in continuing peace talks with Washington after the strike. (Photo by AFP)

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates (AFP) —United States (US) embassies in capitals across the Middle East on Saturday warned their citizens to beware of “unforeseen escalation” in the regional conflict and urged them to be ready to leave.

The warning, posted online by US embassies in Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, came a day after US President Donald Trump threatened to hit Iran “very hard”.

Iran and the United States have been at war since February 28. A period of calm followed a ceasefire, though that collapsed with a return of strikes.

With no end in sight, the war has for months upended the lives of people across the Middle East and rattled global energy markets.

“Americans in the region should consider departing, or be prepared to depart should there be escalation,” said the security alert.

The messages urged citizens to check flight details and to follow safety advice from local authorities.

“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions,” it said.

US citizens in Jordan were told not to visit military bases in the country, which have recently come under Iranian missile attack, and in Israel they were urged to seek the location of the nearest bomb shelter.

“The Iranian regime is unpredictable, as seen by its recent decisions to attack areas in the region without warning or provocations as well as to expand attacks to areas not previously targeted (such as Egypt),” said a post on the US Embassy Jerusalem site.

The US embassy in Beirut said the mission remained on “ordered departure status”, meaning that family members andnon-essential US government personnel were still relocated outside of Lebanon.

– ‘Defensive shield’ –

Iran’s military on Saturday accused Washington of “escalating tensions” in the region.

“Any country serving as defensive shield for criminal and aggressive America will be engulfed by the flames of war,” Ali Abdollahi, head of Iran’s military central command, said in a statement read on state television.

Mohammad Mokhber, adviser to Iran’s supreme leader, also warned against any attacks on Iranian infrastructure.

“You calculate through military equations, but we respond with the logic of history,” he wrote on X.

“Attacking Iran’s infrastructure directly awakens the fault lines on which 250 years of your hegemonic architecture have been built.”

Iran and the US resumed overnight exchanges of fire last month after a days-long lull in fighting, although there were no reported strikes overnight Friday to Saturday.

– ‘Unknown projectile’ –

On Wednesday a drone struck a US-owned gas vessel moored in an Egyptian port, causing a fire. Egypt is investigating but has not yet accused any group of launching the attack.

Meanwhile an “unknown projectile” struck a tanker off the coast of Oman, a British maritime agency said on Saturday, as the United States and Iran vie for control of the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran has effectively maintained control over navigation through Hormuz since the outbreak of the war on February 28, requiring vessels to obtain permission and pay transit fees before using the waterway.

Maritime trade tracking firm Kpler said on Friday that traffic through the Hormuz strait has dropped “sharply”.

“With US and Iranian public positions still at odds, operators are closely monitoring traffic volumes, routing behaviour and any diplomatic developments that could reshape risk across regional shipping lanes in the days ahead,” the firm said on X.

On the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, another waterway that has gained increasing importance as a transit route for Saudi Arabian oil, the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen on Saturday denied seeking to charge ships for passage through it.

The narrow waterway connects the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean and, via the Suez Canal, the Mediterranean.

The Middle East war broke out when the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran, which has retaliated with missile and drone strikes across the region.

On the Lebanon front, Israel’s military on Saturday said it killed three Hezbollah fighters in southern Lebanon, while one of its soldiers was moderately injured during a “close-quarters encounter” with Hezbollah militants.

World.title: Holness: Jamaicans’ Hurricane Melissa resilience reflects spirit of Emancipation
World.content:
Prime Minister of Jamaica Andrew Holness.

Prime Minister Andrew Holness says the rebuilding efforts of Jamaicans following the devastation caused by Hurricane Melissa last October reflect the spirit of our ancestors in their fight to overcome oppression.

In his Emancipation Day message, the prime minister maintained that the same spirit that led our ancestors to freedom will carry Jamaicans through recovery following the Category 5 storm.

“In the months since Hurricane Melissa, communities across Jamaica have borne real loss and taken up the hard work of rebuilding—neighbours helping neighbours, families repairing homes, communities restoring what the storm sought to take,” Holness said.

“The endurance, faith, and cooperation that carried our ancestors out of bondage will carry us through reconstruction,” he continued. “And we are determined to rebuild not only what stood before, but something stronger and more resilient, so that no storm can undo in a night what a generation has built. ”

He also noted that freedom without economic opportunity is incomplete, sharing visions of generational wealth and widened access to education, landownership, housing, employment, and entrepreneurship.

“We honour them when we educate our children, care for our elderly, build honest businesses, protect our communities, and conduct ourselves with dignity. We honour them when we reject prejudice and injustice. We honour them when we refuse to allow the circumstances of our birth to determine the limits of our ambition,” he said

Holness added, “Emancipation is both an inheritance and an instruction. It tells us where we have come from, but it also calls us to decide what we will become.”

See Holness’ full message below:

Prime Minister’s Emancipation Day Message to the Nation

Emancipation Day calls us to remember one of the most consequential turning points in our history. On the first of August 1838, full freedom came to the formerly enslaved people of Jamaica after centuries of bondage, exploitation and injustice.

That freedom was not freely or generously given. It was secured through the courage, resistance, and endurance of generations of our ancestors. Some resisted openly. Others preserved their dignity through faith, family, culture, work, and community. They refused to accept that the condition imposed upon them defined their worth or limited their claim to humanity.

Today, we honour them.

We remember those whose names were recorded in history and the many more whose names are unknown.

We remember the mothers who held families together under brutal conditions; the fathers who struggled to protect and provide; the spiritual leaders who sustained hope; and those who risked everything in the cause of freedom.

Their victory was the assertion of a fundamental truth: that every human being is created with dignity, conscience, and the right to determine the course of his or her own life.

Emancipation gave our ancestors legal freedom, but it did not immediately give them property, education, economic security or equal access to opportunity. They entered freedom with very little material wealth and with institutions still shaped by the inequalities of slavery.

Yet they did not wait passively for others to build a future for them.

They established free villages. They purchased land, built churches and schools, created businesses, cultivated farms, and formed strong communities.

They understood that freedom had to be supported by ownership, education, discipline, cooperation, and faith.

We have seen that same spirit in our own time. In the months since Hurricane Melissa, communities across Jamaica have borne real loss and taken up the hard work of rebuilding—neighbours helping neighbours, families repairing homes, communities restoring what the storm sought to take. The endurance, faith, and cooperation that carried our ancestors out of bondage will carry us through reconstruction. And we are determined to rebuild not only what stood before, but something stronger and more resilient, so that no storm can undo in a night what a generation has built.

True freedom is the capacity to make responsible choices, to provide for one’s family, to own property, to pursue education, to establish a business, to worship according to conscience, and to participate fully in the life of the nation.

Political freedom without economic opportunity is incomplete. Legal rights without personal responsibility cannot produce lasting progress.

The promise of Emancipation must therefore be renewed in every generation through the work of creating a society in which every Jamaican has a fair opportunity to advance.

We must continue to widen access to education, landownership, housing, employment, and entrepreneurship. We must build an economy in which effort is rewarded, enterprise is encouraged, and families can accumulate assets that may be passed from one generation to the next. We must recover that spirit of self-reliance and enterprise.

At the same time, Emancipation reminds us that freedom must be protected from every form of domination. No Jamaican should live under the control of criminals, gangs or violent men who seek to govern communities through fear. A community cannot be truly free when children are afraid to walk to school, when businesses must pay extortion, or when families are forced to remain silent in the presence of wrongdoing. The struggle for freedom therefore continues wherever law-abiding citizens are denied peace, security and opportunity.

We must stand firmly for law, justice, and order. We must strengthen families, support responsible parenting, and teach our children that freedom carries duties as well as rights. We must reject the idea that discipline is oppression, that accountability is hostility, or that personal responsibility can be replaced by permanent dependence.

The strongest tribute we can pay to our ancestors is to use our freedom well.

We honour them when we educate our children, care for our elderly, build honest businesses, protect our communities, and conduct ourselves with dignity. We honour them when we reject prejudice and injustice. We honour them when we refuse to allow the circumstances of our birth to determine the limits of our ambition.

Emancipation is both an inheritance and an instruction. It tells us where we have come from, but it also calls us to decide what we will become.

Let us therefore continue the work of building a Jamaica in which freedom is supported by opportunity, independence by ownership, rights by responsibility, and hope by purposeful action.

May we remain worthy of the sacrifices of those who came before us.

May we preserve the freedom they secured. And may God continue to bless Jamaica, land we love.

World.title: WATCH: Charles defends Barking Lodge aquaculture project, addresses safety concerns
World.content:
Director of St Thomas Farms Limited, Dr Michelle Charles has defended the company’s proposed aquaculture project in Barking Lodge, St Thomas, following residents’ concerns about the development’s proximity to a primary school.

In a statement issued in response to the concerns surrounding the project, Charles sought to clarify what she described as important facts about the development, stressing that the project is being carried out on private property and in compliance with the requirements of the relevant government authorities and regulatory agencies.

Addressing concerns about the aquaculture ponds being constructed behind Barking Lodge Primary School, Charles said: “We wish to assure parents, staff, and residents that no water will be introduced into these ponds until the perimeter fencing has been completed and the area has been properly secured.”

According to Charles, consultations were held with the school’s principal before construction of the ponds began, and student safety has remained a priority throughout the planning process.

Charles also highlighted what she described as the property owners’ longstanding commitment to the Barking Lodge community. As part of that commitment, she said the owners have indicated they are willing to permanently donate the parcel of land currently used as the Barking Lodge Primary School football field. She said the proposed aquaculture ponds are located beyond the football field, ensuring that the recreational space would remain unaffected.

She argued that the project represents an opportunity to balance community investment with economic development, noting that the aquaculture operation has the potential to generate employment, support local contractors and suppliers, create new business opportunities for farmers and entrepreneurs, strengthen Jamaica’s food security, and attract long-term investment to Barking Lodge, New Pera and the wider parish of St Thomas.

Charles described the initiative as having the potential to become one of the first major commercial aquaculture operations on Jamaica’s eastern side. She said responsible investment of this nature could contribute to job creation, skills training, infrastructure improvements and sustained economic growth in an area that has experienced limited commercial development since the decline of the sugar industry.

She also expressed concern that the issue has become increasingly politicised.

“In our view, the focus should not be on opposing lawful development but on ensuring that it proceeds safely, responsibly, and in full compliance with the law,” Charles said.

“The people of Barking Lodge, New Pera, and the wider St Thomas community deserve investment that creates opportunity rather than division,” she added.

St Thomas Eastern Member of Parliament, Rosemarie Shaw is among persons who expressed concerns about the project, noting that her checks with the National Environment and Planning Agency and the St Thomas Municipal Corporation revealed that those agencies were unaware of the development.

(Video by Llewellyn Wynter)

World.title: Sunshine Girls upset Australia to book Commonwealth final spot
World.content:
The Sunshine Girls celebrate after reaching the finals of the Commonwealth Games (Photo: Commonwealth Games Glasgow)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica’s Sunshine Girls scored a sensational one goal 46-45 win over defending champions and world number one ranked Australia in Saturday’s semi-final of the netball competition at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland.

The win was revenge for an equally close loss in the final four years ago in Birmingham, UK and saw the Jamaicans qualify for back-to-back finals.

In Sunday’s final, Jamaica will face New Zealand in a rematch of their Pool B game earlier this week which the Kiwis won 53-48.

New Zealand beat England 61-54 in their semi-final game.

The Sunshine Girls, who snapped Australia’s undefeated run in the competition, led by three goals after the first quarter, 13-10, and held on doggedly despite Australia scoring the last three goals of the game, with Sophie Dwyer missing two attempts in the final two minutes of play.

Jamaica led 23-21 at the half but Australia tied up the scores 35-all going into the fourth quarter before taking the lead 38-37 early in the fourth.

Romelda Aiken-George led the Jamaican scoring with 29 goals from 32 attempts and Shanice Beckford scored 17 from 18 attempts.

Kiera Austin scored 22 goals from 23 attempts, Cora Koenen scored 18 goals from 20 attempts, Sophie Garbin scored four goals and Dwyer one goal.

— Paul A Reid

World.title: New trafficking threat
World.content:
Senior Special Agent at Major Organised Crime and Anti Corruption Agency (MOCA) Shereese Smith participating in a panel discussion during the ‘Conversations on Trafficking’ event held at the Courtyard by Mariott Hotel in New Kingston on Friday. Naphtali Junior

THE growing international threat dubbed cyber factories — where human trafficking victims are held captive to commit online fraud — has made its way to Jamaica.

Minister of National Security and Peace Dr Horace Chang on Friday confirmed Jamaican law enforcement agencies have detected cyber factories operating in the island and are moving quickly to seal the breach.

According to Chang, the Jamaican authorities are fully equipped to prevent this illicit operation from expanding.

Born in Southeast Asia cyber factories, or scam compounds as they are sometimes called, represent an industrial-scale crime economy that turns jobseekers into human trafficking victims, who are then forced to commit various cybercrimes.

According to the ‪International Organisation for Migration (IOM), victims from more than 80 countries are being trafficked to work in these online scam centres.

The revelation of Jamaica being added to that list of countries came on Friday during a ‘Conversations on Trafficking’ staged by the Office of the National Rapporteur on Trafficking (ONRTIP) at the Courtyard by Mariott Hotel in New Kingston to mark World Day Against Trafficking in Persons 2026.

As panellists discussed the rapid expansion of multi-billion-dollar modern slavery networks across Asia, it was confirmed that similar scam-compound cases have now been detected in Jamaica.

When questioned about the domestic prevalence of these human trafficking rings, Chang told the

Jamaica Observer that while their mere presence on the island poses a clear threat, the issue is not widespread and remains under strict monitoring by the relevant authorities.

“We have some good people working quietly and effectively between the various security agencies… MOCA [Major Organised Crime and Anti-Corruption Agency], the Jamaican Constabulary Force, and the JDF [Jamaica Defence Force]. They work together, and we collaborate with our international partners because cybercrime has no boundaries and therefore you can track and find them in this region,” said Chang.

“So it’s not yet as big a threat risk as it is in Southeast Asia, but it’s something that requires continuous monitoring, continuous work, and it means also keeping our own personnel trained and in place at all times,” added Chang.

The security and peace minister argued that, while robust law enforcement deterrence is essential, he also has confidence in public education initiatives such as the ‘Conversations on Trafficking’ forum and other Government-led initiatives that arm citizens with information needed to recognise and avoid these traps.

He further noted that a critical method for keeping human traffickers at bay is for people to actively report suspicious digital activity to law enforcement, rather than simply blocking the accounts when they are detected.

“So, part of what we are hoping is to use… maybe not so much the security, but just to sensitise a wider population so that they will know when to report to the security agencies, in particular the police and MOCA, which are on the front line,” said Chang.

“Tell the parents, ‘Mommy, look at this, look at that,’ to alert somebody else. Show a teacher what this is saying… We need to get that because our team, though limited in numbers and size, are capable and have confidence. Once they get the information, we can work at it. But it’s a rapidly evolving area, especially with artificial intelligence coming up. But we’ll keep working on it,” Chang added.

Meanwhile, event panellist and MOCA Senior Special Agent Shereese Smith told the

Observer that, while extensive data does not exist on who is most vulnerable to these illicit schemes in Jamaica, international monitoring by the agency reveals that women seeking employment are among the primary targets.

“You fall victim to a job offer, you visit this place thinking you’re going to receive a modelling job. But once you land at this location they take your travel documents, you owe them money, you’re in debt now for bringing you there,” she explained.

“And so, you are now required to work for that person. So, they control your movement, they control your finances, they control your communication, and you’re in this space… you are now committing some other crime for these individuals… And when we say they control you, a lot of them is like an armed controller, you know, in terrible conditions with other victims under violence,” she added.

Smith told the Observer that MOCA is currently monitoring the issue and working hard at containing human trafficking and fraud schemes across Jamaica. She urged citizens to report suspicious activity and to use the cyber space with greater awareness and caution.

“If you see this specific agency saying, ‘recruiting, send us your passport, we will cover your flight, your stay, this, your that’, if it is the name is an actual company, reach out to the company itself instead of speaking through that social media platform, just try to verify as much as possible. Or if it’s something that’s suspicious, report it and we will try to get it taken down,” said Smith.

World.title: ‘An investment in the future’
World.content:
Norman Brown, president of the Parade Gardens Community Developmemt CommitteeJoseph wellington

FRIDAY’S official launch of the Community Resilience and Transformation (CREATE) Project signalled hope for residents of four volatile communities across the island.

The communities to benefit from the project are Parade Gardens and Majesty Gardens in the Corporate Area, Norwood in St James, and Grange Hill, Westmoreland.

The project, which costs $36.8 million, is designed to renovate community centres and spaces where residents can gather and bond while engaging in a wide variety of developmental activities and meetings.

These events and activities are expected to go a long way in expanding opportunities for at-risk youth and to support violence prevention in hot-spot communities.

Dalton Spence, president of the Norwood Community Development Committee (CDC), said the usually violent community has started to see a long-needed turnaround with a reduction in shootings and killings.

With the renovation that will take place at community centre, he is expecting crime to be even further reduced.

According to Spence, in the past when the name Norwood was mentioned in any conversation it was most likely because it was being highlighted as a place where shootings and killings occurred often.

“It was always a negative, but now we have changed that. I’m sure nobody is scared to come to Norwood anymore, and so we declare peace in the area,” Spence said.

“It is a privilege to address you on behalf of the Norwood CDC and the residents of Norwood. They are happy for such a moment. I extend our sincere appreciation to the Pan American Development Foundation, the International Narcotics and Law Enforcement, and the Jamaica Constabulary Force. For the people of Norwood, this project represents much more than improvement of a facility. It represents hope. It represents opportunity, and the confidence in a community that has continued to work diligently to improve the lives of its residents.

“Norwood’s CDC is committed to serving our residents, and we have done so. We continue to use this space for community meetings, new development programmes and summer camps. We are going to have our camps in that space. We have educational initiatives. We believe that community development must continue even when resources are limited. The improvement being made will provide a safer and a welcoming space,” he said, “where children, young people, and family can learn and develop their talents.”

Copeland Bailey, past president of the Grange Hill CDC, thanked the stakeholders who invested in the project, pointing out that the renovation of a safe space in his community represents an investment in people, families and the future of Grange Hill overall.

“By restoring this facility, you are creating opportunities that encourage young people to spend their time engaging in productive activities rather than becoming vulnerable to crime, violence, and other negative impacts. Safe community spaces are an important part of crime prevention. They keep young people safe, in terms of belonging, promote teamwork, discipline, leadership, and respect, and bring families and neighbours together,” said Bailey.

He argued that communities are stronger and safer when young people have positive opportunities and supportive environments.

“We want this space to inspire hope, create opportunities, and help guide our young people towards education, employment, and positive things in life. The timing of the renovation could not be better,” Bailey added.

The presidents of the Parade Gardens and Majesty Gardens CDCs were also thankful for the programme.

Jahiem Mitchell from Majesty Gardens said the renovation of the multi-purpose space in the community is happening at the perfect time.

“Once it is to bring the people together, once it is to mend situations, once it is for the development and upliftment of our community, it happens on that multi-purpose court. Its maintenance is indeed our responsibility. This is a gift that we will treasure. This is a gift that we will protect,” Mitchell said.

Meanwhile Norman Brown, president of the Parade Gardens CDC, said the investment in his community is far more than just repairing a building.

“Once renovated, it will form a stronger home for youth development, learning, family support, and positive community engagement. It will provide a safe place where children and young people can build their skills, develop their talents, and access opportunities that encourage positive life choices.

“We look forward to expanding programmes such as our homework support initiative, mentoring activities such as club activities, entrepreneurship and skill development, and other human-focused initiatives that promote education, leadership, and personal growth,” shared Brown.

World.title: Man dies in crash hours after earlier collision
World.content:
The vehicles involved in the fatal crash on Manchester Road in Mandeville Thursday night Kasey Williams

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — Police here say the driver of a Toyota Hiace who died in a two-vehicle crash on Manchester Road on the outskirts of Mandeville on Thursday was involved in another collision less than two hours earlier and was removed from around the steering wheel by a cop.

Police named the crash victim as 47-year-old Junior Samuels, a resident of Bailey’s Pen in Toll Gate, Clarendon.

“He was involved in another crash with a taxi where he collided into the back of that vehicle. A breathalyser was even used to measure if he had any alcohol in his system,” a police source told the Jamaica Observer.

The source said Samuels told a traffic cop that he was recently discharged from hospital.

“He said he was on his way to work and was on some pills as he came out of hospital, after being there for a heart condition. He didn’t look well, and the police waited for the other person to come and drive away the vehicle. Within two hours the man was dead, slumped across the driver’s seat,” the source said on Friday.

Police said about 7:40 pm Samuels was driving a Toyota Hiace minibus southbound out of Mandeville when the vehicle collided with a Honda CRV that was travelling in the opposite direction.

“I saw the van climb the embankment on the left and then went to the other side of the road and climbed the embankment over there too before overturning on top of the Honda CRV. The van basically moved like an out-of-control plane,” one eyewitness told the Observer.

An ambulance was dispatched from the Mandeville Regional Hospital to the scene where checks were made for signs of life on Samuels. He was, however, pronounced dead. His body was removed by Lyn’s Funeral Home undertakers.

Police said the two occupants of the Honda CRV were also examined at the crash scene by staff from the ambulance.

Statistics from the police show that up to 6:00 am Friday there were 186 fatalities from 161 crashes recorded on the Jamaica’s roads compared to 226 fatalities from 195 crashes for the corresponding period last year.

Vice-chairman of the National Road Safety Council Dr Lucien Jones has again urged caution on the roads.

“Seventy-five persons died in June and July. And, according to noted statistician and analyst Dr Parris Lyew-Ayee, during the summer months there has been an upward trend of road fatalities over the years. It is for this reason the National Road Safety Council is warning all road users to be extremely vigilant during the upcoming Emancipendence celebrations, in particular, and during the month of August generally,” Jones said on Friday in an audio release to the media.

“Slow down and live and allow others to reach home safely. Buckle up, both in the front and in the back. Place your infant in a car seat in the back of the car. Do not drink and drive. Do not smoke marijuana and drive. Do not use your cellphone without a hands-free instrument and drive. Do not run the red light. And pedestrians, be very careful on the roads; do not wear dark clothes at night. Let us all try and reach home safely during the holiday celebrations and in August, September, and for the rest of the year,” Jones added.

World.title: Campari Bad Beaches SOS ignites Dream Wknd 2026
World.content:
Montego Bay’s shoreline at Tropical Bliss Beach pulsed with energy Thursday, July 30, as Campari Bad Beaches SOS set the tone for the 2026 edition of Dream Wknd in its new home.

The highly anticipated kick-off party delivered a seamless blend of music, fashion, and vibes, giving proof that the festival’s relocation has only amplified its allure.

From the onset, DJs Dwayne Pow and Pioneer, Coppershot, Creep Chromatic and Fyahman, and Dexta Peppa kept patrons moving with solid mixes that traversed dancehall, soca, hip hop, and international club anthems. Their sets built momentum throughout the evening, creating the perfect runway for the live performances that followed.

The stage came alive with dynamic showcases from Adofo, Qwella, and Jamal, each bringing their own flair to the night. Adofo’s commanding presence, Qwella’s smooth delivery, and Jamal’s high-energy performance ensured the crowd never lost its spark. They elevated the party from a DJ-driven vibe to a full-scale entertainment spectacle.

The atmosphere was electric, with scores of patrons embracing the ‘Sexy Beach Glam’ theme. Sequined ‘fits, flowing resort wear, and bold accessories turned the venue into a runway of Caribbean chic, perfectly complementing the Campari red branding that lit up the beachfront.

Dream Wknd’s Montego Bay debut is off to a dazzling start, and if Campari Bad Beaches SOS is any indication, the rest of the festival promises unforgettable nights of music, fashion, and pure Jamaican energy.

“The energy at the opening party was nothing short of electric, and we are thrilled to be part of this historic first staging of Dream Wknd in Montego Bay. As a major sponsor, Campari is proud to celebrate alongside the thousands of fans who bring this festival to life. Montego Bay offers a vibrant new backdrop that perfectly complements the spirit of Dream Wknd, and we couldn’t be more excited to help shape this new chapter.

“For the rest of the series, people can expect Campari to keep elevating the experience, whether through bold activations, unforgettable moments, or the signature taste that fuels celebration, we’re looking forward to raising the bar with each event and making this Dream Wknd one to remember,” said Jerome Walters, brand manager, Campari.

— Aceion Cunningham

World.title: Ceuta crisis: 22 EU leaders gang up against Spain’s Sánchez over his migration policy
World.content:
In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, the 22 leaders made direct reference to the need for EU-level cooperation on policies such as Madrid’s migrant regularization scheme.

“We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration, by coordinating our action, strengthening our external borders and addressing all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularization of [a] very large number of irregular migrants,” the leaders wrote.

Madrid has pushed back against the claim that the country’s regularization scheme triggered the crisis in Ceuta, and has pointed out that none of the people who illegally entered the exclave would be eligible to benefit from the measure.

“This process is based on very specific conditions, such as proof of residency in Spain before January 1, 2026, and having resided in Spain for five consecutive months at the time of application,” said a spokesperson for the Spanish foreign ministry. Moreover, the deadline for filing applications for the scheme, which was launched in April, was in June.

But those explanations have not appeared to sway the EU leaders who signed the letter to Costa, Von der Leyen and Martin.

“We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay,” they went on.

World.title: Labour holds Greater Manchester mayoralty after counting goes to second round
World.content:
Speaking at the Co-Op Live arena to the east of the city, Craig said she stands “ready to serve” her 3 million constituents.

“Every single decision I take as your mayor of Greater Manchester will pass the test of making your life better,” Craig pledged.

The vote was triggered after three-time mayoral contest winner Burnham resigned the job in June to return to Westminster, where he swiftly claimed leadership of the governing Labour Party and became prime minister. There had been concern that Burnham’s move would allow Reform UK — which performed strongly in local elections in England earlier this year — to seize the mayoralty.

Craig will now be have to deal directly with Burnham, who has promised to devolve more powers to England’s mayors as a part of a devolution package. The post currently comes with powers over transport, policing, and housing.

Turnout for the special election was noticeably lower than when Burnham last ran back in 2024, with only 25 per cent of voters heading to the polls this time, compared to 32 per cent at the last vote. POLITICO witnessed some voters on doorsteps Thursday evening learning of the election for the first time.

Counting continued late into the night as the re-instated supplementary voting system took the contest to a second round for the first time ever.

World.title: Almost all of Ceuta migrants have returned to Morocco, Spain says
World.content:
People gather on a hilltop near Bab Sebta on the Morocco-Spain border, near Ceuta and the Moroccan town of Fnideq on July 30, 2026. | Abdelmajid Bziouat/AFP via Getty Images

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” an official said.

BRUSSELS — More than 48,300 of the approximately 50,000 people who entered the Spanish exclave of Ceuta from Morocco have returned, a Spanish government official told POLITICO.

“Most of the people that came yesterday are now back in Morocco,” said the official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, adding that the situation was “on the path back to normality.”

The influx of migrants could be linked to a recent Spanish court ruling that limited the use of the country’s immediate-return procedure for migrants, the official added.

The European Commission said “there are no onward movements towards the European continent or other member states” by the migrants.

World.title: Trump administration slams Spain’s Sánchez for migrant ‘invasion’ of Ceuta
World.content:
“This unacceptable incident is the direct result of the Spanish Government’s deliberate efforts to enable and facilitate mass illegal migration into Europe. We are considering actions to defend Americans at home and abroad from this threat and stand ready to assist other European allies considering similar options,” wrote the department.

Sánchez will hardly be surprised by the scathing American reaction, having emerged as the fiercest Trump critic among EU leaders, slamming U.S. military action in the Middle East and barring U.S. military planes from using Spanish air bases.

“Thank God POTUS was elected and our country’s border no longer looks like this. These images out of Spain are an unfortunate reminder of the consequences of mass migration and the radical left-wing globalist policies that have enabled the Invasion of the West,” wrote U.S. Vice President JD Vance.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security made the same argument, saying: “If Spain had their own President Trump, this wouldn’t be an issue.”

The U.S. criticism came as the situation in Ceuta escalated into a Europe-wide political flashpoint in little more than a day. Neighboring governments moved to tighten their response on Friday, with France restoring border checks and Italy calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area, exposing divisions over the bloc’s migration policy.

Former Trump adviser and world’s first trillionaire Elon Musk initially shared a video comparing footage from the Ceuta migrant crisis with scenes from the 2013 zombie film “World War Z.” “Wow, the situation in Spain looks crazy!” he posted.

Clarifying the comparison was a joke, he then shared footage from 2023, showing hundreds of Venezuelan migrants attempting to cross into the U.S., captioning it: “This is what America looked like under Biden.”

World.title: Northern Ireland misses a deadline to fix its budget crisis
World.content:
Bryant, a former Anglican priest who’s never held a Cabinet post before, held his first press conference as Northern Ireland secretary shortly before meeting delegations from the region’s two main government parties, Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionists.

Bryant emphasized that the U.K. government expects Stormont to get more bang for its buck by reforming the delivery of local services, most crucially hospital care, where Northern Ireland suffers the worst waiting lists in the entire National Health Service.

“Look, we need to get to a budget,” Bryant said. “And I understand the financial pressures. I know everybody expects me to come with a checkbook. I’m actually coming with a checklist of things that I want to get sorted.”

Sinn Féin, which holds the key finance and economy ministries, has shied from taking any significant decisions on raising local taxes—not that the DUP wouldn’t immediately veto such moves. Nothing much can happen in Northern Ireland’s system of cross-community government unless the largest parties on each side of the divide can agree.

The two parties blame each other for delivering so little and agree that it’s up to the U.K. Treasury to break the budgetary impasse by providing them much more annually to spend. An independent budgetary watchdog, the Northern Ireland Fiscal Council, recently concluded that the region wasn’t being subsidized by English taxpayers to the same levels as in Scotland and Wales — and if it was, Northern Ireland could gain an extra £1 billion to £3.5 billion annually.

While few expect the Burnham administration to come anywhere close to that, both sides in Belfast do expect Bryant to take charge of key budget decisions — which is what his predecessors did when the Northern Ireland Executive collapsed in 2017 from a Sinn Féin walkout, and again in 2022 from a Democratic Unionist walkout.

World.title: London mayor Sadiq Khan accuses Palantir of bypassing procurement rules
World.content:
Palantir claims that Khan’s office blocked the contract unlawfully and “irrationally,” citing comments attributed to the mayor’s spokesperson which referred to the company’s unspecified “values and ethics.”

Louis Mosley, Palantir’s U.K. CEO, has argued that Khan’s decision puts politics above Londoners’ safety, while Met Police Commissioner Mark Rowley has said that the force’s inability to access Palantir’s technology would worsen the impact of cuts to the force’s budget.

In a pre-trial defense statement filed last Thursday and seen by POLITICO, lawyers for MOPAC said Palantir’s claim is “without merit and should be dismissed,” stating that the Met Police “conducted an award process that was unlawful.”

It says the Met Police and Palantir designed a pilot of the technology in 2025 so that the value remained below a £500,000 threshold at which it would have required MOPAC approval. MOPAC, led by Khan’s deputy mayor for policing and crime, oversees the Met Police.

Prior to the conclusion of that pilot in April 2026, the Met Police and Palantir started discussions on directly awarding Palantir a much larger contract to extend the pilot, according to the statement.

The Met Police intended “at each stage” to award the larger contract to Palantir, the statement says, adding that the approach that was “supported/encouraged/assisted” by the company.

World.title: UK to hold budget on Oct. 28, chancellor announces
World.content:
“Fiscal credibility is the bedrock of economic stability and national security,” said the chancellor in the letter. “That is why we will abide by the fiscal rules, ensuring we retain a buffer to protect us against uncertainty and the impact of instability in the Middle East.”

Healey also pledged the budget will move “money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain.”

Burnham announced today that local English mayors will be given powers to retain and spend business rate taxes to boost growth in their regions.

The prime minister said mayors will soon have power over income taxes, but Healey will unveil a whitepaper and a “roadmap” on the topic at the autumn budget.

World.title: UEFA declares to have 'lost confidence' in Infantino over 'shabby, back room, opaque deal'
World.content:
Gianni Infantino's FIFA presidency remains in crisis as football associations around the world targeted his leadership after a controversial private investment plan was dropped on Saturday.

 

“No option should be off the table,” said European soccer body UEFA just hours after FIFA announced it was withdrawing its private equity plan.

FIFA had floated the plan on Tuesday, saying it could raise up to $4.2 billion based on a valuation of $20 billion for a new commercial subsidiary, called the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which it proposed would run events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup.

It said that, if approved, the project could provide each of FIFA's 211 member associations with a one-off payment of $20 million in early 2027, and increase their funding allocation for the 2027-2030 cycle from $8 million to $20 million.

UEFA President Aleksander Čeferin has led the fight against Infantino in a seismic week for FIFA.

In a blistering statement, UEFA declared “the current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA’s confidence but also that of many other members of the football family.”

“We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast-track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game," UEFA said. “We must identify those responsible and hold them to account.

“It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, UEFA will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again.”

UEFA said that Infantino had "failed to deliver" on promises he made when he successfully first sought election in 2016 -- namely to be "transparent" and that FIFA's money was "your (the member associations) money" and "not the money of the FIFA President".

"The shabby, back room, opaque deal he hatched and tried to force through were anything but transparent.

"And with reserves standing at over $5bn, he has also failed to use associations' money for the benefit of the game."

UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin, right, and FIFA President Gianni Infantino pose during the 48th UEFA congress in Paris, Thursday, Feb. 8, 2024. AP Photo/Christophe Ena

CONCACAF calls for 'a comprehensive reckoning with this presidency'

Later Saturday, the governing body for North and Central American and Caribbean soccer (CONCACAF) called for accountability, calling for "a comprehensive reckoning with this presidency" while slamming Infantino's "poor governance and leadership".

Infantino's plan had "advanced outside every established governance framework, without transparency, consultation or due process."

CONCACAF's statement added that FIFA leaders have “a duty of service over power. Where that duty is not upheld, accountability cannot be optional.”

It was not just continental bodies condemning the move.

English football's Football Association (FA) said there should be "a full and robust review of FIFA's leadership and governance to ensure that the global game is run transparently".

The German FA (DFB) called for a complete overhaul within FIFA.

"Together with UEFA and other confederations, we must ensure that a fundamentally different culture takes hold at FIFA — a culture where, above all, decisions are once again discussed and made by members within the governing bodies."

World.title: Ceuta trying to regain calm and return to normality 'with caution'
World.content:
Euronews is reporting from Ceuta, where authorities are working to restore order after the unprecedented influx of migrants. Along the breakwater where at least 60,000 people crossed irregularly, workers have begun installing new protective barriers in an effort to prevent another mass arrival.

 

Despite those efforts, the effects of the crisis remain visible. Euronews found migrants still wandering the streets, while authorities believe an unknown number are hiding in the homes of friends and relatives.

Speaking to Euronews, one resident recalled the moment the crowds arrived.

"Honestly, it was frightening. When that whole crowd came rushing in... yes, we were scared. We really were. Then the Armed Forces arrived—thank God—and they managed to restore some order."

The Ceuta Business Confederation says local businesses have resumed operations, albeit "with caution", after residents spent more than 24 hours sheltering in their homes. During the lockdown, most shops remained closed, leaving parts of the city facing shortages of basic goods, including fresh bread.

Among those still in the city is a young migrant who told Euronews he came in search of a better future.

"I came here to find a new life. My father, my whole family, they're poor. Now we're here, trying to survive, sleeping on the streets. Life is really hard."

He said this is not his first time in Ceuta and that he has no intention of leaving for now.

Normally, the city would now be celebrating its Patron Saint festivities in honour of the Virgin of Africa. This year, however, the celebrations have been cancelled - an extraordinary decision that underlines the scale of the crisis. While authorities are trying to restore normality, the mood in Ceuta remains one of fear, uncertainty and anger, but also compassion, as the city continues to grapple with the aftermath of one of the largest irregular border crossings in its history.

World.title: Germany's small islands: nature and slow living almost on your doorstep
World.content:
Germany's lesser-known islands offer exactly what many people are looking for today: less hustle and bustle, more nature and authentic experiences. Whether it's the Wadden Sea on the North Sea coast, a Baltic Sea beach or quiet countryside, for a short break it is often the smaller islands that provide the greatest relaxation.

 

Hiddensee: Baltic Sea island made for slowing down

Hiddensee in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania may no longer be a real insider tip among island lovers, but it is still far less well known to many travellers than Rügen or Usedom. The island in the Baltic Sea is only about 17 kilometres long, car-free and best explored by bicycle, horse-drawn carriage or on foot.

The long sandy beaches, dune landscapes and the Dornbusch in the north with its lighthouse are particularly appealing.

The west coast of Hiddensee Sebastian Negraszus, Wikimedia Commons

Ummanz: Island feeling without the island stress

Ummanz lies to the west of Rügen, also in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and is one of the quietest islands in the German Baltic Sea. It is linked to Rügen by a bridge, which makes it especially easy to visit for a short stay.

The flat landscape of meadows, salt marshes and small villages is a paradise for nature lovers and photographers. In autumn, thousands of cranes stop here to rest – a spectacular natural spectacle.

Poel: Baltic Sea holiday without mass tourism

Poel lies between Wismar and the island of Rügen and is often underestimated. This Baltic Sea island offers wide beaches, small villages and a laid-back atmosphere.

Cycle tours along the coast, walks along the cliffs and visits to the historic lighthouse in Timmendorf are particularly popular. Poel is a good alternative for anyone wanting the Baltic Sea experience while avoiding the hustle and bustle of larger resorts.

Timmendorf on the island of Poel at sunset. Daniela Kloth, Wikimedia Commons

Vilm: Germany's little nature island

Vilm, off the coast of Rügen, is one of Germany's most strictly protected islands. Only a limited number of visitors are allowed ashore each day. The island is known for its ancient beech forest, untouched nature and its status as a nature reserve. Visits are only possible on guided tours.

Vilm Island nature reserve M. Anarbaev - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php

Neuwerk: Island holiday in the middle of the Wadden Sea

The small island of Neuwerk belongs politically to Hamburg, but lies around 100 kilometres away in the Wadden Sea off the coast of Lower Saxony. It forms part of the Hamburg Wadden Sea National Park.

At low tide, the island can be reached on foot or by horse-drawn wagon across the mudflats. The historic lighthouse dating back to the 14th century is Neuwerk's landmark. Anyone staying overnight experiences something special: almost complete silence at night and a spectacular starry sky.

East Frisia: A nature paradise with plenty of peace

Baltrum is the smallest of the inhabited East Frisian islands and is often referred to as the "Sleeping Beauty of the North Sea". With an area of less than seven square kilometres, it is easy to explore entirely on foot.

Palisade wall as coastal protection on the East Frisian island of Baltrum. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/

There are no cars here; instead, bicycles, horse-drawn carts and the sound of the sea set the pace. Walks across the mudflats, long strolls along the beach and sweeping views over the North Sea make Baltrum an ideal destination for a short escape.

Langeoog is one of the better-known East Frisian islands, but still feels much quieter than the big North Sea hotspots. The car-free island offers endless sandy beaches, dunes and a rich birdlife.

A short trip to Langeoog is particularly worthwhile in spring or autumn, when there are fewer visitors and walks by the sea are especially impressive.

Spiekeroog is one of the quietest of the East Frisian islands. The car-free island is known for its unspoilt dunes, old lime-tree avenues and its kilometre-long sandy beach. Unlike some of its neighbours, Spiekeroog relies less on large holiday complexes and more on nature, peace and relaxation. Walks through the dunes, mudflat excursions and bike rides are especially popular.

Wangerooge is the easternmost of the inhabited East Frisian islands and is ideal for a long weekend. The island is car-free and, alongside its beaches, offers protected natural areas where you can see seabirds and seals. A particular highlight is the journey on the island railway from the harbour to the village.

Juist, at around 17 kilometres long, is one of the longest East Frisian islands but only a few kilometres wide. With horse-drawn carriages instead of cars, it is wonderfully quiet. Its wide sandbank, the Wadden Sea and endless horizons make Juist a favourite with nature lovers.

The Foto Fitti, Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 Unported license.

Arngast is no longer a classic holiday island, but it is an intriguing destination for outings. The former island in the Jade Bay near Wilhelmshaven is best known for the Arngast lighthouse, which stands in the middle of the Wadden Sea. At low tide, you can discover this unique landscape on guided mudflat walks.

Islands in southern Germany: Time out on Lake Chiemsee

It's not only the North Sea and Baltic Sea that offer island experiences. Southern Germany also has some remarkable islands – right in the foothills of the Bavarian Alps. The Chiemsee islands show that you don't necessarily have to head to the sea for an island escape.

Fraueninsel: Monastery, gardens and Bavarian island charm

Fraueninsel is probably the best-known island on Lake Chiemsee and also one of the most atmospheric. Covering just 15 hectares or so, the island is car-free and easy to explore on foot. Its centrepiece is the historic Benedictine convent Frauenwörth, usually called Frauenchiemsee Abbey, which is still home to nuns today. Founded in 782 by Bavarian Duke Tassilo III, it is one of the oldest surviving convents for women in Germany.

Frauenchiemsee Abbey Allie Caulfield, Chiemsee, Schliersee 025, CC BY 2.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php

Alongside the convent, small gardens, old fishermen's houses, narrow paths and numerous arts and crafts shops shape the island's appearance. The combination of lake, mountains and historic architecture gives Fraueninsel its very special atmosphere.

Krautinsel: The quiet nature haven on Lake Chiemsee

Krautinsel is the smallest and at the same time the most original of the three main Chiemsee islands. It is uninhabited and serves primarily as a natural habitat. Its name goes back to its former use: vegetables – especially cabbage – were once grown here to supply the inhabitants of the neighbouring islands.

Today, Krautinsel is above all a retreat for plants and wildlife. The flat, green island with its meadows and reed beds offers a glimpse of how pristine the Chiemsee landscape once was. Landing on the island is not possible – the best way to see it is from a boat or by circling it during a trip on the lake.

It shows that island experiences do not always have to be about beaches and swimming.

Herreninsel: Royal history and nature trails

Herreninsel, at around 230 hectares, is the largest of the Chiemsee islands and is famous for Herrenchiemsee Palace. The Bavarian King Ludwig II began building the palace in 1878, modelled on Versailles – a homage to the French King Louis XIV.

Ferry landing stage on Herrenchiemsee Island By Jannis Raabe - Own work, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=64923231

Away from this main tourist attraction, large parts of Herreninsel are covered by forests and meadows, criss-crossed by quiet walking paths. Anyone who leaves the main routes behind will find peaceful spots with views over the lake and towards the Alps.

World.title: Hamburg celebrates Pride with increased security one week after deadly Berlin attack
World.content:
Hamburg celebrated its annual Pride event, one of Germany's biggest, with increased security on Saturday, one week after a deadly attack near Berlin's pride parade that shocked the country.

 

Organisers expected around 250,000 people to attend the parade, which this year has the motto "Queer in solidarity. Take a stand — for a future without fear."

A late addition to the trucks taking part was one representing the Berlin Pride event — or Christopher Street Day, CSD for short, as the parades are known in Germany. People on that truck were asked to wear dark clothing as a sign of respect for the victims of last week's attack, where one person was killed and 29 others injured.

A reveller holds a placard during the Hamburg Pride 2026, the Christopher Street Day (CSD) parade, in Hamburg, Germany, Saturday Aug. 1, 2026. Georg Wendt/dpa via AP

Late on July 25, a man plowed a van into people a few hundred metres from the closing party of the Berlin Pride event before cutting others with what appears to have been a machete.

The 21-year-old suspect, Abdul Ballout, was killed in a confrontation with police on Sunday. Investigators later found a video in which a person believed to be the suspect claimed responsibility and pledged allegiance to the Islamic State group.

Prosecutors have said Ballout, who was born in Germany and has Lebanese roots, travelled to Lebanon in 2025 with the goal of going to Syria to join IS. He made contact with several people who were presumed members.

Hamburg's police chief said earlier this week that roughly twice as many officers as last year would protect the Hamburg event.

A police officer stands on Steindamm at the edge of Hamburg Pride 2026, the Christopher Street Day (CSD) parade, in Hamburg, Germany, Saturday Aug. 1, 2026. Georg Wendt/dpa via AP

“After the brutal attack on the CSD in Berlin, many are unsure in the queer community but also in society whether here and today is the right place,” Hamburg's deputy mayor, Katharina Fegebank, told RTL television.

“I say, now more than ever, let’s all take to the streets, stand up for diversity, for freedom, for an open society, and above all, in full solidarity with and for the queer community," she added.

"Well, when something like that happens, we all have to show that we’re not afraid, that we won’t let it get us down," said Petra Schwab, who was attending Saturday's Pride in Hamburg.

World.title: Wildfires in Europe: blazes continue to spread in France and Greece
World.content:
A wildfire in France's Provence region continued spreading on Saturday as overnight efforts successfully stopped the blazes from reaching the nearby towns of Correns and Montfort-sur-Argens.

 

Some 1,300 firefighters have been deployed to tackle the blaze, which has flared up again in the Gros Bessillon area, burning approximately 1,250 more hectares since Friday. By the end of the week, authorities said a total of 4,500 hectares had been burnt.

Despite the difficulties, 2,500 people were still unable to return home.

Meanwhile, authorities say France's largest wildfire in 70 years has been brought under control near the southwestern city of Bordeaux.

The Gironde fire has burned 420 square kilometres of pine forest west of the city, an area four times the size of Paris.

Firefighters said it remained contained within that perimeter Saturday, meaning flames had not broken beyond its existing boundaries. But it had not been declared “fixed” — the point at which crews determine that a fire is no longer advancing — and active sectors and buried hot spots persisted.

Twenty French departments were under an orange heat warning Saturday, mostly in the east and southeast. Temperatures of 35 to 39 degree celsius were forecast around the Mediterranean, while eight departments faced a high forest-fire risk.

Residents evacuated in Greece

In Greece, hundreds of firefighters on Saturday were battling to save a popular coastal resort northwest of Athens as violent winds lashed the country, hampering operations.

More than 400 firefighters, backed by several dozen specialised aircraft, were battling blazes in the area of Porto Germeno, the country's fire department said.

According to meteo.gr, the weather service of the National Observatory of Athens, winds up to 130 kilometres per hour were recorded Saturday.

The fire broke out Friday near the neighbouring coastal village of Agios Vasileios. Residents initially ignored a civil protection call to evacuate, and some 300 people had to be rescued by sea.

Wildfires have flared in several parts of the country this week, including on the popular island of Crete, and three firefighters have so far lost their lives.

World.title: Find in German cave: 40,000-year-old mammoth ivory bird figures discovered
World.content:
The two figurines, discovered by a team from the University of Tübingen in the lower layers of the cave, are thought to have been made by people of the Aurignacian culture, who lived in the region during the Upper Palaeolithic.

 

The better preserved of the two carvings depicts a bird at rest, possibly brooding. The other shows a bird with outstretched wings, although the left wing has broken off. Archaeologists found the two figurines only about a metre and a half apart.

Miniature carvings made from mammoth ivory

Both sculptures are so small they would fit on a fingernail and weigh just 1.3 and 0.7 grams respectively. One of them – a bird with outspread wings and a length of only two centimetres – is currently regarded as the smallest known Ice Age artwork ever discovered in the region.

One of the bird figures bears parallel lines on its wing, which are thought to represent feathers. Ralf Ehmann, Universität Tübingen

"Mammoth ivory was not simply used here to create a simplified form of a bird's body," explains Nicholas Conard, an archaeologist at the University of Tübingen and head of the excavations, in a statement. "Detailed observations of nature were translated into figurines whose richness of detail even allows us to investigate which bird species is depicted and what it is doing."

The resting bird, shown stretched out and lying flat, may depict a bird brooding or sitting on a nest of eggs. The second figurine, with its wings spread and neck extended, could show a bird in courtship display, taking off or landing on water.

Ptarmigan or capercaillie?

Archaeologists are still not entirely certain either about the exact species of bird or the behaviours portrayed. One possibility is that the figurines show ptarmigan – a cold-adapted species whose bones are frequently found at prehistoric sites in the region.

However, they might also represent larger, pheasant-like birds such as the capercaillie, a woodland species known for its striking appearance and elaborate courtship rituals. The detailed carvings allow comparisons of body shape, posture and the depiction of plumage, but the tiny dimensions and stylised execution of the figurines make a definitive identification difficult.

What is clear is that both species were already present in Europe during the Ice Age.

Hohle Fels cave (often also called Hohler Fels) was inhabited during the Aurignacian period (around 43,000 to 28,000 years ago) by early Homo sapiens, at a time when Neanderthals had already disappeared from Europe.

In this period, humans experienced a remarkable cultural and artistic flowering and created some of the oldest known musical instruments, items of jewellery and figurative artworks. Among the cave's most famous finds is the "Venus of Hohle Fels", a roughly 41,000-year-old ivory figure of a woman with accentuated breasts and hips, regarded as one of the oldest examples of figurative art in Europe.

Hohle Fels is one of six caves in the Swabian Jura that enjoy special protection as part of a UNESCO World Heritage site. The region is considered one of the most important archaeological landscapes for studying the beginnings of human art in Europe.

Since archaeological excavations began there in the 1860s, numerous finds dating from between 33,000 and 43,000 years ago have been uncovered, including some of the earliest known musical instruments.

The figurines will remain on display at the Museum of Prehistory and Ice Age Art in Blaubeuren until 4 April 2027.

World.title: Mountaineer Nirmal Purja killed with all members of expedition in Pakistan avalanche
World.content:
Renowned mountaineer Nirmal Purja has been confirmed dead in an avalanche accident in Pakistan, his climbing company Elite Expeditions said in a social media post on Saturday.

 

The avalanche struck on Thursday, cutting off contact with the international expedition led by 43-year-old British-Nepali climber Purja on Broad Peak in northern Pakistan.

"It is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak," Purja's company Elite Expeditions said on social media.

"We have also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive," it added.

The remains recovered so far, flown by helicopter to a hospital for formal identification, included an American woman, an Omani woman and a Nepali man, the regional government said in a statement released on Friday night.

Lost contact since Thursday

The team lost contact with their base camp Thursday after an avalanche struck Broad Peak as they attempted to scale the mountain, said Karrar Haidri, vice president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan on Friday.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah offered his condolences over the "tragic" deaths of Purja and the other climbers, which he said "has shocked us".

"The physical journey of all the deceased climbers... has been interrupted, but the history of their courage, dedication, and contributions will always remain inspiring," Shah said in a statement on social media.

Broad Peak Illuminated at Daybreak, from Concordia Camp, Pakistan. Anne Dirkse via Wikimedia Commons

Police in the mountainous northern Gilgit-Baltistan region said in a statement that high-altitude porters and rescue teams were carrying out a second day of the operation on Saturday after the search was paused due to difficult weather conditions a day earlier.

Rescuers and military helicopters had been scouring the area and teams stayed at the base camp overnight, according to the regional government.

"The rescue operation is being conducted under extremely challenging terrain and high-altitude weather conditions by the Pakistani army in coordination with local high-altitude climbers and rescuers," it said.

Powerful avalanche

The avalanche struck while the mountaineers were on a mission to summit Broad Peak 8,047 metres on Thursday and while the team was ascending at an altitude of around 6,600 metres, according to regional authorities.

The expedition comprised 10 people, including Purja, five Nepalis, a Pakistani, an Omani, an American, and a climber from China.

"Data from their tracking devices indicates that they were thrown hundreds of metres down the mountainside," Naila Kiani, from Pakistan's Alpine Club, told Le Monde newspaper.

Elite Expedition announced death of Nirmal Purja in avalanche in Pakistan this Saturday. Elite Expedition social media post

Fida Ali, a climber in the area who worked closely with Purja since 2023, said their focus for the climbing season was summiting Broad Peak, but they had first tackled another mountain, G2, in harsh weather.

Ali also joined the expedition to Broad Peak in its initial stages but returned early to accompany a Russian climber who was feeling the effects of exhaustion - narrowly avoiding the fatal avalanche.

"I wanted to go with him (Purja) but couldn't and came back with her. I was part of the team but survived," he said.

Record high peaks climb

Purja had written on X this week that he was close to becoming the first person to climb all 14 "super peaks" twice without oxygen.

"Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down," he wrote.

He had climbed all 14 "eight-thousanders" (peaks above 8,000 metres) in six months and six days between April and October 2019, then a record.

Broad Peak is the world's 12th highest mountain, located in the Karakoram range in northern Pakistan, and is regarded as one of the toughest and most technical climbs of all the 8,000-metre-plus ascents.

World.title: Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea
World.content:
Intensifying clashes between Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea are threatening a crucial trade artery responsible for nearly a third of the world's wheat supply, stoking fears of soaring prices and shortages.

Advertising

Earlier in July, a Russian cruise missile struck the grain carrier Golden Leo, claiming ten lives. This marked the deadliest blow yet in a mounting campaign by both Russian and Ukrainian forces targeting cargo ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

"This is a new development in recent months," claims shipping analyst Yoruk Isik, who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. Isik warns that cargo vessels are caught in a deadly tit-for-tat.

"Ukraine has been targeting Russian seaborne bulkers in particular, the ones transporting stolen grain from the occupied territories of Ukraine," explains Isik, "Russia retaliated and hit Ukraine's civilian port infrastructure in Odesa; a mid-sized vessel carrying corn out of Odesa was totally sunk, other vessels were damaged, and sailors died," he adds.

Turkey’s Shipowners’ Association, having logged 136 incidents involving commercial vessels in recent months, is now urging its members to avoid the Black Sea altogether.

Beyond its role as a key channel for Russian oil, the Black Sea is a lifeline for global grain exports, with Russia and Ukraine among the top suppliers.

"It is very important to note that most of Russia's agricultural commodities are exported through the Black Sea, and that almost all of Ukraine's agricultural commodities are shipped via Ukraine's ports," warns Isik.

Bad timing for harvest

Around a third of the world's wheat moves through these waters. The surge in attacks across the Black Sea and the neighbouring Sea of Azov has brought exports to a near standstill.

"No port is officially closed, but almost no shipowner wants to go there, so trade is close to zero," claims Istanbul-based international grain dealer Can Atbasoglu. "Sellers want buyers to handle the vessels, and buyers want sellers to handle the vessels, but shipowners don't want to risk it."

This deadlock arrives at the worst possible moment: harvest time. "Normally, Russian sellers would have sold all their August cargoes by now; I don't know if anybody has any sales on their books at present," says Atbasoglu.

Turkey agrees deal to clear Black Sea of mines that threaten Ukrainian exports

Wheat prices are already reacting. "The price in Romania is, say, 20-25 percent higher – that's the clearest effect we're seeing. But everybody is waiting for some kind of intervention, and soon," adds Atbasoglu.

Turkey now leads a NATO mission, along with Bulgaria and Romania, to safeguard navigation in the Black Sea. However, former Turkish ambassador and navigation rights expert Mithat Rende believes Ankara will be wary of any effort to enforce passage for commercial ships. "It's very important that the Ukrainian war should not be transformed into a regional war," cautions Rende.

"Where would it stop? Would you fire missiles and intercept Russian missiles in the Black Sea? They (Russia) already accuse all of us of fighting Russia as NATO. It's very important to avoid such operations," he adds.

Full impact yet to be felt

Rende argues Ankara’s priority is diplomacy, having played a pivotal role in brokering the 2022 United Nations-backed grain export deal after Russian forces blocked Ukrainian shipments. "Turkey maintained a dialogue with both the Russian and the Ukrainian sides at the same time," says Rende, "But is there political will for a ceasefire now? I don't see it at present."

Grain trader Atbasoglu warns the full impact of the disruption is not yet reflected in prices. "Buyers are still not fully reacting. It's seen more as an August, or at the latest a September issue, and the markets still want to believe both sides will get together and talk," he says.

However, Atbasoglu cautions that time may be running out. "In 2022, Ukraine was completely closed off, and there was a major panic. We saw the effect: wheat prices jumped 50 percent in 2022, and we could expect something similar if this continues," he concludes.

Africa and the Middle East, which are heavily reliant on Black Sea grain, are beginning to seek pricier alternatives. Europe, too, may soon feel the strain, as drought-hit wheat harvests threaten to push global food prices even higher.

World.title: Homemade bomb goes off outside upscale Moscow restaurant state officials say
World.content:
Russian authorities said the blast occurred outside a restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square when a woman allegedly carrying explosives was stopped by a security guard.

An explosion at a restaurant in central Moscow killed at least three people, including the suspected bomber on Saturday night, authorities said.

Russia's Anti-Terrorism Committee said a woman carrying "a homemade explosive device" tried to enter the restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square but was stopped by a security guard.

The device exploded at the entrance, killing the woman, the guard and a restaurant patron.

What we know about the explosion?

State news agency RIA Novosti reported that at least 21 other people were injured in the blast, which occurred shortly before 8 p.m. local time (5 p,m. UTC).

The restaurant's website said the venue had been closed on Saturday for a private event.

The explosion occurred at an Italian restaurant located in one of ​Moscow's seven Stalin-era skyscrapers Image: Sergei Vedyashkin/Moscow News Agency/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Heavily armed law enforcement officers sealed off the area and launched an investigation.

Authorities did not immediately identify those they believed to be behind the attack.

Russia has faced several attacks since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. They blamed a ‌series of assassinations and attempted killings on Kyiv.
