World.title: How Trans-Caspian Cable Fits Kazakhstan’s Evolving Connectivity Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA — For decades, Kazakhstan’s connectivity strategy was measured in highways, railways and pipelines. Today, that vision is expanding. As global competition increasingly depends on the movement of data alongside the movement of goods, the country is investing in a new layer of strategic infrastructure — one designed not to carry cargo, but information.

Among the clearest examples of this shift is the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable project. The first-ever underwater telecommunications link across the Caspian Sea will connect Aktau and Sumqayit, creating a new digital corridor between Central Asia, the South Caucasus and Europe.

The project reflects a broader vision articulated by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who has increasingly framed Kazakhstan’s connectivity agenda as extending beyond physical transport routes to include cross-border digital infrastructure. In his September 2024 State of the Nation Address, he called for the project to be completed, describing it as essential for “creating a digital infrastructure linked with international corridors and cross-border data flows.”

Several months later, speaking at an informal meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Organization of Turkic States in Budapest, Tokayev expanded that vision beyond Kazakhstan.

“This project will significantly improve digital communication between our countries and will be a strategic step towards strengthening regional integration. Such initiatives open up opportunities to create a new digital corridor across the Eurasian continent,” he said.

The regional context continues to evolve. As the cable enters its final construction phase, regional leaders are once again gathering, this time in Cholpon-Ata for an informal Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, underscoring how cooperation between the countries increasingly extends across transport, energy and digital connectivity.

Nearly two years after Tokayev first identified the project as a strategic priority, it is entering its most tangible phase. Kazakhstan is now carrying out the final stages of the project, with commercial commissioning expected by the end of 2026. The latest phase has shifted from engineering preparation to offshore construction.

According to the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development’s release from July 31, regulatory, customs and organizational procedures have been completed, including the approval of equipment required for the offshore works, allowing construction to proceed without administrative delays.

Preparatory work in 2025 included desktop and offshore engineering surveys, selection of the optimal route avoiding anchorage zones and military training areas, environmental approvals from the Mangystau Region authorities, and the production and factory testing in China of a specially armored submarine cable equipped with ROPA optical amplifiers.

With the planning phase complete, attention has shifted from engineering design to execution at sea. The cable, previously delivered from China to the port of Kuryk together with three cable baskets weighing a combined 600 tons, was transported to Baku aboard a specialized logistics vessel. It has now been transferred into the cable tank of the cable-laying vessel, which has departed Baku and is laying the line toward Aktau.

The operation is being carried out by a cable-laying vessel with a displacement exceeding 20,000 tons and equipped with dynamic positioning technology to ensure precise installation on the seabed. Around 70 crew members are involved, including technical supervisors and representatives of Kazakhtelecom. The project is being implemented by CaspiLink B.V., the joint venture established by Kazakhtelecom and AzerTelecom.

A dedicated jointing room has also been installed onboard to allow engineers to repair or reconnect the cable if required during installation. Both the Kazakh and Azerbaijani cable ends have already undergone testing. Subject to favorable weather conditions, installation of the submarine cable is expected to be completed within the next 15 to 20 days, while the overall commissioning process remains on schedule for completion by the end of 2026.

The significance of the project, however, extends well beyond the technical operation. As economies become more deeply integrated through both physical and digital infrastructure, international corridors are no longer defined solely by the goods they carry. They are increasingly shaped by the data they enable to move across borders. While the cable spans just 380 kilometers across the Caspian seabed, the vision behind it reaches much further. The Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable reflects Kazakhstan’s ambition to remain an important link in the movement of both goods and data across Eurasia.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Air Taxis, Energy Security and Middle Corridor
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from international media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest highlights the country’s plans to launch Central Asia’s first air taxi service, developments in energy security, transport connectivity and regional diplomacy.



Speaking alongside Putin, Kazakh President calls for freeze of Ukraine war

Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said on Saturday ​that a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine might be reached ‌if the sides froze the conflict and resumed negotiations, reported Reuters on July 25.

Speaking alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin at a Russia-Kazakhstan forum in the Siberian ​city of Omsk, Tokayev praised Putin’s “utmost diplomatic flexibility.”

“If I may offer my humble opinion, since I have been asked, perhaps it is time to freeze this conflict and return to the Istanbul formula 2.0,” he said.

Moscow ​and Kyiv participated in talks in Istanbul soon after Russia’s full-scale invasion in early 2022 and again in 2025, though the discussions failed ​to produce a breakthrough.

Tokayev proposes launching digital transport corridor between Kazakhstan and Russia

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has proposed launching a pilot digital transport corridor between Kazakhstan and Russia to further develop logistics and boost bilateral trade, reported Trend on July 25.

According to the press service of the President of Kazakhstan, Tokayev made the proposal while addressing the 22nd Kazakhstan-Russia Interregional Cooperation Forum in Omsk.

The president said Kazakhstan and Russia have unique opportunities to shape Eurasia’s transport and logistics architecture.

“Kazakhstan and Russia, which share the world’s longest continuous land border, are destined to play a leading role in developing the transport and logistics architecture of the Eurasian continent,” Tokayev said.

US, Kazakhstan discuss energy security, Caspian oil exports

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Kazakh Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev held high-level talks Wednesday on regional energy security and the stability of global oil supply chains, reported ED News on July 29.

“The two officials discussed the importance of energy security, including the reliable and uninterrupted export of Kazakhstan-origin oil via the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), for regional stability and prosperity,” said State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott.

Rubio expressed gratitude for Kazakhstan’s support of US President Donald Trump’s peace initiatives and signaled interest in deeper economic ties, he added.

The Kazakh Foreign Ministry confirmed the conversation covered the “Enhanced Strategic Partnership” and preparations for Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s upcoming trip to the US for the G20 Summit in December.

Middle Corridor opens new route for Kazakh exports

Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ) has organized the first-ever multimodal shipment of mineral fertilizers from the city of Ekibastuz to the United Kingdom, AzerNEWS reported on July 28.

The shipment is being carried via the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor, using both rail and maritime transport. The cargo will travel through Kazakhstan, across the Caspian Sea, and onward through Azerbaijan and Georgia before being transported by sea from the ports of Poti and Batumi to the Port of Felixstowe in the United Kingdom.

The new route will enable Kazakhstan’s fertilizer producers to increase exports to the UK market. The use of the Middle Corridor will also help diversify logistics routes and ensure more reliable cargo deliveries.

Kazakhstan set to become first Central Asian country to launch air taxi service

Kazakhstan is preparing to become the first country in Central Asia to introduce electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) air taxis into its transport system, reported Reuters Connect on July 24.

“The Prosperity eVTOL aircraft, developed by Chinese manufacturer AutoFlight, was unveiled during a demonstration flight at the Kazanat Hippodrome in Astana. The event was organized by Kazakhstan’s Alatau Advanced Air Group (AAAG) in cooperation with AutoFlight.

The aircraft can carry one pilot and five passengers, reach speeds of up to 200 kilometers (124 miles) per hour, and travel about 200 kilometers (124 miles) on a single charge.

The air taxi service is expected to launch in Alatau, a new city being built from the ground up under Kazakhstan’s digital city concept,” reads the article.

World.title: Kazakhstan Joins Top Five Gold Buyers Amid Reserve Strategy Shift
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan ranked among the world’s five largest central bank gold buyers in the second quarter of 2026, purchasing 15 tons of the precious metal as monetary authorities worldwide accelerated efforts to strengthen reserves amid persistent geopolitical uncertainty and shifting global financial conditions.

According to the latest World Gold Council (WGC) report, the National Bank of Kazakhstan (NBK) was the fourth-largest purchaser globally during the quarter, behind only Poland (51 tons), China (33 tons) and Uzbekistan (16 tons). Jordan and the Czech Republic each added six tons, while Ghana, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates and the Kyrgyz Republic made smaller purchases.

Kazakhstan’s acquisition came during a record quarter for central bank demand. Global official sector purchases reached 289 tons between April and June, the strongest second-quarter result on record and a sharp rebound from just 57 tons in the first quarter. The WGC attributes the recovery to a combination of geopolitical tensions, lower gold prices compared with first-quarter peaks, and central banks’ continued efforts to diversify reserve assets.

The trend appears far from temporary. According to a recent World Gold Council survey, 89% of central banks expect global official gold reserves to increase over the next year, while a record 45% plan to expand their own holdings.

For Kazakhstan, the latest purchases continue a long-term strategy rather than representing a short-term reaction to market volatility.

According to Amir Aktanov, an analyst at Halyk Finance’s Analytical Center, central banks have remained net buyers of gold for 15 consecutive years, purchasing more than 1,000 tons annually over the past three years. He also described sustained official demand as one of the key drivers behind the metal’s recent rally.

Kazakhstan has been one of the most consistent participants in that trend. Between 2011 and 2021, the National Bank steadily expanded its gold reserves, purchasing more than 335 tons over the decade. Although the regulator shifted its reserve management strategy in recent years, it also announced in February 2025 that it had suspended gold sales from its foreign exchange reserves, citing the complex geopolitical situation worldwide.

The renewed purchases in the second quarter suggest that reserve diversification remains a priority as policymakers seek assets perceived as resilient during periods of economic and geopolitical uncertainty. The broader gold market reflects the same dynamics.

Total global gold demand, including over-the-counter trading, remained stable year-on-year at 1,269 tons during the second quarter, while demand for the first half of 2026 increased 2% to 2,522 tons. In value terms, however, global demand reached a record $380 billion, highlighting the impact of elevated prices.

Kazakhstan’s position among the world’s largest buyers underscores both the strategic importance of gold in its reserve policy and the broader shift among central banks toward assets viewed as relatively insulated from geopolitical and financial shocks.

With official institutions expected to remain major buyers through the coming year, central bank demand is likely to continue providing structural support for gold prices, even as market attention shifts between inflation, interest rates and global political risks.

World.title: Russian woman faces prison after calling Armenians ‘rat-like’ people
World.content:
Russian calls Armenians ‘rats’

A criminal case has been opened in Armenia against Russian national Nadezhda Pirozhkova. A blogger who has lived in Armenia for the past year and a half, Pirozhkova came under fire after criticising Vardavar, the Armenian tradition of pouring water over one another on the holiday. She described the custom as an act of aggression. In another video, she referred to Armenians as a “rat-like people”.

Armenia’s Investigative Committee has initiated criminal proceedings against Pirozhkova under the article on “public statements aimed at inciting hatred and discrimination through the use of the internet”. Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for a prison sentence of up to four years under this article. If Pirozhkova is found guilty in court, she could therefore face imprisonment.

For now, however, she has been banned from leaving her place of residence as a preventive measure. The blogger may leave Yerevan only with written permission from a prosecutor or a judge.

Vardavar is one of the principal feasts of the Armenian Apostolic Church, celebrating the Transfiguration of Jesus Christ, although its origins date back to pagan times. It is virtually impossible to stay dry on the streets that day, but taking offence is not customary, as drenching someone with water is considered a way of congratulating them on the holiday. The water is believed to bring health, good fortune and purification.

Pirozhkova’s Instagram posts sparked outrage among social media users—not only Armenians, but also fellow Russians.

Many have not only criticised Pirozhkova but have also called on law enforcement authorities to punish her as severely as possible or deport her from the country.

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian did not rule out the possibility that certain actors interested in damaging Armenia’s image as a tourist destination were behind the spread of such videos. He pointed to the large number of Russian tourists visiting Armenia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Armenia received 1.042 million foreign visitors, around 40% of whom were from Russia.

“It’s interesting, isn’t it? On the one hand, the Russian government imposes trade restrictions [on imports of Armenian products and goods], while on the other, Russians happily travel to Armenia, enjoying its nature, its people and, why not, its traditions,” Yerkanian said.

What else Pirozhkova said

In a video about Vardavar, the Russian blogger said that the holiday made her want to leave Yerevan more than anything else. She described the tradition of pouring water over one another as “the height of tactlessness”. In her view, Armenians do not understand the concept of “personal boundaries” and routinely violate them.

Pirozhkova argued that splashing passers-by with water was disrespectful towards those who did not wish to take part in the celebration.

“If I’m in your country, I’m not obliged to follow your traditions. This is a direct manifestation of aggression.“

Following the video, Pirozhkova has periodically posted about the wave of online abuse directed at her. She has also publicly apologised several times, saying:

“I understand that many people saw it as disrespect towards the Armenian people. And I’m truly sorry. That was never my intention, and it still isn’t.”

At the same time, the blogger has acknowledged that she is using the controversy to promote her Instagram page.

“People recognise me now. Why shouldn’t I make use of something I’ve been through after putting in so much effort? I’ve worked hard for this. Why shouldn’t a person take advantage of circumstances and situations they have rightfully earned? I just want to change my life.“

Foreign nationals are required to respect Armenia’s national customs and traditions

The legal status of foreign nationals in Armenia is governed by the Law on Foreigners. Article 5 of the law states that foreigners in Armenia enjoy the same rights, freedoms and obligations as Armenian citizens. At the same time, it stipulates that “foreigners in the Republic of Armenia are obliged to respect the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Armenia, other legal acts, as well as national customs and traditions.”

The same article also provides that foreign nationals bear the same legal responsibility as Armenian citizens while in Armenia.

Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for penalties for “public statements aimed at inciting or promoting hatred, discrimination, intolerance or hostility against an individual or group of persons on the grounds of race, nationality or ethnicity, as well as the dissemination of materials or objects for that purpose.”

The available penalties include fines, community service, restriction of liberty and imprisonment.

Under Article 329, offences committed “through publicly displayed works, the mass media, or information and communication technologies” are punishable by one to four years’ imprisonment

Commentary

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian said in an interview with a local television channel::

“After the Russian blogger publicly apologised, this story could have ended there. But some social media users continued calling on the Armenian law enforcement authorities to examine Nadezhda Pirozhkova’s actions and determine whether they amounted to a criminal offence. The authorities decided to respond to those calls.

Perhaps there was no need to be so severe. The court will, of course, take all mitigating circumstances into account.

Perhaps we should not politicise everything. It is obvious that the aim was not to incite ethnic hatred but simply to increase her audience through provocative videos.

In two weeks, the video attracted more than 250,000 views and over 5,000 comments. As a result, the number of followers on her page increased more than fifteen-fold.

In other words, this blogger simply found a ridiculous and foolish way to grow her audience.

Nevertheless, perhaps such cases should be monitored more closely, because this is not an isolated incident.

In recent weeks, there have been several similar cases in which foreign bloggers, particularly Russians, have made remarks discrediting Armenians and damaging Armenia’s reputation as a tourist destination.

There was one case in which a young woman accused an Armenian taxi driver of attempting to rape her. I also recall another similar incident, and there are probably many more. But what is more important?

Notably, these videos are deliberately amplified by non-existent users. An army of fake accounts is spreading this material in pursuit of a specific objective.

It cannot be ruled out that certain forces are behind these fake accounts and are interested in ensuring that Armenia is not perceived as a safe destination for tourists.

Every tourist who enjoys visiting the country indirectly becomes its ‘agent of influence’. Perhaps that is exactly what some people dislike.

I don’t know whether it is a coincidence, but it was precisely during those days that the Russian Foreign Ministry added Armenia to its list of countries where Russians cannot feel safe, citing the possibility that the Armenian authorities could extradite them to third countries. Perhaps it is a coincidence—or perhaps it is not.”

Social media reaction

“If, after a year and a half of living in Armenia, she still allows herself to speak like this, it cannot be dismissed as an accident or naivety.”

“The police should investigate her actions. She’s a planted agent.”

“She should be fined heavily and deported.”

“She should be tried and deported from our country. It’s a matter of the nation’s dignity.”

“If an Armenian had behaved like this in Russia, he would already have disappeared.”

“Foreign visitors are obliged to obey the law, respect the country and its people, and behave like guests.”

World.title: Meet Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver: Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver are young pine martens and the newest residents of Tbilisi Zoo. A local resident found the orphaned cubs alone in an attic and took them home after discovering they had no mother.



However, pine martens are wild predators with powerful teeth and strong natural instincts. Once the cubs had grown up, releasing them back into the wild was no longer an option. Contact with humans had altered their natural behaviour, leaving them unable to survive on their own. Their rescuer therefore turned to Tbilisi Zoo for help.

Konstantin Pkhakadze, head of the zoo’s exotic animals department, said the pine martens arrived at Tbilisi Zoo about a month ago. He said such cases are quite common. People often assume that young animals found alone have been orphaned and need rescuing, but that is not always the case.

In most instances, the mother is nearby, hunting, searching for food or moving her young to a new location. Pkhakadze said intervening at that stage is the biggest mistake people can make. They should not even approach the cubs, as the mother may detect the scent of humans, see it as a threat and never return to her offspring.

Tbilisi Zoo currently has very limited capacity to take in new animals. Its existing site is overcrowded, while most of its resources are being directed towards the construction of a new zoo.

Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver were initially housed in the zoo’s exotics pavilion. However, the small enclosed space was unsuitable for such active and energetic animals. Zoo staff therefore built a temporary outdoor enclosure, giving the pine martens more space, fresh air and room to move freely.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.

Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.content:
Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

Major reconstruction work has been completed in the South Ossetian capital, Tskhinval. The city centre has been renovated, dozens of streets repaired, and new utility networks installed.

World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: German broadcaster ARD investigates Georgia’s rise as a crypto hub
World.content:
Crypto mining in Georgia

“Crypto war: How Putin is using bitcoin to wage war against us” is the title of a 45-minute investigative documentary by German public broadcaster ARD, which portrays Georgia as a major cryptocurrency mining hub and an alleged transit route used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions.

The documentary focuses on bitcoin mining and crypto systems which, the journalists argue, have enabled Russia to adapt to international financial restrictions.

Georgia’s favourable conditions for crypto industry

The investigation’s authors say Georgia has developed a particularly favourable legal and tax environment for the cryptocurrency industry over many years. They argue that this was closely linked to political and economic decisions taken during the rule of the Georgian Dream party and its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, turning the country into what they describe as one of the world’s cryptocurrency “grey zones”.

The documentary focuses in particular on the free industrial zones in Poti and Rustavi. According to the journalists, Russia can no longer sell natural gas to Europe at pre-sanctions levels, with some of that gas instead being used to generate low-cost electricity. The filmmakers argue that this electricity powers large-scale bitcoin mining infrastructure, the ultimate financial benefits of which serve Russia’s interests.

The German journalists say they travelled to Georgia and visited cryptocurrency mining facilities themselves, including infrastructure in the Rustavi Free Industrial Zone.

Russia said using cryptocurrency to circumvent sanctions

Nino Bakradze, founder of the investigative journalism organisation iFact, says in the documentary that Russia has not been completely cut off from the international financial system and is increasingly using cryptocurrency for cross-border transactions.

Nino Bakradze

She says iFact investigated exports of dual-use goods to Russia by conducting an undercover experiment. The organisation contacted a Russian trading company and asked whether it could ship around 30 drones to Russia. According to Bakradze, the company replied that such a shipment was possible and said it had carried out similar transactions before despite the risks posed by sanctions.

Bakradze says the investigation found that companies involved in such transactions use cryptocurrency to settle payments in order to circumvent sanctions, often without being detected by Western authorities.

‘Bitcoin mining in Georgia is profitable’

The documentary also features local bitcoin miner Nikoloz Museridze, who says the main advantage of mining bitcoin in Georgia is the country’s relatively low electricity prices.

Nikoloz Museridze

Museridze says his mining farm consumes about 2 megawatts of electricity. He estimates that, at this capacity, it takes about a year to mine one bitcoin, while the cost of producing a single bitcoin in Georgia is around $30,000-$40,000.

The miner describes bitcoin as “borderless money” that can be transferred anywhere in the world at any time and which, he claims, cannot be blocked or frozen.

World.title: Nauru withdraws recognition of occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Nauru says it has formally withdrawn its recognition of the self-proclaimed republics of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

“The Government of the Republic of Nauru declares that it has withdrawn its recognition of the ‘Republic of South Ossetia’ and the ‘Republic of Abkhazia’ as independent states.

Accordingly, the Republic of Nauru has immediately terminated diplomatic relations with South Ossetia and Abkhazia,” the Nauru government said in a statement.

On 29 July, Nauru severed diplomatic relations with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation on the basis of shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

The self-proclaimed Abkhaz foreign ministry claimed that Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure” to end diplomatic relations with Abkhazia.

“The development of cooperation between the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of Nauru has consistently encountered resistance from Georgia and its Western partners. As joint initiatives turned into practice, a campaign of aggressive external pressure was unleashed against the Republic of Nauru.

For many years, states maintaining diplomatic relations with the Republic of Abkhazia have faced external pressure aimed at abandoning their independently determined foreign policy course. Small states, with limited resources to counter large-scale political, diplomatic, and economic instruments of influence, are particularly vulnerable to such pressure.

Such practice contradicts the fundamental principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in their internal affairs.

The Republic of Abkhazia remains committed to strengthening its international subject status, protecting its national interests, and developing mutually beneficial cooperation with states that share the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, and international law,” the statement said.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and Georgia’s Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to support the move backed by Moscow.

Nauru is a small Pacific island state in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 sq km (8 sq miles), it is home to around 12,000-13,000 people.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: Labor's Secret Harbour by-election campaign walks fine line on pork barrelling
World.content:
All might be fair in love and war, but politics is normally a more regulated affair.

But where exactly those lines should be drawn — especially in the heat of a hotly-contested by-election — is often more in the eye of the beholder.

Take the location of the government's media events in the past few weeks.

Ordinarily, leaders would be hard-pressed to find a reason to ever be in the electorate of Secret Harbour.

But when applications for the WA Student Assistance Payment opened last month, suddenly the best place to talk about it was Port Kennedy.

Georgia Tree's Secret Harbour by-election campaign has been boosted by some funding announcements in the electorate. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

What about the expansion of the full-time kindy pilot program? Wouldn't you know it, one of the schools was Comet Bay Primary School, neatly within the electorate.

On Wednesday, the government announced a $5 million expansion of electrical training facilities at Rockingham TAFE — which candidate Georgia Tree claimed to have "secured" in the 20 days since being preselected.

The following day, the premier swung by to announce $3 million for nine public schools — all in the electorate.

"I'm proud that I've secured funding for local public schools across Secret Harbour," Ms Tree said in a statement.

Georgia Tree announcing the expansion of Rockingham TAFE last week. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

She can't claim full credit though — at least $600,000 had already been pledged by the area's former member, Paul Papalia, during last year's election campaign.

'Bit sus'

One Nation WA leader Rod Caddies questioned those announcements, and how Tree could claim credit for an extra $1 million committed by the government to Lakelands Youth Park.

"What caught my attention was how it was announced," he said in a social media video titled 'BIT SUS'.

"Not through an official government media statement, not by a minister or department, but via a Facebook video on the Labor candidate's campaign page.

"To me, that looks dangerously close to targeted pork barrelling and in-kind taxpayer-funded contributions dressed up as community investment."

So is it?

Premier on the defensive

The premier was defensive on Thursday when it was put to him that the education announcement had already been funded in May's budget, given it was part of a broader funding scheme for public schools.

"You can't say on the one hand that this [announcement] is just you doing what you're always doing … [and] on the other hand saying it's pork barrelling," he told reporters.

"What we've said is this is a demonstration of our $6.4 billion investment pipeline for schools right across WA."

But he was pressed on the matter by a reporter.

Premier Roger Cook and Georgia Tree in Rockingham prior to a press conference. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

"It's one or the other, isn't it? Either it wasn't being done before or it's being done because you're worried about a by-election," he was asked.

"Well obviously we're taking advantage of a by-election to highlight what we are doing for this community, and to highlight how effective Georgia Tree is in representing this community," the premier replied.

Labor in 'fight for our lives' as by-election opens door to One Nation assault Paul Papalia's resignation for family reasons sparks a by-election in the WA minister and Labor stalwart's southern Perth seat at a time when disgruntled voters are increasingly turning to One Nation.

That's effectively an acknowledgement that Labor is doing what political parties have done for a very long time: use their position in government to campaign in a by-election.

Because many of these announcements have been framed as government – not Labor party events – despite being for both purposes.

And while they are legitimate parts of the government’s work, their promotion to benefit Tree’s campaign is aided by taxpayer-funded drivers and staff.

No rules broken

That's not to say it isn't within the rules.

"What an incumbent government has is all the resources of government, and that means that it can allocate funding, especially funding that is already in the system," Notre Dame University politics professor Martin Drum said.

"The hardest thing for a sitting government to do is to bypass appropriate processes and approvals.

" Many of these announcements will have already been through some form of approval process or some form of assessment before the campaign. "

Martin Drum says there is now more scrutiny on these type of funding announcements due to social media. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

But he did acknowledge it was a "very fine line" between genuine government funding and pork barrelling — which can present an opportunity for scrutiny from other candidates, particularly on social media.

"Previously those types of platforms weren't necessarily available to candidates, so there's greater scrutiny now probably in that respect than there used to be."

Train station promise

That's certainly a big element of the Secret Harbour contest, as well as one of the area's biggest issues: stalled plans to build Karnup Station along the Mandurah train line.

Then-opposition leader Mark McGowan first promised it in 2012, but by the time Labor got into government and started working on delivering Metronet there was no federal funding for it.

More candidates emerge in by-election that will test One Nation's popularity Here's everything you need to know about the Secret Harbour by-election, which is shaping up as one of the most closely-watched political contests in WA for some time.

That's because then-prime minister Scott Morrison announced funding for a nearby station in Lakelands instead in 2019.

Federal Labor MP Madeleine King, whose seat includes the proposed location for Karnup, described it as "cynical pork barrelling" at the time, because Lakelands is within the neighbouring electorate held by Liberal MP Andrew Hastie.

Nearly seven years on, there are no firm plans for the Lakelands project.

On Monday, Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said a timeline would become clearer once planning for housing near the station was completed.

For her part, Tree has said pressuring Saffioti for the station would be one of her top priorities if elected.

That lack of clear progress created an opening for Liberal candidate Ryan Robertson, who promised this week the Liberals would build the station.

WA Liberal candidate for the Secret Harbour by-election, Ryan Robertson taking questions about a potential Karnup train station. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

But that relies on the party winning government at the 2029 election, which still looks like an ambitious goal, especially if One Nation continues to eat their lunch.

Countdown is on

The minor party's efforts could be helped if they can convince voters Labor isn't genuine in their commitment to the seat and is just trying to buy votes.

At the same time though, many in the electorate have voiced displeasure at feeling forgotten on account of being a safe Labor seat for so long.

Can Georgia Tree hold onto Secret Harbour for Roger Cook and Labor? (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Some extra money might be welcome, no matter how they get it.

Whether it's fair — or crosses a line — will be up to voters in just under a month's time.

World.title: Quick hits: Sprinter's surprise, a bored prince, and a stunning upset
World.content:
An Australian sprinter receives a surprise visit, Jamaica celebrates in style after beating the Diamonds and Prince George looks bored at the cycling.

Here are the quick hits from day nine of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Surprise guests shock Aussie sprinter

Chloe Mannix-Power (right) had some fans she was not expecting to see in the stands. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Chloe Mannix-Power somewhat controversially missed out on an individual 100-metre berth at these Games, but hit the track for the first time in the women's 4x100m heats.

In the moments after she and teammates Ebony Lane, Monique Hanlon and Georgia Harris made it through to the women's 4x100m final, Mannix-Power looked up into the stands and received quite a shock.

"I thought [my parents] were at home watching on the lounge, but no they're up in the top of the grandstand cheering me on," she said.

"My parents love a surprise moment, they've done it before, so to be honest I kind of had a little feeling they would be up there, but they never tell me they're here until the end of the race."

Mannix-Power later helped Australia finish fourth in the final.

2. Prince George bored?

Prince William, Princess Catherine and their three children took in a few of the sports on day nine.

Prince George, however, seemed as though he wanted to be anywhere else when they visited the velodrome.

Prince George watches on at the velodrome. (AP: Andrew Milligan)

Earlier, the royals watched on as the Diamonds lost 46-45 to Jamaica in a major upset in the netball semifinals.

The Prince and Princess of Wales took to Instagram to thank the athletes for putting on a show.

The Prince and Princess of Wales and their family watching the netball at the Hydro in Glasgow. (Getty Images)

"Incredible atmosphere at the Commonwealth Games today," a post from their official Instagram account read.

"Watching world-class talent compete and seeing the power of sport to bring people together is truly special.

"Thank you to everyone involved for such a wonderful day."

3. 'Absolute scenes'

Jamaica celebrates its win over the Diamonds. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Not only did the Royals take in Jamaica's shock victory, but they also witnessed some of the wildest celebrations seen at the Commonwealth Games.

After Sophie Dwyer missed the shot that would have sent the semifinal to extra time, the entire Jamaican squad celebrated like they never had before.

We lost count of how many social media videos featured the caption: "Absolute scenes."

Loading Instagram content

For the Jamaicans, this was personal.

They were still hurting from their loss to the Diamonds in the 2022 Commonwealth Games final in Birmingham.

"We're carrying a bit of vengeance from the last Commonwealth Games," Jamaica captain Shamera Sterling-Humphrey said.

"We've graduated from bronze medals. We didn't want bronze this year."

Jamaica faces New Zealand in the final, while the Diamonds meet England in the bronze medal play-off.

4. Montag admits to being 'selfish'

Elizabeth McMillen led Jemima Montag for most of the race, but did not win gold. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

It was an Australian sweep of the medals in the women's 10,000m race walk, but the fight for the gold medal between teammates was a fierce one.

Australian Elizabeth McMillen and Jemima Montag broke clear from the pack early and led for the entire race.

McMillen was at the front, with Montag her shadow just behind.

Montag's strategy was to use McMillen as protection from the wind, a tactic which worked to perfection.

McMillen's lead for the better part of 23 laps of the 25-lap race, before Montag ducked out from behind her and put on the burners in a decisive attack to claim gold.

It was a move she had no regrets over.

"In a race you have to be selfish. Unfortunately it's an individual sport, not a team," Montag said.

"If it was cycling or something with drafting, where you do change the lead around then absolutely.

"But as much as I would love to, sometimes you have to forget it's a teammate that you care about and just remember it's another competitor and it's another body that in front of you and to ultimately be selfish."

McMillen was not particularly happy, but understood.

"What can you do? That's racing for you," McMillen said.

"I did look back a few times thinking, 'Are you going to help out here?', but no. I was the rabbit today, so what are you going to do?"

5. Indian boxer explains celebration

Arundhati Choudhary celebrates in her unique way. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

India boxer Arundhati Choudhary is a beacon of positivity inside and outside the ring.

Choudhary, who won gold in the women's 70-kilogram category in Glasgow, takes inspiration from a Hindu deity, Lord Rama.

This is why she opts for a bow and arrow celebration.

"In India we have Lord Rama, who killed negativity with his bow," Choudhary explained.

"Last year I was suffering from surgery and my family was also suffering from many problems.

"So I just throw the bow and arrow and shoot all the negativity out."

World.title: Radical idea to stop dust storms in this outback city has been a success for 50 years
World.content:
Doug Daws remembers when colossal dust storms would regularly strike his outback hometown, grinding life to a halt and sending people sprinting indoors.

"You could hear the wind coming, and you'd say, 'quick, quick, get inside, the Esperance doctor's coming', and you had to race inside and close all the windows and doors," he said.

"Never really worked … the dust was very, very bad."

Doug Daws remembers the huge columns of red dust moving towards the city, but the grey dust was worse, in his opinion. (ABC Goldifelds: Nicholas R Ward)

For decades, Kalgoorlie-Boulder, 700 kilometres east of Perth, was plagued by choking clouds of dust blowing off the treeless plains north of the city, and from mine tailings in the south.

Mr Daws has lived in the mining city his whole life and thinks people today do not appreciate how bad the dust was.

"The storms were fairly fierce," Mr Daws said.

"We have no problem now, really, to speak of; it's so small, it's infinitesimal."

Dust storms had been a problem since the 1890s and

"During some times of the day, all traffic and business were suspended," the Morning Herald reported on October 17, 1898. (Supplied: Eastern Goldfields Historical Society)

"A lot of people just said, 'Oh, you're in a mining town, you're an outback town, you've just got to accept it,'" Mr Daws said

"Well, we have a saying here … we just get shit done."

A man for all seasons

In 1973, a man called Julian Grill arrived in Kalgoorlie-Boulder from another historic town: Broken Hill.

Mr Grill arrived with a radical idea to stop the dust.

Before going onto state politics, Julian Grill spearheaded a controversial anti-dust initiative in Kalgoorlie-Boulder in the 1970's. (Lee Griffith/Pool/The West Australian, file photo: AAP)

"He was a very persuasive talker, and he convinced us that we should give it a go," Mr Daws recalled.

"And to his absolute credit, he and the blokes out of the AG [agriculture] department … came up with a workable solution."

Mr Daws was Boulder shire president at the time and remembered thinking the idea was far-fetched, but the town was struggling with a slump in gold prices, so he thought they did not have much to lose.

With a $10,000 state grant, the committee set about meticulously studying dust. (1981 Department of Conservation and Environment Report)

From there, Mr Grill became chair of the newly established Goldfields Dust Abatement Committee.

A lesson in history

Severe dust storms dated back to the region's gold rush in the 1890s, when tens of thousands flocked to the area.

One of the earliest recorded storms was in 1894, two years after the first gold discoveries.

In 1894 the Coolgardie Miner described one of the storms: "A dust storm of unexampled severity passed over the town on Saturday last, and endured the whole day … causing almost total suspension of business." (Supplied: JJ Dwyer/Eastern Goldfields Historical Society)

It was a problem being created and worsened by mining; in the early days the new industry needed wood for tunnels, pumps and heating.

In less than a decade, locals had cleared land around Kalgoorlie-Boulder, and small railways spread out hundreds of kilometres to gather timber.

The almost complete clear-felling of forests around Kalgoorlie-Boulder meant dust storms could move unimpeded across the region (Supplied: Eastern Goldfields Historical Society)

The deforestation destabilised the region's fine dusty topsoil.

As the miners kept digging for gold, tailings were created and left piles of grey dirt which the wind picked up and carried into town.

The region's early mining industry had an almost insatiable need for timber to frame tunnels, run steam turbines and heat houses. (Supplied: Gwalia Museum)

The beginning of the end

The studies confirmed that dust storms were primarily coming from this deforestation and mine refuse.

The committee came up with a plan that Mr Daws said seemed "nuts".

The process was slow but monitoring showed by the 1980s it was working. (1981 Department of Conservation and Environment Report)

Wood chips were spread over the desert floor, saplings planted in arid shrubland and mine tailings were covered in rocks.

To block dust hitting the city from the north, six reserves were created which would become 3,500 hectares of forest.

With limited funds, the committee bought a woodchipper to preserve ground moisture in reserves. (1981 Department of Conservation and Environment report)

The reserve was controversial, with 300 saplings being destroyed by vandals and forcing the committee to fence off the area.

Researchers tried novel strategies to see what would work to reduce the dust. (1981 Department of Conservation and Environment report)

"We went out and built these zones and forbade people from going there with threats when we had absolutely no legislative protection or authority to do so," Mr Daws said.

"But sometimes you just gotta go and do things, don't you?"

The Eastern Goldfields was once covered in hundreds of tailing dumps. (1981 Department of Conservation and Environment report)

Next, the committee needed to stabilise hundreds of mine tailings. Most methods were prohibitively expensive, so in the late 80s, almost all tailings were taken and put into a single storage area.

By 1981, the dust storms still hit, but as they got closer to town, the severity had reduced.

In the 1970s, hundreds of square kilometres surround Kalgoorlie were clear-felled but the forest has returned. (ABC Goldfields-Esperance: Nathan Morris)

Working for the next generation

It took 20 years for the dust abatement to take full effect.

While dust still impacts the region, the levels are usually well below the 50 micrograms per cubic metre national air quality recommendations.

A tree planting day by Kalgoorlie-Boulder Urban Landcare Group this year. (ABC Goldifelds: Nicholas R Ward)

In 1994, with its mission largely complete, the committee turned into the Kalgoorlie-Boulder Urban Land Care Group (KBULCG).

Today, it is focused on greening efforts, conducting plantings around town and maintaining the huge reserves that still protect the area.

The once controversial forest is now a popular recreation area for locals, parts now hosting walking trails, playgrounds and picnic areas.

Kim Eckert planting a tree at the KBULCG planting day. (ABC Goldifelds: Nicholas R Ward)

KBULCG chief executive Kim Eckhert said the town would be very different today without the committee.

"It was a radical plan, and it just shows you what foresight they had back in those days to understand the impact of all of that," Ms Eckhert said.

Today, the group is largely volunteer-run, with hundreds of locals donating their time.

KBULCG volunteer Krishan Coona says he joined because it was an opportunity to connect with the community and help the environment. (ABC Goldifelds: Nicholas R Ward)

For Mr Daws, tackling the dust is still one of his proudest achievements.

"I just happened to be there at the time, as I said, a bit reluctantly, was drawn into it, but we backed Julian, it worked, we're proud of that," Mr Daws said.

"The dust problem in Kalgoorlie now is basically non-existent.

"People that say, 'oh, it's very dusty here', quite frankly, don't know what they're talking about."

World.title: Courts jailing parents of US school shooters marks legal turning point
World.content:
For the third time in US history, a parent has been held criminally responsible for the murderous actions of their child.

Colin Gray, 55, was sentenced in the state of Georgia on Thursday local time to 15 years in prison for second-degree murder, two days after his son Colt Gray was jailed for life over a school shooting.

Prosecutors argued the father abetted his son's crimes by providing him with the weapon he ultimately used to kill four people and injure nine others.

Gray has become just the third parent in US history to be sentenced to prison for negligence that led to the crimes of a child. (AP: Supplied/Hyosub Shin/Atlanta Journal-Constitution)

They also argued the father ignored clear red flags of his son's deteriorating mental health before the shooting.

Legal experts have suggested Gray's jailing marks a turning point in American prosecutors pursuing a crackdown on parents for the criminal actions of their children.

How the Apalachee High School shooting unfolded

On September 4, 2024, then-14-year-old Colt Gray brought an AR-15-style assault rifle to school hidden in his backpack.

Driven by a desire to achieve a level of notoriety associated with infamous US school shooters before him, he began firing indiscriminately in a classroom and hallway.

Two 14-year-old students, Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo, and two teachers, Richard Aspinwall and Cristina Irimie, were shot dead.

Colt Gray pleaded guilty to 55 counts, including murder. (AP: Jason Getz/Atlanta Journal-Constitution/Pool)

A third teacher and eight other students were injured, including seven hit by gunfire.

Prosecutors argued the teenager had planned the shooting for some time, and wrote a detailed step-by-step guide for himself — including estimates of how many people he aimed to kill and injure.

Investigators previously interviewed Colt and his father more than a year earlier over an online threat linked to the teen, which he denied.

In the wake of the Apalachee High School shooting, authorities found a shrine in Colt's bedroom dedicated to Nikolas Cruz, the shooter in the 2018 Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School massacre in Florida.

Teen gets life for school shooting A judge in the US has sentenced a teenager who killed two students and two teachers in a shooting at Apalachee High School in Georgia to serve life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Colt told one investigator he had experienced uncontrollable urges and heard people tell him to do things.

He said right before the shooting he felt things were getting really bad and he feared he was going to be attacked. He repeatedly mentioned believing teachers, and possibly students, were plotting against him.

On Tuesday, local time, the 16-year-old — who pleaded guilty to 55 counts including murder and assault charges — was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Judge says father 'failed as a parent'

In sentencing Colin Gray to 15 years in prison, Georgia Judge Nicholas Primm said he was faced by a "nearly impossible task" to penalise the 55-year-old without his decision being skewed by emotion.

He said punishing crimes of negligence was particularly challenging because there was no intent by Gray to commit a crime.

"My heart aches for everyone that was there that day, for all of you that have been impacted by it," he said.

"But the law requires that I set aside emotion. I don't get to sentence with passion.

" You were convicted because the warning lights were flashing brighter and brighter and you didn't get him help and you didn't remove his access to the guns. "

During the father's jury trial, prosecutors said he had given his son the assault rifle as a Christmas gift along with ammunition, a gun sight and other shooting accessories.

Marcee Gray, the teen's mother who was separated from his father, told investigators she argued with her estranged husband weeks before the shooting, asking him to secure his guns and restrict their son's access.

Gray's defence lawyer asked Judge Primm for a 10-year prison sentence, followed by 10 years on probation, while prosecutors initially pushed for an 80-year term.

Prosecutors argued Colin Gray knew of a shrine his son Colt had created in his bedroom in this house, dedicated to notorious school shooter Nikolas Cruz. (Reuters: Elijah Nouvelage)

The defence team argued Colt Gray "actively hid the depth of his involvement" in the online community obsessed with mass shooters from his parents and others, and the red flags raised by prosecutors were outliers among happier moments.

Prosecutors argued the father had simply ignored his son's "substantial and unjustifiable risk."

In handing down the 15-year prison term, Judge Primm said there would have been no crime if Colt had not brought a gun to school and shot people, but his father could have locked up or restricted access to the weapon and ammunition and sought counselling for the teenager.

Why lawyers are pursuing child school shooters' parents

Colin Gray is the latest US parent to be prosecuted for a mass shooting committed by a child, in what is becoming an emerging legal strategy employed by prosecutors in a bid to tackle gun violence in American schools.

Jennifer and James Crumbley were the first US parents jailed over shootings conducted by their son, Ethan, who killed four students and injured others at Michigan's Oxford High School in 2021.

They were also unaware of their son's plans and had gifted him a gun before the shooting.

Michigan school shooter Ethan Crumbley's parents, Jennifer and James, were the first two American parents in US legal history to be held criminally responsible for their child's actions. (Reuters: Supplied/Oakland County Sheriff's Office)

Rachel Fiset, a lawyer at the US-based ZFZ Law firm, told ABC NewsRadio the jail terms represent a new push by American prosecutors to hold parents legally responsible for the criminal actions of their children.

"The judge was considering that it's fairly unusual circumstances that someone who didn't pull the trigger or wasn't even present at the scene was being convinced of murder, even under these types of circumstances," she said.

"The idea here is: they're handling dangerous weapons at home, and if you are going to handle dangerous weapons at home, you need to be aware of what your children are doing.

"It is charging the parents with responsibility over the child, which we do in all kinds of aspects of life of course, but it is extending it to intentional crimes the children might commit that parents would have an obligation to try to stop."

Loading...

Harry Melkonian, a legal expert from the US Studies Centre in Sydney, told the ABC that American prosecutors had become more motivated to pursue parents of child criminals because school violence had "become a drastic situation".

"It's a means of trying to stop this kind of violence," he said.

"One of the purposes of criminal law is deterrence, to try to prevent crimes.

" The American society is undoubtedly fed up with shootings at schools and churches and synagogues and mosques. It's got to stop. "

He compared the relation of Colin Gray to his son's actions to the legal definition of someone committing a conspiracy to another person's crime.

Mr Melkonian also said the rulings in Georgia and Michigan could provide a legal precedent for similar court decisions in the future, but that they would need to satisfy the "extreme" conditions of cases such as Gray's.

"The facts are really extreme … The facts, as we know them, are of people really behaving badly," he said.

"I don't think you're going to find many situations of such extreme parental idiocy."

ABC/AP

World.title: 'Pattern of missteps': Football bodies launch stunning Infantino rebuke
World.content:
Successfully stopping Gianni Infantino's FIFA plan to sell World Cup profits to private investors was the first half of a high-stakes game in global soccer politics.

The second half kicked off overnight with what seemed a clear aim of ending Infantino's decade-long presidency.

"No option should be off the table," said European soccer body UEFA, whose president Aleksander Čeferin has led the fight against Infantino in a seismic week for FIFA.

"The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family."

Aleksander Čeferin (left) has been a vocal critic of Gianni Infantino's latest quest to privatise part of FIFA. (Getty Images: Nicolò Campo/LightRocket)

After that comment, the governing body for North and Central American and Caribbean soccer (CONCACAF) called for accountability, saying: "A [World Cup] proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident. It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first. This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A full review of this leadership must now take place."

Mr Infantino had proposed creating a $US20 billion ($28.5 billion) company to run the World Cup with private investors but drew backlash that grew every day since Tuesday's announcement.

The FIFA president was forced to scrap the plan early Saturday after his senior adviser who sat on a White House panel resigned and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), joined Europe and North America in opposing it.

UEFA's blistering statement

UEFA, the governing body of European soccer, issued its blistering statement hours after FIFA announced it was withdrawing its private equity plan.

"We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast-track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game," UEFA said.

"We must identify those responsible and hold them to account.

"It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, UEFA will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again."

Lise Klaveness (right) looks on as Gianni Infantino takes a selfie with a fan during the World Cup. (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

Norwegian soccer federation president Lise Klaveness, an elected member of the UEFA executive committee, said steps must be taken to protect the integrity of the sport.

"The entire framework of international football cooperation was unnecessarily put at risk in pursuit of individual interests rather than the best interests of the game," Mr Klaveness said.

"This has been visible to many for a long time, including those of us elected to positions intended to safeguard checks and balances and provide ongoing oversight. We have to recognise that these mechanisms have not worked well enough."

Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa (right) also criticised the way the privatisation plan had been rolled out. (Getty Images: Kevin C. Cox)

The president of the AFC, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, said, "The future of global football must always be shaped through proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established governance structures of our game."

Mr Infantino's audacious bid fell apart after UEFA's 55-member nations agreed Thursday to boycott the World Cup and all other FIFA competitions. CONCACAF and the AFC also said they opposed the plan.

CONCACAF's statement added that FIFA leaders have "a duty of service over power. Where that duty is not upheld, accountability cannot be optional".

FIFA's internal revolt

There was also an internal revolt.

Mr Infantino's senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned and urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.

Hours later, FIFA chief operating officer Kevin Lamour issued a statement to the Associated Press, saying FIFA staff were deceived by Infantino's lack of openness in planning the sale over recent months and that the project must not continue.

Kevin Lamour says the FIFA plan is a project of "one person". (Getty Images: Joosep Martinson)

"It is the project of one person," wrote Mr Lamour, a longtime colleague of Mr Infantino at both FIFA and UEFA.

"Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."

Mr Infantino had proposed spinning off FIFA's commercial businesses — including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women — into a $US20 billion subsidiary with 20 per cent owned by private investors.

The "anchor investor", described by FIFA, is a New York-based investment firm launched by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

This is not Infantino's first big plan to flop

A tumultuous week in international soccer is at least the third time Mr Infantino has rocked it with an ambitious plan many in the sport saw as reckless.

But the fallout from FIFA's Joshua Kushner-backed plan is the first time UEFA has acted quickly to create momentum for removing the man who was its former long-time employee.

In 2018, Mr Infantino pushed a secretive offer of $US25 billion from Japan's SoftBank to create new competitions, which posed a long-term risk to continental events for clubs and national teams.

Vladimir Putin awarded an Order of Friendship to Gianni Infantino after the 2018 World Cup in Russia. (Getty Images: Mikhail Metzel/TASS)

In 2021, Mr Infantino proposed playing World Cups every two years instead of four — an idea that also angered the International Olympic Committee where he is an elected member.

Both plans created big rifts in the sport and were eventually dropped by FIFA.

Despite the turmoil, Mr Infantino was re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.

The third time is shaping up to be different.

November 18 is the deadline for candidates to enter the next presidential contest, exactly four months ahead of the vote in Rabat, Morocco, where FIFA has its African headquarters.

FIFA statutes allow Mr Infantino one more four-year term in office. The failed spin-off venture seemed like a way to create a commissioner-like role for Mr Infantino beyond 2031, likely paying much more than his current annual salary and a bonus deal of more than $US6 million.

Gianni Infantino with Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani and Jordan's Crown Prince Hussein at the FIFA Arab Cup 2025. (Getty Images: Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto)

It would take 106 votes to ensure a majority in a contested election. Continents surely do not vote uniformly en bloc, but most of Europe's 55, plus Asia's 46 and CONCACAF's 35 FIFA members would be a solid base.

The Qatar FA issued a statement in support of Infantino on Saturday.

Its president, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa bin Ahmed Al Thani, said: "We welcome FIFA President Gianni Infantino's decision to withdraw the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal in the interest of the global football community.

"While the proposal had merit, we applaud the wisdom behind prioritising unity among Member Associations. The Qatar Football Association fully supports president Infantino's efforts to continue growing and strengthening the game globally."
