World.title: One final clean sweep proves Aussie track stars are the real deal
World.content:
The main event for most of the crowd at Scotstoun Stadium lived up to the hype.

Scottish world record holder Josh Kerr utterly bossed a chaotic men's mile final, teaching Australian hope Cameron Myers a lesson in competition racing.

Twenty-year-old Myers came into the Games in phenomenal form and pledged to not let the hometown favourite out of his sight in the final, but once he was boxed in and Kerr got a break, it was curtains with half a lap to go.

Josh Kerr lit up Scotstoun. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

"He smashed me," a visibly disappointed Myers said.

The inexperienced young gun pledged to learn from it and clearly enjoyed his time in the "electric" atmosphere.

But the finale for a historic athletics program for Australia came about half an hour later, when three Australian stars lined up in the women's mile.

We're used to see it in the swimming, but this time it was an international track meet that staged a replay of the Australian championships as Abbey Caldwell, Jess Hull and Claudia Hollingsworth went around the track four times.

Stunning day of Comm Games success for Australia Australia stuns the field to claim gold in the men's 4x100m relay for the first time since 1974 on a packed night final night of athletics action.

When they ran the equivalent 1,500 metres at the national championships in April, it was a debacle.

Hollingsworth tripped Hull, which held up Caldwell, who was pipped by Sarah Billings.

Hull and Caldwell lodged protests, Hollingsworth was disqualified, and Billings was installed as national champion.

After her unusual elevation to the crown, Billings chose to only race the 800m in Glasgow, winning bronze, and her competitors from that night in Sydney stepped in as the clear fastest milers in the country.

The women pulled off the triumph Camweon Myers (right) could not. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

Lining up in the Commonwealth Games final right next to Hull, Caldwell burst off the line, while Hull held back and watched as Hollingsworth settled into the pack ahead of her.

Like the nats, it was a slow race, raising the risk of another late calamity.

Instead, with 200 metres to go, Caldwell burst clear and Hull joined her.

Hull couldn't match Caldwell but, just like when she won silver behind Rose Davies in the 5,000m, she was beaming as her teammate crossed the line ahead of her.

Abbey Caldwell crossed ahead of Jess Hull, the woman who paved the path for her. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Meanwhile, the in-stadium announcer broke the news that the podium sweep was on as Hollingsworth, seemingly boxed in with the typically rambunctious peloton, found the space and energy to burst past Naomi Korir and claim bronze.

Caldwell had predicted a podium sweep before the athletics program started in a manner portraying matter-of-fact confidence, rather than arrogant bluster.

Even after the prediction came true, it was the importance of their presence on the start line, 9.34 metres behind the spot where Caldwell snared gold 4 minutes and 39.31 seconds later, that Hull remarked upon.

"The Aussies are a force; on that start line we're a threat," she said.

"We've done it at Commonwealth level and the next step is to do it at [world] championships, get three of us in the final and then the odds are pretty high that you're gonna bring home a couple of medals."

The women's middle distance has been the jewel in the Australian track crown before the sprinters joined the party in the past couple of years.

But this podium sweep in the first female Commonwealth mile in history, Caldwell said, truly "put [them] on the map".

"We are the best and I think we can prove that we are the best and we will come and compete for those [Olympic and world] medals," she said.

"We do all wanna keep competing and we are worldwide competitors.

"Jess paved that path for us; we're here to compete internationally, we've accomplished the Commonwealth and now we move onto the big world stage."

If Glasgow 2026 was the coming-out party for Australia's new short-track guns, it marked the coming of age for Caldwell, Hull, Hollingsworth and Billings, who were holding up the tartan long before it was cool.

World.title: Why Eastern Rosellas is the perfect earworm
World.content:
It's the viral song about a beloved Australian bird that you can't get out of your head.

But what makes Eastern Rosellas, performed by Miles Phillips and his dad Joel, so catchy?

The hit song has clocked up thousands of likes and reposts on social media and inspired covers from across the world, including Australian musicians Meg Washington, Ball Park Music and Ben Lee.

If you ask the experts, there is a distinct formula that lodges the one-minute thirty-nine-second song in the minds of people everywhere.

Musicians, however, simply believe it might just be the wholesome antidote we all need at the moment.

Childhood innocence

One of the artists to cover the song is Aussie musician Ben Lee.

According to Lee, the way Eastern Rosellas has taken off says a lot about what the Australian audience is craving right now.

Loading Instagram content

"It's really interesting how music and art in general have become increasingly corporatised over recent decades," he said.

"We often feel like the algorithm isn't just picking what we get to consume, but in a way it's influencing what's getting made.

"There's something about this experience that we're having with Eastern Rosellas where it's connecting us back to this childlike innocence and the reason we love songs and music in the first place.

" It's incredibly pure. "

Seven-year-old Miles told the ABC's BTN he came up with the idea for the song while feeding the birds at his grandparents' house on Raymond Island.

Miles was inspired while feeding the birds at his grandparents' house. (Supplied: Chris Farrell)

In a world where AI is encroaching on the arts, Lee said the human side to the song offers something a computer can't provide.

"Something like this is completely unpredictable," he said.

" In its nature it is chaotic, and I love that because I don't want to live in a world where everything is predictable, and everything's algorithmic, and everything is just like a composite of things before it. "

Repetition and relaxation

Music cognition researcher and professor of music at the University of New South Wales, Emery Schubert, said there might actually be a bit of science to go along with Lee's theory on how a composer can get an audience hooked.

"There's a very simple reason why songs are potentially good for earworm creation, and that's because there's a section of the song that is an exact repetition," he said.

"It's a very simple formula and a lot of songs do use it.

" When you repeat something identically in a song … when you're relaxing, your brain doesn't worry about the order of the song, and it often goes for the simplest progression. "

Professor Emery Schubert says "contiguous repetition" is key to creating an earworm. (Supplied: UNSW Sydney)

Professor Schubert said this repetition, known in the music world as "contiguous repetition", is the only characteristic a songwriter needs to make a track earworm-able.

"A segment of the song is exactly repeated immediately after the first playing of that segment," Professor Schubert said.

"That will jump into people's minds because, even when they're not thinking, in particular when they're not really thinking hard about anything in particular, that's most likely to come up."

Colour in darkness

While experts might argue that there is a magic formula to create an earworm on loop in your mind, Lee said the timing and authenticity have played a larger role than any musical pattern could.

Ben Lee says the youthful innocence of the Eastern Rosellas is what has captured the hearts of Australia. (Supplied: Kim Magic)

"There's something about how dark the present moment is, whether it's politically [or] economically," he said.

"Things are quite unnerving for people.

World.title: Sopranos star Vincent Pastore dies aged 80
World.content:
Mob drama star Vincent Pastore, known for playing Salvatore “Big Pussy” Bonpensiero in The Sopranos, has died at age 80.

Bob McGowan, who had managed Pastore since his run on the HBO series, learned of his death on Saturday from another client and actor on the show, Vincent Curatola.

He said Pastore had been found in his home on New York’s City Island, and had not been heard from for several days.

Mr McGowan said he had been trying to reach Pastore about a possible job.

"He was the most loyal client and he always gave to charity," Mr McGowan said.

"He was the kind of guy who would help anybody, which is rare in my business."

Mr Pastore began appearing in movies in the 1980s and had roles in films such as Goodfellas and Awakenings, both in 1990.

He often played gangsters.

And it was one of those roles for which he is best known: his 30-episode run as Salvatore “Big Pussy” Bonpensiero, the friend of Tony Soprano who becomes an FBI informant in The Sopranos.

In a 2019 interview with the ABC Radio Sydney Breakfast, he described Bonpensiero’s character as "a rat who got a lot of people in trouble".

Mr Pastore was born in the Bronx and grew up in suburban New Rochelle, New York.

He enlisted in the Navy during the Vietnam War and later attended Pace University, according to his biography on IMDb.

He has a daughter, Renee Pastore.

World.title: State Department warns US citizens to be ready to leave Middle East as Iran tensions boil
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war State Department warns US citizens to be ready to leave Middle East as Iran tensions boil Samy Magdi and Aamer Madhani August 2, 2026 — 10:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US State Department has issued new security alerts for Americans in 10 countries in the Middle East region to be “prepared to depart” due to the escalating tensions with Iran. The warnings – covering Bahrain, Israel, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – urged American citizens to prepare for possible flight cancellations, temporary airspace closures and other travel disruptions. Donald Trump, pictured with CIA director John Ratcliffe last week. Reuters via AP The warning came after US President Donald Trump warned on Friday (US time) that US forces would hit Iran “very hard” until the country could not take any more. Speaking to reporters during a meeting with members of his cabinet at the Camp David presidential retreat in Maryland, Trump said, “we just want to win” in Iran. He signalled that he expected American military action to continue for some time.



Related Article Middle East at war Trump’s Gaza deal sparks questions on whether Israel, Hamas will comply Later that day, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt expressed the administration’s frustration anew, accusing Tehran of last month signing a memorandum of understanding on a truce but then quickly “broke it, shot at commercial ships, and killed American soldiers”. Trump has repeatedly threatened to step up attacks on Iran in recent weeks, signalling the possibility of targeting critical infrastructure like power plants and bridges, but has yet to follow through. The US conducted a “heavy wave of strikes” last Wednesday, according to US Central Command, though no further strikes have been reported in the last few days. US Air Force B1 bombers pictured at RAF Fairford in the UK last week. Getty Images



According to CNN, Trump is under significant political pressure to end the war, which is deeply unpopular in the US. Only 28 per cent of Americans approve of his handling of the conflict, which has caused economic pain, including rising fuel prices. The effects of the war have rippled far beyond the Gulf, driving up inflation worldwide while threatening to engulf more of the Middle East. New attacks on Kuwait Meanwhile, Kuwait’s military on Saturday said its forces were responding to Iranian drone attacks. In a statement, Defence Ministry spokesman Major General Saud Abdulaziz Al-Otaibi said the drones hit a number of vital facilities, including a government structure in the country’s north. He said there were no casualties.



Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Dumb and dumber: Trump and Putin are both losing wars to smaller enemies Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Separately, the British Royal Navy said a tanker was struck, and another explosion hit close to a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman. No casualties were reported in either incident, it said. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organisation said an unknown projectile hit the vessel on Friday some 20 kilometres north-east of Lima, Oman. The attack damaged the vessel’s engine room. A day later, the group said a large splash and an explosion were reported near another tanker while it was sailing about 38 kilometres north-west of the city of Khasab. Separately, crude oil appeared to be leaking and spreading in recent days from a sanctioned tanker grounded off the coast of Oman, close to a marine protected area, satellite images reviewed by the Associated Press show.



Iran has repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to transit through the Strait of Hormuz without its authorisation as part of the ongoing conflict. Yemen’s Houthi rebels forced eight Saudi ships to reroute from the Bab el-Mandeb strait after the Iranian-backed group announced a blockade on Saudi shipping in the choke point. Brigadier General Yahya Saree, the military spokesperson for the Houthis, said in a statement on Friday that the vessels changed course to the Cape of Good Hope around Africa to avert the blockade. World.title: Sentencing loophole failing sexual assault victims
World.content:
NationalNSWCourts Sentencing loophole failing sexual assault victims The Herald's View August 2, 2026 — 9:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The justice system often exacts a heavy toll on victim-survivors of sexual offences. Historically low conviction rates for rape and the likelihood of a long and re-traumatising court process deter some complainants from ever coming forward. Even if they decide to report their attacker and prosecutors secure a conviction in court, there is no guarantee that victims will regard the sentence handed down by the court as reflective of the gravity of the crime. There is still work to do for victim-survivors. Sexual assault conviction rates remain low. Marija Ercecgovac Sentencing statistics obtained exclusively by this masthead’s court reporter Clare Sibthorpe from the Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research paint a worrying picture in this respect. They show community correction orders (CCOs) – effectively good behaviour bonds – made up nearly 4 per cent, or 19, of NSW sentences where the principal offence was unlawful sexual penetration of an adult. The figures cover a four-year period to March 2026.



The use of CCOs for some convicted rapists appears to be an unintended consequence of sentencing reforms by the former NSW Liberal government, which took effect in 2018 and were billed by the then Attorney-General Mark Speakman as “tough and smart”. Those reforms took a sentencing option known as an intensive correction order (ICO) off the table for offenders sentenced to imprisonment for serious crimes including sexual assault. The changes were designed to ensure those offenders went to prison rather than serving a sentence in the community. An ICO, imposed for up to two years, is tougher than a CCO. It is categorised as a custodial sentence, even though it is served in the community. It involves strict supervision and potentially home detention. Speakman said when introducing the reforms that the government “considers that an offence that is serious enough to warrant a prison sentence of more than two years should be served in full‑time custody”, rather than by way of an ICO.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Serious sexual offenders are walking free on community orders But, in a shock to many complainants, it now appears that judges in some cases are opting for a much more lenient CCO for some convicted rapists. The legislation does not rule it out. David Heilpern, Southern Cross University dean of Law and former magistrate of 22 years, told Sibthorpe that it was “outrageous” for a convicted rapist to avoid jail. Heilpern said parliament could not have imagined its “zero tolerance” decision to remove ICOs for serious crimes, including sexual assault, would mean some judges resorted to the lower CCOs instead of imprisonment. “A CCO is what you get for a second shoplift or pushing and shoving in a pub,” he said.



Sexual intercourse without consent carries a maximum prison term of 14 years with a standard non-parole period of seven years. It appears contrary to parliament’s will for the courts to decide that an order akin to a good behaviour bond reflects the gravity of that crime in all but rare cases. But the legislature has been unclear, and banning ICOs appears to have distorted sentencing outcomes. Heilpern’s strongly worded comments are a wake-up call that further, careful reform may be required. The Sun-Herald does not support mandatory sentencing but an urgent review of the provisions by the Minns government is essential. World.title: Parliament and pineapple on pizza: Milton Dick’s plan to future-proof democracy
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Parliament and pineapple on pizza: Milton Dick’s plan to future-proof democracy Rob Harris August 2, 2026 — 9:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Milton Dick has spent the past four years refereeing one of Australia’s rowdiest workplaces. But the Speaker of the House of Representatives has set himself a mission that stretches far beyond keeping order in question time. His focus is on a campaign to improve civics education, arguing Australians need a better understanding of the institutions that underpin democracy as trust is tested by misinformation, social media and growing global instability. Milton Dick is embarking on an ambitious campaign to improve civics education Alex Ellinghausen “As the Speaker, I need to protect democracy – whatever happens in the chamber, but also outside the chamber as well,” the 54-year-old says. “We have a duty of care to fight for it.” The Labor MP for Oxley, a seat previously held by former governor-general Bill Hayden and One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, has made school visits a defining feature of his speakership, travelling to classrooms across the country – from remote Indigenous communities to tiny schools with two students and island communities off Tasmania. This term, he wants to visit all 150 federal electorates.



His drive comes as democracies around the world grapple with declining public trust, political polarisation and online misinformation. Australia remains one of the world’s strongest democracies, Dick says, but that should never be taken for granted. The Economist Intelligence Unit’s Democracy Index ranks Australia among the world’s strongest democracies, but Dick says those achievements cannot be assumed. Globally, only 31 countries are classified as liberal democracies, with three-quarters of the world’s population now living under authoritarian rule. Speaker Milton Dick has spoken about Australian democracy at more than 200 schools during his time as Speaker of the House. Alex Ellinghausen Dick wants nationally consistent civics education in years 6 and 10, arguing every student should leave school with a basic understanding of how governments are formed, how courts operate, how elections are run and why independent institutions matter. The call comes as national testing shows Australian students’ understanding of democracy is deteriorating. The Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority found civics and citizenship results had fallen to their lowest levels in two decades, with just 28 per cent of year 10 students meeting the national proficiency standard in 2024, down from 38 per cent in 2019.



“I’m not talking about politics,” Dick says. “I’m talking about teaching democracy ... it’s the meat and potatoes. More than ever, with the rise of social media and the impacts we’re seeing around the world, we’ve got to protect what we’ve got here and fight for it.” Last month, Governor-General Sam Mostyn joined Dick for his 200th school visit since he became Speaker, at her old school in Canberra, Curtin Primary. Governor-General Sam Mostyn takes a selfie together with Speaker Milton Dick. Alex Ellinghausen One of the more light-hearted moments comes when Dick asks students, as he does everywhere, to vote on whether pineapple belongs on pizza. The mock ballot sparks lively debate while introducing children to voting and parliamentary procedure. Mostyn politely abstained, observing the political neutrality of her office.



The classroom visits have convinced Dick younger Australians are more engaged than they are often given credit for. Once discussions turn to who makes laws, why people vote and how governments are formed, students quickly become active participants. Related Article Opinion

Indigenous The ghost of Bob Hawke supports Pauline Hanson? I saw first-hand how wrong that notion is Tony Wright Associate editor and special writer “They get it,” he says. “I ask them who thinks they could be a member of parliament or do my job as Speaker. Only a handful put their hands up. I tell them that’s okay because I didn’t put my hand up either when my local member asked me that question at primary school.” Dick insists the program is deliberately bipartisan, regularly inviting government, opposition and crossbench MPs into classrooms, so students see democracy rather than party politics. The mission reflects his belief that public service begins with understanding civic responsibility.



Dick traces that commitment to his parents, Allan, a World War II naval veteran, butcher and taxi driver, and Joan, a nurse and midwife, who instilled a strong sense of service and respect for others. His brother, Cameron, was deputy premier of Queensland under Annastacia Palaszczuk. “I’ve worked out my why,” Dick says. “My why is to hopefully do my bit to promote democracy and support civics.” The Speaker is also expanding parliament’s outreach beyond schools. Every federal MP will receive a ceremonial mace to use when visiting classrooms, while a new National Youth Parliament will bring young Australians to Canberra to experience the legislative process first-hand. To mark the 125th anniversary of the Australian flag, Dick has taken one flown above Parliament House on a national road trip, using it to teach students about Australia’s history and democratic traditions. New Speaker Milton Dick pledged to build respect in the chamber and in the parliament more broadly Alex Ellinghausen



He says many are surprised to learn the flag was chosen through a public competition. Dick hopes descendants of the winning designers – including Perth artist Annie Dorrington and 14-year-old Melbourne schoolboy Ivor Evans – will be tracked down to attend anniversary commemorations in September. “Their names have been banished from our history books,” he says. “I think it’s I think it’s high-time that we recognised those young people.” Australia, he argues, has much to be proud of, from compulsory voting and an independent electoral system to a democratic tradition that extended political rights earlier than many comparable nations. And his message is simple: democracy survives not only through the laws that protect it, but through generations who understand why it matters. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Be it a HQ Holden or a Wallabies jersey, Lonergan’s no stranger to playing the long game
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Be it a HQ Holden or a Wallabies jersey, Lonergan’s no stranger to playing the long game Iain Payten August 2, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ryan Lonergan doesn’t mind chipping away on a long-term project. Take the 1974 HQ Holden gathering dust in a shed on the family farm in Williamsdale, south of Canberra. Lonergan bought the car as a 16-year-old, with the plan to do it up and drive it to his school formal. When that deadline came and went, the Wallabies halfback changed it to the formal of his younger brother, Lachlan. Ryan Lonergan had a long apprenticeship before finally landing a Wallabies jersey. Steven Siewert “No chance,” Ryan says. “It’s still sitting in the shed. It runs ... just. “But unfortunately, it is a bit on the backburner. I get a lot of stick for it just sitting in the shed, particularly from my brother.



“I’ve pretty much finished all the work; I’ve done it all myself so it’s not tip-top or anything, but yeah, I’ll finish it off eventually. We’ll get there.” For the record, Ryan is now 28 and Lachlan is 26. Since those teenage days, the brothers have gone on to become Brumbies and Wallabies. But the fact that Lachlan, a hooker, played for the ACT three years after his brother, but then made his debut for Australia five full years before him points to the other long-term project in Ryan’s life: becoming a Wallaby. That mission, thankfully, has been more successful than getting the Holden back on the road. But for a long time it felt just as elusive for Lonergan, who endured the longest apprenticeship of any Australian player in the Super Rugby era – 93 games over nine seasons – before making his Wallabies debut last year. The only other players even close, Jed Holloway and Sam Talakai, were in the 70-game range.



“I’d probably rather it not be my story, but I do think it’s a good way to do it,” Lonergan says. “I think it teaches you a bit of resilience. And then, when you’re here, I feel I’m ready.” Lonergan made his debut for the Brumbies in 2017, having played for Australian Schoolboys in 2016 and then captained the Junior Wallabies. Nothing out of the ordinary so far for a rising star. But unlike others in the cohort who then pushed up to national honours, Lonergan had to settle in for a long wait. A very long wait. Ryan Lonergan played 93 games for the Brumbies before being selected for Australia. Getty Images He became a key player and captained the Brumbies in many successful seasons. But, further up, the Wallabies halfback trio of Jake Gordon, Nic White and Tate McDermott was rusted on. Issak Fines-Leleiwasa even leap-frogged Lonergan for the gig in 2023. Before long, Lonergan was owner of the unwanted tag: “Australia’s best player without a Test cap”.



“I just tried to keep chipping away, really,” Lonergan said. “I saw a lot of people, and they fly through it all. They’ll debut in Super Rugby, and then they debut for the Wallabies the same year or whatever. And sometimes it goes really well, sometimes it doesn’t. So you see both sides of it. “It didn’t really bother me too much. I’ve thought I’ve just got to keep getting better. Maybe more recently, it probably started to annoy me a little bit more, because I thought I was more ready. But early on in those days, I would be in a camp, and I was thinking, ‘Oh jeez, actually, I’m still probably not quite ready’. Ryan Lonergan on the charge against Ireland. Getty Images “In the last couple of years, yeah, I was starting to get a little bit more frustrated, because I’m a bit of a realist and I felt I was ready, and I kept missing out. But again, I just kept chipping away.” Lonergan’s saintly patience eventually paid off. When White retired last year, he became Wallaby No.993 at Eden Park against the All Blacks.



“My old man’s always been a big believer in just keep working hard and good things will come,” Lonergan said. Ryan Lonergan passing at Wallabies training at North Sydney Oval. Audrey Richardson It’s fair to say good things came for the Wallabies as much as they did for Lonergan. For many Australian players in the modern game, waiting nine seasons for a Test jersey would be five seasons too long. Many would have seen a closed door and gone overseas long ago. “It crossed my mind [to go overseas], but I also thought I was just on the point of, right, now I’m ready, so I felt I would have been doing myself an injustice if I was to work that hard and then just give up on it,” he said. Lonergan entered Test rugby as an experienced, game-controlling halfback and barely blinked. At 27, he knew his game perfectly, and after Gordon suffered a season-ending injury in May, Lonergan moved into the Wallabies team in July.



In all three July Tests, he was one of the best players in gold. And in a sign of his influence, the Wallabies were mostly on top when Lonergan was on the field, but fell away when he was replaced. In 33 minutes (before injury) against Ireland and 58-minute stints against France and Italy, the Wallabies had a combined score of 70-46. With Lonergan off the paddock, the Wallabies were collectively outscored 29-24. Using the plus-minus stat common in basketball, the Wallabies are plus 24 with Lonergan and minus five without him. It’s not all on bench halfback McDermott, of course, given the team undergoes multiple changes in the last half hour of matches. But there was no mistaking the overall shifts in fluency and momentum. “I’m happy with where my game’s at. It’s not complete though, so I’ll just try to keep dragging that same mindset through and keep trying to get better,” Lonergan says. “It took me a long time to get here, so I guess I’m just grateful for it to be happening.



Related Article Commonwealth Games Kennedy ended a 64-year sprint drought – but he needs to play two footy codes to match this great “I could have thrown the toys out of the cot and said I was good enough when I wasn’t, but then I’d just stay the player I was. I just kept chipping away. You get better if you’re willing to keep putting in work.“ The Lonergan work ethic comes from mum Jenny and dad Tom, who is a builder and a farmer on the 600-acre cattle and sheep property where the boys grew up doing chores and kicking at homemade footy posts. The brothers still love nothing more than chipping in and doing some fencing. “Whether I recognised it or not when I was younger, it really rubbed off on us,” Lonergan says. “Growing up on a farm taught us a work ethic. And then, don’t complain too much, just get on with it. It’s worked pretty well so far.”

World.title: This was the event of the Games. An Australian had a ‘terrrible’ race and won silver
World.content:
SportAthleticsCommonwealth Games This was the event of the Games. An Australian had a ‘terrrible’ race and won silver Michael Gleeson August 2, 2026 — 9:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Scroll down for a complete Commonwealth Games medal tally Glasgow: The Commonwealth Games were patched together at the 11th hour in an attempt to salvage an anachronistic concept. To do so, organisers resurrected an anachronistic distance, loved by Americans (who aren’t here) and by nostalgists. They raced a mile in Glasgow, not the 1500 metres, an imperial reach back to the Empire Games. It would be very retro, but for the fact that it sounds too modern a term. Josh Myers wins silver in the men’s mile. AP Photo/Kin Cheung On Sunday morning (AEST), the Games then delivered two cinematically perfect mile races worthy of being raced in white singlets on a beach with a Chariots of Fire soundtrack.



In the men’s mile, Australia’s Cameron Myers discovered what happens when potential collides with experience. In the event of the Games, the callow Myers, who has swept all records before him to reach his 20th birthday, confronted the Scot Josh Kerr who last month broke the world record, and was racing on his home track before a crowd who figured frigid conditions perfect for suntanning. He could not have roused them to a giddier state had he stood on the blocks with his face painted blue, screaming that no one would ever take his freedom. The men’s mile final was the race of the Games. Getty Images Myers is on a trajectory to go past Kerr, but finding a trajectory can be easier than finding a path through a thicket of mile runners on a blue track. Myers ran a terrible race. And won silver.



Related Article Opinion

Commonwealth Games Glasgow may have saved the Commonwealth Games, but it made a crucial mistake Michael Gleeson Sports columnist He was cranky with himself afterwards, not so much for the fact he lost, but for the fact he didn’t give himself a serious chance to win. Losing to the new world record holder Kerr cannot be a surprise, but running a clunky race yet still coming second made it a moment not for celebration, but self-flagellation. “I mean it’s good, a silver [medal], but I want to be challenging. The reality was that with 50 metres to go he was five, ten metres clear so, to me, it doesn’t even feel like I was racing him, I was racing the other guys,” Myers said. “You know, I don’t want to be the best of the rest. I want to be challenging to win a race.



“I could feel the energy. It was electric. I mean, I was introduced right next to Kerr, and it felt like the stadium erupted. Even when he walked out, he was one spot behind me, and you can just feel the energy that he’s bringing, and the fact that he was able to deliver under so much pressure, it’s full credit to the athlete. Related Article Commonwealth Games Three venues in five hours: How the royals spent a day at the Commonwealth Games “It’s definitely one of the most physical [races] but I haven’t had too much experience in those races.” Myers was stuck where he didn’t want to be and couldn’t get out. He waited, saw Kerr break and still found a way to work to the lead of the chasing pack, but by that stage he was no chance of reining Kerr in. Still, he found a way to salvage a silver medal, running 3:55.26 behind Kerr, who won in 3:54.12. It was not dissimilar to Nina Kennedy the night earlier when the Olympic champion performed well below herself in the pole vault and still won silver.



“I got drafted lane one, which sucks. I mean, my plan was to go to the front and sort of control it, just run a comfortable but fast speed, and I couldn’t really do that because I couldn’t get out at any point,” Myers said. “I looked to my right to see if I could get out around and I just had nowhere to go, so I had to change my plan on the go, which was to sit and just remain as comfortable as possible. Australians swept the podium in the women’s mile, Abbey Caldwell taking gold from Jess Hull and Claudia Hollingsworth. Getty Images “I got to a good spot at the bell, but like inevitably, when Kerr made his move he had a jump on me and you can’t give someone a jump at this level, and he smashed me in the end.” If the men’s race offered the Empire a sense of warm reassurance, then the women’s race was an assertion that Australia might have rudely chosen not to host these Games but the Commonwealth Games are now undoubtedly owned by Australia.



The Australians swept the podium: Abbey Caldwell taking gold from Jess Hull and Claudia Hollingsworth in silver and bronze. Related Article Live

Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games as it happened: Marschall wins third consecutive gold and sets a Games record after Australia sweep the podium in the women’s mile; Historic gold in men’s relay The women, two of whom clashed – or rather, accidentally collided – at the national championships only months ago in dramatic fashion now shared a podium. “We had a moment together in the second China Diamond League meet when we were cooling down, and I just said, all that matters this year is that we’re going to sweep that Commonwealth podium, and we all ran our own race tonight, and we’ve executed that, and we’ve done it,” Hull said. Hollingsworth added: “It’s incredible to have all three green and gold on the podium, it is just so exciting. I hope everyone keeps watching us because we’ve got big things coming, and it’s so exciting to do it all together.



“It’s so exciting to be up there together, and we both said that at the end of the race, we gave each other such a big hug, and just know we put it all together. We just know we’re such good competitors and good friends, and to step on the podium together is really, really special.” Hull said sweeping the podium was not a comment on the quality of the Commonwealth Games but a statement to the world about Australian middle-distance running. “The Aussies are a force, you know. Like if we are on that start line, we’re a threat. So I think we’ve done it at Commonwealth level now, and then the next step is to do it at championships. To get three of us into the final then the odds are pretty high that you’re going to bring home a couple of medals.” Get around our Commonwealth Games coverage

World.title: State Department warns US citizens to be ready to leave Middle East as Iran tensions boil
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war State Department warns US citizens to be ready to leave Middle East as Iran tensions boil Samy Magdi and Aamer Madhani August 2, 2026 — 10:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US State Department has issued new security alerts for Americans in 10 countries in the Middle East region to be “prepared to depart” due to the escalating tensions with Iran. The warnings – covering Bahrain, Israel, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates – urged American citizens to prepare for possible flight cancellations, temporary airspace closures and other travel disruptions. Donald Trump, pictured with CIA director John Ratcliffe last week. Reuters via AP The warning came after US President Donald Trump warned on Friday (US time) that US forces would hit Iran “very hard” until the country could not take any more. Speaking to reporters during a meeting with members of his cabinet at the Camp David presidential retreat in Maryland, Trump said, “we just want to win” in Iran. He signalled that he expected American military action to continue for some time.



Related Article Middle East at war Trump’s Gaza deal sparks questions on whether Israel, Hamas will comply Later that day, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt expressed the administration’s frustration anew, accusing Tehran of last month signing a memorandum of understanding on a truce but then quickly “broke it, shot at commercial ships, and killed American soldiers”. Trump has repeatedly threatened to step up attacks on Iran in recent weeks, signalling the possibility of targeting critical infrastructure like power plants and bridges, but has yet to follow through. The US conducted a “heavy wave of strikes” last Wednesday, according to US Central Command, though no further strikes have been reported in the last few days. US Air Force B1 bombers pictured at RAF Fairford in the UK last week. Getty Images



According to CNN, Trump is under significant political pressure to end the war, which is deeply unpopular in the US. Only 28 per cent of Americans approve of his handling of the conflict, which has caused economic pain, including rising fuel prices. The effects of the war have rippled far beyond the Gulf, driving up inflation worldwide while threatening to engulf more of the Middle East. New attacks on Kuwait Meanwhile, Kuwait’s military on Saturday said its forces were responding to Iranian drone attacks. In a statement, Defence Ministry spokesman Major General Saud Abdulaziz Al-Otaibi said the drones hit a number of vital facilities, including a government structure in the country’s north. He said there were no casualties.



Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Dumb and dumber: Trump and Putin are both losing wars to smaller enemies Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Separately, the British Royal Navy said a tanker was struck, and another explosion hit close to a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman. No casualties were reported in either incident, it said. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organisation said an unknown projectile hit the vessel on Friday some 20 kilometres north-east of Lima, Oman. The attack damaged the vessel’s engine room. A day later, the group said a large splash and an explosion were reported near another tanker while it was sailing about 38 kilometres north-west of the city of Khasab. Separately, crude oil appeared to be leaking and spreading in recent days from a sanctioned tanker grounded off the coast of Oman, close to a marine protected area, satellite images reviewed by the Associated Press show.



Iran has repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to transit through the Strait of Hormuz without its authorisation as part of the ongoing conflict. Yemen’s Houthi rebels forced eight Saudi ships to reroute from the Bab el-Mandeb strait after the Iranian-backed group announced a blockade on Saudi shipping in the choke point. Brigadier General Yahya Saree, the military spokesperson for the Houthis, said in a statement on Friday that the vessels changed course to the Cape of Good Hope around Africa to avert the blockade. World.title: Sentencing loophole failing sexual assault victims
World.content:
NationalNSWCourts Sentencing loophole failing sexual assault victims The Herald's View August 2, 2026 — 9:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The justice system often exacts a heavy toll on victim-survivors of sexual offences. Historically low conviction rates for rape and the likelihood of a long and re-traumatising court process deter some complainants from ever coming forward. Even if they decide to report their attacker and prosecutors secure a conviction in court, there is no guarantee that victims will regard the sentence handed down by the court as reflective of the gravity of the crime. There is still work to do for victim-survivors. Sexual assault conviction rates remain low. Marija Ercecgovac Sentencing statistics obtained exclusively by this masthead’s court reporter Clare Sibthorpe from the Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research paint a worrying picture in this respect. They show community correction orders (CCOs) – effectively good behaviour bonds – made up nearly 4 per cent, or 19, of NSW sentences where the principal offence was unlawful sexual penetration of an adult. The figures cover a four-year period to March 2026.



The use of CCOs for some convicted rapists appears to be an unintended consequence of sentencing reforms by the former NSW Liberal government, which took effect in 2018 and were billed by the then Attorney-General Mark Speakman as “tough and smart”. Those reforms took a sentencing option known as an intensive correction order (ICO) off the table for offenders sentenced to imprisonment for serious crimes including sexual assault. The changes were designed to ensure those offenders went to prison rather than serving a sentence in the community. An ICO, imposed for up to two years, is tougher than a CCO. It is categorised as a custodial sentence, even though it is served in the community. It involves strict supervision and potentially home detention. Speakman said when introducing the reforms that the government “considers that an offence that is serious enough to warrant a prison sentence of more than two years should be served in full‑time custody”, rather than by way of an ICO.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime Serious sexual offenders are walking free on community orders But, in a shock to many complainants, it now appears that judges in some cases are opting for a much more lenient CCO for some convicted rapists. The legislation does not rule it out. David Heilpern, Southern Cross University dean of Law and former magistrate of 22 years, told Sibthorpe that it was “outrageous” for a convicted rapist to avoid jail. Heilpern said parliament could not have imagined its “zero tolerance” decision to remove ICOs for serious crimes, including sexual assault, would mean some judges resorted to the lower CCOs instead of imprisonment. “A CCO is what you get for a second shoplift or pushing and shoving in a pub,” he said.



Sexual intercourse without consent carries a maximum prison term of 14 years with a standard non-parole period of seven years. It appears contrary to parliament’s will for the courts to decide that an order akin to a good behaviour bond reflects the gravity of that crime in all but rare cases. But the legislature has been unclear, and banning ICOs appears to have distorted sentencing outcomes. Heilpern’s strongly worded comments are a wake-up call that further, careful reform may be required. The Sun-Herald does not support mandatory sentencing but an urgent review of the provisions by the Minns government is essential. World.title: Parliament and pineapple on pizza: Milton Dick’s plan to future-proof democracy
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Parliament and pineapple on pizza: Milton Dick’s plan to future-proof democracy Rob Harris August 2, 2026 — 9:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Milton Dick has spent the past four years refereeing one of Australia’s rowdiest workplaces. But the Speaker of the House of Representatives has set himself a mission that stretches far beyond keeping order in question time. His focus is on a campaign to improve civics education, arguing Australians need a better understanding of the institutions that underpin democracy as trust is tested by misinformation, social media and growing global instability. Milton Dick is embarking on an ambitious campaign to improve civics education Alex Ellinghausen “As the Speaker, I need to protect democracy – whatever happens in the chamber, but also outside the chamber as well,” the 54-year-old says. “We have a duty of care to fight for it.” The Labor MP for Oxley, a seat previously held by former governor-general Bill Hayden and One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, has made school visits a defining feature of his speakership, travelling to classrooms across the country – from remote Indigenous communities to tiny schools with two students and island communities off Tasmania. This term, he wants to visit all 150 federal electorates.



His drive comes as democracies around the world grapple with declining public trust, political polarisation and online misinformation. Australia remains one of the world’s strongest democracies, Dick says, but that should never be taken for granted. The Economist Intelligence Unit’s Democracy Index ranks Australia among the world’s strongest democracies, but Dick says those achievements cannot be assumed. Globally, only 31 countries are classified as liberal democracies, with three-quarters of the world’s population now living under authoritarian rule. Speaker Milton Dick has spoken about Australian democracy at more than 200 schools during his time as Speaker of the House. Alex Ellinghausen Dick wants nationally consistent civics education in years 6 and 10, arguing every student should leave school with a basic understanding of how governments are formed, how courts operate, how elections are run and why independent institutions matter. The call comes as national testing shows Australian students’ understanding of democracy is deteriorating. The Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority found civics and citizenship results had fallen to their lowest levels in two decades, with just 28 per cent of year 10 students meeting the national proficiency standard in 2024, down from 38 per cent in 2019.



“I’m not talking about politics,” Dick says. “I’m talking about teaching democracy ... it’s the meat and potatoes. More than ever, with the rise of social media and the impacts we’re seeing around the world, we’ve got to protect what we’ve got here and fight for it.” Last month, Governor-General Sam Mostyn joined Dick for his 200th school visit since he became Speaker, at her old school in Canberra, Curtin Primary. Governor-General Sam Mostyn takes a selfie together with Speaker Milton Dick. Alex Ellinghausen One of the more light-hearted moments comes when Dick asks students, as he does everywhere, to vote on whether pineapple belongs on pizza. The mock ballot sparks lively debate while introducing children to voting and parliamentary procedure. Mostyn politely abstained, observing the political neutrality of her office.



The classroom visits have convinced Dick younger Australians are more engaged than they are often given credit for. Once discussions turn to who makes laws, why people vote and how governments are formed, students quickly become active participants. Related Article Opinion

Indigenous The ghost of Bob Hawke supports Pauline Hanson? I saw first-hand how wrong that notion is Tony Wright Associate editor and special writer “They get it,” he says. “I ask them who thinks they could be a member of parliament or do my job as Speaker. Only a handful put their hands up. I tell them that’s okay because I didn’t put my hand up either when my local member asked me that question at primary school.” Dick insists the program is deliberately bipartisan, regularly inviting government, opposition and crossbench MPs into classrooms, so students see democracy rather than party politics. The mission reflects his belief that public service begins with understanding civic responsibility.



Dick traces that commitment to his parents, Allan, a World War II naval veteran, butcher and taxi driver, and Joan, a nurse and midwife, who instilled a strong sense of service and respect for others. His brother, Cameron, was deputy premier of Queensland under Annastacia Palaszczuk. “I’ve worked out my why,” Dick says. “My why is to hopefully do my bit to promote democracy and support civics.” The Speaker is also expanding parliament’s outreach beyond schools. Every federal MP will receive a ceremonial mace to use when visiting classrooms, while a new National Youth Parliament will bring young Australians to Canberra to experience the legislative process first-hand. To mark the 125th anniversary of the Australian flag, Dick has taken one flown above Parliament House on a national road trip, using it to teach students about Australia’s history and democratic traditions. New Speaker Milton Dick pledged to build respect in the chamber and in the parliament more broadly Alex Ellinghausen



He says many are surprised to learn the flag was chosen through a public competition. Dick hopes descendants of the winning designers – including Perth artist Annie Dorrington and 14-year-old Melbourne schoolboy Ivor Evans – will be tracked down to attend anniversary commemorations in September. “Their names have been banished from our history books,” he says. “I think it’s I think it’s high-time that we recognised those young people.” Australia, he argues, has much to be proud of, from compulsory voting and an independent electoral system to a democratic tradition that extended political rights earlier than many comparable nations. And his message is simple: democracy survives not only through the laws that protect it, but through generations who understand why it matters. World.title: Be it a HQ Holden or a Wallabies jersey, Lonergan’s no stranger to playing the long game
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Be it a HQ Holden or a Wallabies jersey, Lonergan’s no stranger to playing the long game Iain Payten August 2, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ryan Lonergan doesn’t mind chipping away on a long-term project. Take the 1974 HQ Holden gathering dust in a shed on the family farm in Williamsdale, south of Canberra. Lonergan bought the car as a 16-year-old, with the plan to do it up and drive it to his school formal. When that deadline came and went, the Wallabies halfback changed it to the formal of his younger brother, Lachlan. Ryan Lonergan had a long apprenticeship before finally landing a Wallabies jersey. Steven Siewert “No chance,” Ryan says. “It’s still sitting in the shed. It runs ... just. “But unfortunately, it is a bit on the backburner. I get a lot of stick for it just sitting in the shed, particularly from my brother.



“I’ve pretty much finished all the work; I’ve done it all myself so it’s not tip-top or anything, but yeah, I’ll finish it off eventually. We’ll get there.” For the record, Ryan is now 28 and Lachlan is 26. Since those teenage days, the brothers have gone on to become Brumbies and Wallabies. But the fact that Lachlan, a hooker, played for the ACT three years after his brother, but then made his debut for Australia five full years before him points to the other long-term project in Ryan’s life: becoming a Wallaby. That mission, thankfully, has been more successful than getting the Holden back on the road. But for a long time it felt just as elusive for Lonergan, who endured the longest apprenticeship of any Australian player in the Super Rugby era – 93 games over nine seasons – before making his Wallabies debut last year. The only other players even close, Jed Holloway and Sam Talakai, were in the 70-game range.



“I’d probably rather it not be my story, but I do think it’s a good way to do it,” Lonergan says. “I think it teaches you a bit of resilience. And then, when you’re here, I feel I’m ready.” Lonergan made his debut for the Brumbies in 2017, having played for Australian Schoolboys in 2016 and then captained the Junior Wallabies. Nothing out of the ordinary so far for a rising star. But unlike others in the cohort who then pushed up to national honours, Lonergan had to settle in for a long wait. A very long wait. Ryan Lonergan played 93 games for the Brumbies before being selected for Australia. Getty Images He became a key player and captained the Brumbies in many successful seasons. But, further up, the Wallabies halfback trio of Jake Gordon, Nic White and Tate McDermott was rusted on. Issak Fines-Leleiwasa even leap-frogged Lonergan for the gig in 2023. Before long, Lonergan was owner of the unwanted tag: “Australia’s best player without a Test cap”.



“I just tried to keep chipping away, really,” Lonergan said. “I saw a lot of people, and they fly through it all. They’ll debut in Super Rugby, and then they debut for the Wallabies the same year or whatever. And sometimes it goes really well, sometimes it doesn’t. So you see both sides of it. “It didn’t really bother me too much. I’ve thought I’ve just got to keep getting better. Maybe more recently, it probably started to annoy me a little bit more, because I thought I was more ready. But early on in those days, I would be in a camp, and I was thinking, ‘Oh jeez, actually, I’m still probably not quite ready’. Ryan Lonergan on the charge against Ireland. Getty Images “In the last couple of years, yeah, I was starting to get a little bit more frustrated, because I’m a bit of a realist and I felt I was ready, and I kept missing out. But again, I just kept chipping away.” Lonergan’s saintly patience eventually paid off. When White retired last year, he became Wallaby No.993 at Eden Park against the All Blacks.



“My old man’s always been a big believer in just keep working hard and good things will come,” Lonergan said. Ryan Lonergan passing at Wallabies training at North Sydney Oval. Audrey Richardson It’s fair to say good things came for the Wallabies as much as they did for Lonergan. For many Australian players in the modern game, waiting nine seasons for a Test jersey would be five seasons too long. Many would have seen a closed door and gone overseas long ago. “It crossed my mind [to go overseas], but I also thought I was just on the point of, right, now I’m ready, so I felt I would have been doing myself an injustice if I was to work that hard and then just give up on it,” he said. Lonergan entered Test rugby as an experienced, game-controlling halfback and barely blinked. At 27, he knew his game perfectly, and after Gordon suffered a season-ending injury in May, Lonergan moved into the Wallabies team in July.



In all three July Tests, he was one of the best players in gold. And in a sign of his influence, the Wallabies were mostly on top when Lonergan was on the field, but fell away when he was replaced. In 33 minutes (before injury) against Ireland and 58-minute stints against France and Italy, the Wallabies had a combined score of 70-46. With Lonergan off the paddock, the Wallabies were collectively outscored 29-24. Using the plus-minus stat common in basketball, the Wallabies are plus 24 with Lonergan and minus five without him. It’s not all on bench halfback McDermott, of course, given the team undergoes multiple changes in the last half hour of matches. But there was no mistaking the overall shifts in fluency and momentum. “I’m happy with where my game’s at. It’s not complete though, so I’ll just try to keep dragging that same mindset through and keep trying to get better,” Lonergan says. “It took me a long time to get here, so I guess I’m just grateful for it to be happening.



Related Article Commonwealth Games Kennedy ended a 64-year sprint drought – but he needs to play two footy codes to match this great “I could have thrown the toys out of the cot and said I was good enough when I wasn’t, but then I’d just stay the player I was. I just kept chipping away. You get better if you’re willing to keep putting in work.“ The Lonergan work ethic comes from mum Jenny and dad Tom, who is a builder and a farmer on the 600-acre cattle and sheep property where the boys grew up doing chores and kicking at homemade footy posts. The brothers still love nothing more than chipping in and doing some fencing. “Whether I recognised it or not when I was younger, it really rubbed off on us,” Lonergan says. “Growing up on a farm taught us a work ethic. And then, don’t complain too much, just get on with it. It’s worked pretty well so far.”
